blocks.text: Part B: the theory questions, each with its practical

blocks.label: The scenario, as the course text prints it
blocks.printed:
(12 marks)A. A conference organiser needs a program (using JOptionPane only, for all input/output) that prices tickets for a 3-day conference and produces a sales summary. Implement the following four methods.

i.    Create a method that takes in a day number. Use a switch statement to return a base ticket price for Day 1, Day 2, or Day 3 (pick any three distinct prices and state them clearly). If the day number is not 1, 2, or 3, throw an IllegalArgumentException.

ii.   Create a method that takes in a tier and a number of days attending. Use nested if-else statements (not a switch, and not independent/separate if checks) to return a discount percentage:

•  Gold, attending all 3 days -> 25%

•  Gold, attending 1-2 days -> 15%

•  Silver, attending all 3 days -> 15%

•  Silver, attending 1-2 days -> 5%

•  Bronze (any days) -> 0%

•  Any tier string that is not "Gold" or "Silver" must be treated as "Bronze"

The nesting must reflect that "days attending" is only checked within each tier branch, not as a separate top-level check.

iii.  Create a method that takes in a base price total and a discount percentage and applies the discount to the base price total. If the discounted amount is below 50.0, the method should return 50.0 instead (a price floor).

iv.  main()

•  Ask the user for the number of attendees N (a positive integer).

•  Loop exactly N times. In each iteration, ask for that attendee's number of days attending (an integer from 1 to 3, inclusive) and tier. For each day from 1 up to that attendee's days attending, call the method from part (i) and add the result to that attendee's running base price total (a running total that starts at 0 for each new attendee). Then call the method from part (ii) to get the discount percentage, and the method from part (iii) to get that attendee's final price.

•  Accumulate: (a) total revenue across all attendees, and (b) a running count of how many attendees were Gold, Silver, and Bronze.

v.   After the loop, show one summary dialog with total revenue and the three tier counts.

blocks.label: What you are asked
blocks.html: Shape: Write a program. A full program, marked on structure as much as on logic. The two papers set this shape 17 times between them, 1 of them on this topic.

blocks.label: Break it down first
blocks.question: What is this question actually asking, what have you been given, and what do the marks tell you about how much to write? Decide, then check.
blocks.answer:
GivenA complete pricing specification and the structure of the four methods.
Asked forFour methods plus a main, with the control structure of each dictated: switch in part i, nested if-else in part ii.
The marks12 marks. The structural constraints are marked, so a correct answer written the wrong way loses marks.
WatchPart ii spells out the nesting it wants and then repeats it in a separate sentence, which is the examiner telling you where the marks are. Tier is the outer test, days the inner. Anything not "Gold" or "Silver" falls to Bronze, so that is the else branch, not a third named case.
Taught inUnits 4.2, 4.3, 5.4, 9.4 and F.11.

blocks.label: Part 1: the answer you write in the hall
blocks.tag: write yours first, then open this
blocks.problem: Write your answer to the question above in your book first. It carries 12 marks, so write one clear point for every mark. Then open the model answer and mark yourself against it.
blocks.answer:
Q5 a · conference ticket pricing · 12 MARKS
  1. takes a day number, uses a switch to return a base price for Day 1, 2 or 3 (pick any three distinct prices and state them clearly); any other day throws IllegalArgumentException;
  2. takes a tier and days attending, and uses nested if-else to return a discount: Gold 3 days 25%, Gold 1-2 days 15%, Silver 3 days 15%, Silver 1-2 days 5%, Bronze 0%, and any tier that is not "Gold" or "Silver" is Bronze. The nesting must reflect that days are only checked within each tier branch;
  3. takes a base total and a discount percentage, applies it, and returns 50.0 if the result would fall below 50.0 (a price floor);
  4. main(): ask for N attendees; loop N times asking days and tier; sum the day prices into a per-attendee base total; get the discount; get the final price; accumulate total revenue and a count of Gold, Silver and Bronze; then show one summary dialog.
Must memorise · Choose prices that let the floor fire

The question lets you pick the three prices. That freedom is a trap with a right answer.

Pick 15000, 12000 and 9000 and part 3's price floor can never fire. The largest possible discount is 25%, so nothing ever falls near 50.0. You will have written a floor you cannot demonstrate and the examiner cannot see work.

Pick 30.0, 25.0 and 20.0 and the floor becomes live: one Gold day is 30, less 15% is 25.50, which is below 50.0, so the method returns 50.0. The 50.0 floor is itself the hint about the scale the examiner had in mind.

MEMORY HOOK: when a question lets you choose the numbers, choose numbers that make every rule visible. A rule that never fires is a rule you cannot be shown to have written correctly.

Teach · What "nested, not separate" actually means here

Part 2 is unusually explicit: nested if-else, not a switch, not independent if checks, and "the nesting must reflect that days attending is only checked within each tier branch, not as a separate top-level check."

So the shape is forced. The tier decides the branch; the days are examined inside it:

What the question demandsWhat loses the mark
if (Gold) { if (days == 3) 25 else 15 }
else if (Silver) { if (days == 3) 15 else 5 }
else { 0 }		 if (Gold && days == 3) 25;
if (Gold && days < 3) 15;
if (Silver && days == 3) 15;
Right answers, wrong structure: days is tested at the top level, four separate times. This is what "not independent checks" forbids.

Why the final else is the whole Bronze rule. "Any tier string that is not Gold or Silver must be treated as Bronze" is not an extra check you add: it is what a bare else already means. Write else if (tier.equals("Bronze")) and you have broken the rule, because "Platinum" would then match nothing and fall through with no discount assigned. The bare else catches Bronze, Platinum, "gold" in lower case, and an empty string, which is exactly what was asked (Unit 4.4).

The same else must also do the counting. If "Platinum" is treated as Bronze for the discount, it is a Bronze attendee in the summary too. Count it anywhere else and your dialog contradicts your own pricing.

Code · question five, part a · VERIFIED ON THE JVM
import java.util.Scanner;public class ConferenceTickets {    // Part i: a switch returning the base price for a day. Any other day is illegal.    static double basePriceForDay(int day) {        switch (day) {            case 1:  return 30.0;            case 2:  return 25.0;            case 3:  return 20.0;            default: throw new IllegalArgumentException(                         "Day must be 1, 2 or 3 but was " + day);        }    }    // Part ii: NESTED if-else. Days are only examined inside a tier branch.    static double discountPercent(String tier, int daysAttending) {        if (tier.equals("Gold")) {            if (daysAttending == 3) {                return 25.0;            } else {                return 15.0;            }        } else if (tier.equals("Silver")) {            if (daysAttending == 3) {                return 15.0;            } else {                return 5.0;            }        } else {            return 0.0;        }    }    // Part iii: apply the discount, with a price floor of 50.0.    static double applyDiscount(double baseTotal, double percent) {        double discounted = baseTotal - (baseTotal * percent / 100.0);        if (discounted < 50.0) {            return 50.0;        }        return discounted;    }    public static void main(String[] args) {        Scanner in = new Scanner(System.in);        int attendees = Integer.parseInt(in.nextLine());        double totalRevenue = 0;        int goldCount = 0, silverCount = 0, bronzeCount = 0;        for (int a = 1; a <= attendees; a++) {            int days = Integer.parseInt(in.nextLine());            String tier = in.nextLine();            double baseTotal = 0;            for (int d = 1; d <= days; d++) {                baseTotal += basePriceForDay(d);            }            double percent = discountPercent(tier, days);            double finalPrice = applyDiscount(baseTotal, percent);            totalRevenue += finalPrice;            if (tier.equals("Gold")) {                goldCount++;            } else if (tier.equals("Silver")) {                silverCount++;            } else {                bronzeCount++;            }            System.out.println("Attendee " + a + ": " + tier + ", " + days                + " day(s), base "                + baseTotal + ", discount " + percent + "%, pays " + finalPrice);        }        System.out.println("SUMMARY");        System.out.println("Total revenue: " + totalRevenue);        System.out.println("Gold: " + goldCount + ", Silver: " + silverCount            + ", Bronze: " + bronzeCount);    }}
OutputAttendee 1: Gold, 3 day(s), base 75.0, discount 25.0%, pays 56.25
Attendee 2: Gold, 1 day(s), base 30.0, discount 15.0%, pays 50.0
Attendee 3: Silver, 2 day(s), base 55.0, discount 5.0%, pays 52.25
Attendee 4: Bronze, 1 day(s), base 30.0, discount 0.0%, pays 50.0
Attendee 5: Platinum, 3 day(s), base 75.0, discount 0.0%, pays 75.0
SUMMARY
Total revenue: 283.5
Gold: 2, Silver: 1, Bronze: 2

Read attendees 2 and 4: both would have paid less than 50 and both paid exactly 50.0, so the floor is visibly working. Read attendee 5: "Platinum" got a 0% discount and was counted as Bronze, so the two Bronze rules agree. Input is a Scanner here so the run can be printed; in the hall, every prompt is JOptionPane.showInputDialog and the summary is one showMessageDialog (F.11).

Trap · The switch must return, or fall through

Part 1's method must give back a price for 1, 2 and 3 and throw otherwise. Writing return inside each case is what makes that safe: a return leaves the method immediately, so no break is needed and there is no fall-through to worry about (Unit 4.3).

Use double price; with assignments instead and you must not forget the breaks, and the compiler will additionally complain that price "might not have been initialized" unless every path assigns it. The default: throw is what convinces the compiler every path is covered: an exception is a legitimate way to leave a method that promised to return a double, because it does not return at all.

Note also that throw needs no throws clause here. IllegalArgumentException is unchecked (Unit 10.1), which is Q1 B's distinction being examined a second time on the same paper.

blocks.text: Part 2: the method behind these, taught from nothing

blocks.label: Work it frame by frame
blocks.tag: for a reader who has never read the course

frames.teach:
The eight primitives are byte, short, int, long, float, double, char, boolean. Whole numbers are int, decimals are double, and everything else is a special case.

public class Divide {    public static void main(String[] args) {        int a = 7, b = 2;        System.out.println(a / b);        double wrong = a / b;        System.out.println(wrong);        double right = (double) a / b;        System.out.println(right);    }}
Output3
3.0
3.5
frames.ask: What do you think this prints, before you look?

frames.teach:
int divided by int is an int, and the fraction is thrown away at the moment of division. Storing the answer in a double afterwards is too late, which is why the second line still prints 3.0.

The fix is to cast BEFORE dividing, or to make one side a double literal: (double) a / b, or a / 2.0.
frames.ask: Now the other arithmetic trap. What does the modulus operator give you, and what is it used for in every exam question about digits?

frames.check: The remainder. n % 10 is the last digit and n / 10 drops it.
frames.teach:
% gives the remainder, and the pair n % 10 and n / 10 is how you take a number apart digit by digit: the first gives the last digit, the second removes it.

public class Digits {    public static void main(String[] args) {        int n = 407, sum = 0;        while (n > 0) {            int digit = n % 10;            sum += digit * digit * digit;            n = n / 10;        }        System.out.println(sum);    }}
Output407
frames.ask: Armstrong numbers, perfect numbers, palindromes and digit counts are all built on that pair. What does this print?

frames.teach:
It prints 407, because 4 cubed plus 0 cubed plus 7 cubed is 407: that is an Armstrong number, and it is a past question in Topic Three.

Now the increment trap. i++ uses the value THEN adds one; ++i adds one THEN uses it.

public class Increment {    public static void main(String[] args) {        int i = 5;        System.out.println(i++);        System.out.println(i);        System.out.println(++i);    }}
Output5
6
7
frames.ask: So what does this print?

frames.teach:
5, then 6, then 7. Read it as: post increment hands over the old value, pre increment hands over the new one.

One more operator trap: + joins when either side is a String. "total: " + 1 + 2 gives "total: 12", because it works left to right. Bracket the arithmetic.
frames.ask: Now input. This paper's Section C says JOptionPane only. What does showInputDialog return?

frames.teach:
A String, always, exactly like Scanner's nextLine. So it must be parsed: Integer.parseInt(text) or Double.parseDouble(text). Forgetting that is the single most common lost mark in Section C.

The pattern to memorise, since it is not compiled here only because it opens a window:

import javax.swing.JOptionPane;public class Fees {    public static void main(String[] args) {        String text = JOptionPane.showInputDialog("How many hours?");        int hours = Integer.parseInt(text);        double fee = hours * 150.0;        JOptionPane.showMessageDialog(null, "Fee: " + fee);        System.exit(0);    }}
frames.ask: Two more lines in that skeleton earn marks. Which, and why?

frames.teach:
import javax.swing.JOptionPane; at the top, and System.exit(0); at the end, which closes the program after the last dialog. Both are on the mark scheme, and both are one line each.

For printed output, printf formats: %d whole number, %.2f two decimals, %s string, %n newline.

blocks.big: "int divided by int is an int. 7 / 2 is 3, and no amount of storing it in a double fixes it after the fact."
blocks.sub: Cast one side first, or use a double literal. JOptionPane reads a String, so parse it with Integer.parseInt or Double.parseDouble.

blocks.printed:
[10 Marks]D. An Armstrong number (also called a narcissistic number) is a positive integer that is equal to the sum of its own digits, each raised to the power of the total number of digits in the number. For example, 153 is an Armstrong number because 1³ + 5³ + 3³ = 1 + 125 + 27 = 153.

i.    State the five outputs for this code (you can show your workings but make the answer bold)

ii.   Retain other things but change the For Loop to While loop and the While loops to For loops.

blocks.label: What you are asked
blocks.html:
Shape: Write a program. A full program, marked on structure as much as on logic. The two papers set this shape 17 times between them, 5 of them on this topic.

And the subject repeats: a program over the digits of a number is also set in 2025/2026, Question Two, 10 marks, 2025/2026, Question Six, 12 marks, 2024/2025, Question Six, 7.5 marks.

blocks.label: Break it down first
blocks.question: What is this question actually asking, what have you been given, and what do the marks tell you about how much to write? Decide, then check.
blocks.answer:
GivenA definition, a worked example, and a working program.
Asked forTwo separate tasks: trace five outputs, then rewrite every loop as the other kind. Part ii is worth doing even if part i defeats you.
The marks10 marks between them, the largest single block on the paper.
WatchPart ii says "Retain other things": change only the loop machinery, not the logic or the variable names. Note the swap is both ways, the for becomes a while and the two while loops become for loops.
Taught inUnits 4.4 to 4.6 and 3.6.

blocks.label: Part 1: the answer you write in the hall
blocks.tag: write yours first, then open this
blocks.problem: Write your answer to the question above in your book first. It carries 10 marks, so write one clear point for every mark. Then open the model answer and mark yourself against it.
blocks.answer:
Q1 d i · state the five outputs · 10 MARKS, PART ONE

The answer. Compute each digit cubed (all five are 3-digit numbers, so the power is 3):

nsum of digits3= n?Output
37027 + 343 + 0 = 370yes370 -> ARMSTRONG
37127 + 343 + 1 = 371yes371 -> ARMSTRONG
37227 + 343 + 8 = 378no372 -> NOT ARMSTRONG
40764 + 0 + 343 = 407yes407 -> ARMSTRONG
40864 + 0 + 512 = 576no408 -> NOT ARMSTRONG

The arithmetic: 33 = 27, 73 = 343, 03 = 0, 13 = 1, 23 = 8, 43 = 64, 83 = 512. Three of the five are Armstrong numbers, which is worth noticing: the examiner chose 370, 371 and 407 because they are the three three-digit Armstrong numbers next to each other, and 372 and 408 as near misses.

Code · confirmed by running the paper's own code · VERIFIED ON THE JVM
public class ArmstrongChecker {    public static void main(String[] args) {        int[] numbers = {370, 371, 372, 407, 408};        for (int idx = 0; idx < numbers.length; idx++) {            int n = numbers[idx], digits = 0, temp = n, sum = 0;            while (temp > 0) { digits++; temp /= 10; }            temp = n;            while (temp > 0) {                int d = temp % 10, power = 1;                for (int p = 0; p < digits; p++) power *= d;                sum += power;                temp /= 10;            }            System.out.println(n + " -> "                + (sum == n ? "ARMSTRONG" : "NOT ARMSTRONG"));        }    }}
Output370 -> ARMSTRONG
371 -> ARMSTRONG
372 -> NOT ARMSTRONG
407 -> ARMSTRONG
408 -> NOT ARMSTRONG
Q1 d ii · convert the loops · 10 MARKS, PART TWO

Read it precisely. The original has three loops:

LoopCurrentlyBecomes
the outer one over idxforwhile
counting the digitswhilefor
summing the powerswhilefor
the inner p loopforwhile

"The For Loop" (singular) is the outer one; "the While loops" (plural) are the two digit loops. The innermost p loop is also a for, so convert it too: the safest reading is that every for becomes a while and every while becomes a for. Apply Unit 4.6's recipe to each.

Code · every loop converted, same output · VERIFIED ON THE JVM
public class ArmstrongConverted {    public static void main(String[] args) {        int[] numbers = {370, 371, 372, 407, 408};        // FOR -> WHILE: init out, condition in, update at the bottom        int idx = 0;        while (idx < numbers.length) {            int n = numbers[idx], digits = 0, temp = n, sum = 0;            // WHILE -> FOR: no init needed, temp is the counter            for (; temp > 0; temp /= 10) {                digits++;            }            temp = n;            // WHILE -> FOR            for (; temp > 0; temp /= 10) {                int d = temp % 10, power = 1;                // FOR -> WHILE                int p = 0;                while (p < digits) {                    power *= d;                    p++;                }                sum += power;            }            System.out.println(n + " -> "                + (sum == n ? "ARMSTRONG" : "NOT ARMSTRONG"));            idx++;                      // the update, at the bottom        }    }}
Output370 -> ARMSTRONG
371 -> ARMSTRONG
372 -> NOT ARMSTRONG
407 -> ARMSTRONG
408 -> NOT ARMSTRONG

Identical output to the original. That is the test of a conversion: same program, different clothes.

Two points a marker looks for. The for (; temp > 0; temp /= 10) has an empty initialisation, which is legal and is the honest conversion: the original while had nothing to initialise, because temp already existed. Do not invent a variable to fill the slot. And idx++ sits at the bottom of the while body, which is Unit 4.6's step 3 and the one people forget: leave it out and the program runs forever.

A number whose proper divisors sum to more than the number itself is called abundant, and one whose proper divisors sum to less than the number itself is called deficient.

Q2 d i · state the output · 10 MARKS, PART ONE

The answer: Perfect: 2, Abundant: 5, Deficient: 23

The reasoning, which is worth writing out because "no need to show workings" does not mean "do not check":

ClassCountWhich
Perfect26 (1+2+3 = 6) and 28 (1+2+4+7+14 = 28)
Abundant512 (16), 18 (21), 20 (22), 24 (36), 30 (42)
Deficient23everything else, including every prime, and 1

Two checks that catch mistakes. 2 + 5 + 23 = 30, so every number is classified exactly once. And 1 is deficient: its proper divisors sum to 0, because 1 has no proper divisor, and the loop for (div = 1; div < num; div++) never runs for num = 1. Forget that and you get 22, not 23.

Code · confirmed, with the classification printed · VERIFIED ON THE JVM
public class NumberClassifier {    public static void main(String[] args) {        int perfectCount = 0, abundantCount = 0, deficientCount = 0;        for (int num = 1; num <= 30; num++) {            int sum = 0;            for (int div = 1; div < num; div++) {                if (num % div == 0) sum += div;            }            if (sum == num) perfectCount++;            else if (sum > num) abundantCount++;            else deficientCount++;        }        System.out.println("Perfect: " + perfectCount + ", Abundant: " + abundantCount            + ", Deficient: " + deficientCount);        System.out.println("check: " + (perfectCount + abundantCount + deficientCount)            + " numbers classified");    }}
OutputPerfect: 2, Abundant: 5, Deficient: 23
check: 30 numbers classified
Code · q2 d ii · for loops converted to while loops · VERIFIED ON THE JVM
public class NumberClassifierWhile {    public static void main(String[] args) {        int perfectCount = 0, abundantCount = 0, deficientCount = 0;        int num = 1;                        // 1. init above        while (num <= 30) {                 // 2. condition            int sum = 0;            int div = 1;                    // the inner one too            while (div < num) {                if (num % div == 0) sum += div;                div++;                      // 3. update at the bottom            }            if (sum == num) perfectCount++;            else if (sum > num) abundantCount++;            else deficientCount++;            num++;                          // 3. update at the bottom        }        System.out.println("Perfect: " + perfectCount + ", Abundant: " + abundantCount            + ", Deficient: " + deficientCount);    }}
OutputPerfect: 2, Abundant: 5, Deficient: 23

Identical output, which is the whole test. Note int sum = 0; stays inside the outer loop: it must be reset for every number, and moving it out is the classic way to wreck this conversion. The recipe only moves the loop's own three parts; everything else stays exactly where it was, which is what "retain other things" means.

blocks.printed:
(12 marks)A. Design and implement a program, using JOptionPane only for input and output, that classifies a single user-supplied positive integer N according to its digit pattern (Palindrome).

Definition: A number is a palindrome if it reads the same forwards and backwards (i.e. it is equal to its own digit-reversed value). For example, 4884 and 7 are palindromes; 4821 is not.

Constraints: The entire task must be implemented inside main() only, using loops and nested/chained if-else and/or switch logic. No arrays and no user-defined helper methods are permitted; everything must be inline.

i.    Using a loop built only on the % and / operators (no converting N to a String or array), compute, in the same loop:

•  the digit sum of N, and

•  the value of N with its digits reversed (e.g. for N = 4821, the reversed value is 1284).

ii.   Determine whether N is a palindrome by comparing N directly to the reversed value computed in step 1.

iii.  Inline in main() (not a separate method), determine whether the digit sum from step 1 is itself a prime number. Use a loop that tests divisibility only up to the square root of the digit sum.

iv.  Using nested/chained conditional logic, classify N into exactly one of the following categories, checked strictly in this priority order:

•  "PALINDROME-PRIME-SUM": if N is a palindrome AND its digit sum is prime

•  "PALINDROME": if N is a palindrome but its digit sum is not prime

•  "HARSHAD": if N is not a palindrome but N is exactly divisible by its own digit sum

•  "STANDARD": in every other case

v.   Display N, its digit sum, its reversed value, and its final classification in a single JOptionPane message dialog.

blocks.answer:
Q6 a · classify a number by its digit pattern · 12 MARKS
  1. in one loop, built only on % and / (no converting N to a String or array), compute both the digit sum of N and N with its digits reversed;
  2. N is a palindrome if it equals its reversed value;
  3. inline, decide whether the digit sum is prime, testing divisibility only up to its square root;
  4. classify, strictly in this priority order: PALINDROME-PRIME-SUM (palindrome and sum prime), PALINDROME (palindrome, sum not prime), HARSHAD (not a palindrome, but N divides exactly by its digit sum), STANDARD otherwise;
  5. show N, its digit sum, its reversed value and its classification in a single dialog.
Must memorise · The digit loop, and the copy that saves it

Peeling digits off a number is three lines you should be able to write without thinking:

int digit = temp % 10;   takes the last digit
reversed = reversed * 10 + digit;   pushes it onto the right of the answer
temp = temp / 10;   drops the last digit

Loop while (temp > 0). Both answers fall out of one pass.

The line the marks hang on is int temp = n;. The loop destroys whatever it walks: temp ends at 0. Walk n itself and by step 2 there is nothing left to compare the reversed value against, and nothing left to divide in step 4. Copy it, consume the copy.

reversed * 10 + digit is worth a moment. Take 4821: the loop pulls 1, then 2, then 8, then 4. Start at 0, and each step shifts what you have one place left and drops the new digit into the units: 1, then 12, then 128, then 1284. The digits come off backwards, which is exactly why pushing them on in the order they arrive reverses the number.

MEMORY HOOK: % takes the last digit, / removes it. Every digit problem in this course is those two lines and a loop.

Teach · The square root test, without Math.sqrt

Part 3 says test divisibility only up to the square root of the digit sum. The clean way needs no square root at all:

boolean sumIsPrime = (digitSum >= 2);for (int f = 2; f * f <= digitSum; f++) {    if (digitSum % f == 0) { sumIsPrime = false; break; }}

f * f <= digitSum is "f is at most the square root of digitSum", squared on both sides. It stays in whole numbers, so there is no Math.sqrt, no double, and no floating-point comparison to get wrong at the boundary (Unit 3.6).

Why stopping at the square root is correct, not just faster. If digitSum = a * b, then a and b cannot both be above the square root, or their product would exceed digitSum. So every factor pairs with one at or below the square root. Find none there and there are none at all.

And the initialiser is the whole edge case. digitSum >= 2 is what makes 1 not prime and 0 not prime. The loop cannot help you: for digitSum = 1 it never runs, so whatever you started with survives. Start at true and the program declares 1 prime, and then N = 1 (a palindrome with digit sum 1) is misclassified. See the table below, last row.

Code · question six, part a · VERIFIED ON THE JVM
import java.util.Scanner;public class PalindromeClassifier {    public static void main(String[] args) {        Scanner in = new Scanner(System.in);        int n = Integer.parseInt(in.nextLine());        // Step i: ONE loop, using only % and /, computing BOTH the digit sum and        // the reversed value. temp is consumed; n must survive for step ii.        int temp = n;        int digitSum = 0;        int reversed = 0;        while (temp > 0) {            int digit = temp % 10;            digitSum = digitSum + digit;            reversed = reversed * 10 + digit;            temp = temp / 10;        }        // Step ii: palindrome is a comparison against the ORIGINAL n.        boolean isPalindrome = (n == reversed);        // Step iii: is digitSum prime? Test factors only up to its square root.        boolean sumIsPrime = (digitSum >= 2);        for (int f = 2; f * f <= digitSum; f++) {            if (digitSum % f == 0) {                sumIsPrime = false;                break;            }        }        // Step iv: classify, in the paper's priority order.        String classification;        if (isPalindrome) {            if (sumIsPrime) {                classification = "PALINDROME-PRIME-SUM";            } else {                classification = "PALINDROME";            }        } else if (n % digitSum == 0) {            classification = "HARSHAD";        } else {            classification = "STANDARD";        }        // Step v: one dialog with all four facts.        String message = "N: " + n                       + "\nDigit sum: " + digitSum                       + "\nReversed: " + reversed                       + "\nClassification: " + classification;        System.out.println(message);    }}
OutputN: 4884
Digit sum: 24
Reversed: 4884
Classification: PALINDROME

4884 is the paper's own example. It is a palindrome, and 24 = 2 × 12 is not prime, so it is PALINDROME and not PALINDROME-PRIME-SUM. That is the priority order doing its job.

Code · the same statements, run over every case · SO THE TABLE IS REAL

This is not the exam answer: the question forbids helper methods and demands a single N. It is the identical block of statements with a loop around it, so that every row below is real output rather than someone's arithmetic.

import java.util.Scanner;// The SAME statements as the answer, with a loop around them, so that every row// of the table in this book is real output rather than someone's arithmetic.public class ClassifierBench {    public static void main(String[] args) {        Scanner in = new Scanner(System.in);        System.out.println("     N | sum | reversed | classification");        while (in.hasNextLine()) {            String line = in.nextLine();            if (line.isEmpty()) {                continue;            }            int n = Integer.parseInt(line);            int temp = n, digitSum = 0, reversed = 0;            while (temp > 0) {                int digit = temp % 10;                digitSum = digitSum + digit;                reversed = reversed * 10 + digit;                temp = temp / 10;            }            boolean isPalindrome = (n == reversed);            boolean sumIsPrime = (digitSum >= 2);            for (int f = 2; f * f <= digitSum; f++) {                if (digitSum % f == 0) {                    sumIsPrime = false;                    break;                }            }            String classification;            if (isPalindrome) {                classification = sumIsPrime ? "PALINDROME-PRIME-SUM" : "PALINDROME";            } else if (n % digitSum == 0) {                classification = "HARSHAD";            } else {                classification = "STANDARD";            }            System.out.printf("%6d | %3d | %8d | %s%n", n, digitSum, reversed,                classification);        }    }}
Output     N | sum | reversed | classification
  4884 |  24 |     4884 | PALINDROME
     7 |   7 |        7 | PALINDROME-PRIME-SUM
  4821 |  15 |     1284 | STANDARD
    21 |   3 |       12 | HARSHAD
   131 |   5 |      131 | PALINDROME-PRIME-SUM
     1 |   1 |        1 | PALINDROME

Six rows, and every branch of part 4 is exercised. 4884 and 4821 are the paper's own two examples and both come out as the paper says. 7 is its one-digit palindrome. 4821: the digit sum is 15 and 4821 = 15 × 321 + 6, so it is not a Harshad number either, and it falls to STANDARD. 1 is the row worth staring at: a palindrome whose digit sum is 1, and 1 is not prime, so PALINDROME. Get the initialiser wrong and this row alone would read PALINDROME-PRIME-SUM.

Trap · "Priority order" means else-if, not four ifs

Part 4 says checked strictly in this priority order and exactly one category. Both phrases point at the same structure: one chain, where reaching a test means every test above it already failed.

Write four independent ifs and a palindrome with a prime digit sum matches the first, then falls into the others too, and your single dialog reports whichever assignment landed last. The chain is what makes "exactly one" true, and it is also what makes HARSHAD's rule readable: HARSHAD never has to say "and is not a palindrome", because it is only ever reached when the palindrome test failed. The order does that work, which is precisely why the question fixes it (Unit 4.2).

Watch n % digitSum in the HARSHAD test. It is safe here only because N is a positive integer, so digitSum is at least 1 and never 0. Take that guarantee away and it throws ArithmeticException (Unit 3.6): a division by zero hiding in a remainder.

Q1 c · dry run sumseries with 3, 4, 5, 7 · 4 MARKS

The answer is 0. For all four values.

Must memorise · Four values, one answer, and that is the question

j and j + 1 are both int, so j / (j + 1) is integer division.

j is always smaller than j + 1. A smaller int divided by a larger int is always 0. Every term is 0. The sum is 0.

1/2 is 0. 2/3 is 0. 3/4 is 0. Not 0.5, 0.67, 0.75: 0, because integer division throws the remainder away (Unit 3.6). It does not round; it truncates.

Why the examiner gave you four values. Being handed 3, 4, 5 and 7 shouts "four different answers". It is bait. The four values are there so that you either notice the types once and answer all four in one line, or trace fractions by hand for ten minutes and write four confident wrong numbers.

MEMORY HOOK: int / int is an int. Before you trace any division, look at the two types. One double anywhere on top and the answer changes completely: 1.0 / 2 is 0.5.

Code · the paper's own method, run · VERIFIED ON THE JVM
public class SumSeriesTrace {    // exactly as the paper prints it    public static int sumSeries(int i) {        int sum = 0;        for (int j = 1; j <= i; j++) {            sum += j / (j + 1);        }        return sum;    }    public static void main(String[] args) {        System.out.println("sumSeries(3) = " + sumSeries(3));        System.out.println("sumSeries(4) = " + sumSeries(4));        System.out.println("sumSeries(5) = " + sumSeries(5));        System.out.println("sumSeries(7) = " + sumSeries(7));        System.out.println("and the terms themselves: 1/2 = " + (1 / 2)            + ", 2/3 = " + (2 / 3) + ", 3/4 = " + (3 / 4));        System.out.println("with a double on top:     1.0/2 = " + (1.0 / 2));    }}
OutputsumSeries(3) = 0
sumSeries(4) = 0
sumSeries(5) = 0
sumSeries(7) = 0
and the terms themselves: 1/2 = 0, 2/3 = 0, 3/4 = 0
with a double on top:     1.0/2 = 0.5

Four inputs, one answer. The last two lines are the whole explanation: every term really is 0, and the single change that would rescue the method is a double on top.

Dry run · How to write this up for 4 marks

Do not just write "0" four times. Show the trace for one value and generalise; that is what the marks are for.

sumSeries(3): the loop runs for j = 1, 2, 3
jj / (j + 1)in real arithmeticas int divisionsum
11 / 20.500

Then one sentence: "for any i, every term j/(j+1) has j < j+1, so integer division gives 0 every time; therefore sumSeries returns 0 for 3, 4, 5 and 7 alike." That sentence is the answer to all four values, and it is worth more than four traced tables.

blocks.answer:
Q4 a · describe decision making, looping and branching · 3 MARKS

Model answer. These are the three families of control structure (Unit 4.1): the statements that decide which code runs and how often, rather than doing the work themselves.

  1. Decision-making. Choosing between paths by testing a condition, so that some code runs and some does not: if, if-else, the if-else ladder, and switch.
  2. Looping (iteration). Repeating a block while a condition holds: for, while and do-while. The do-while is the one that always runs at least once, because it tests at the bottom.
  3. Branching (jumping). Transferring control out of the normal flow: break leaves a loop or a switch case, continue skips to the next iteration, and return leaves the method entirely.

Where the marks are: name the actual keywords. "Looping means repeating" is the idea; "for, while, do-while, and do-while tests at the bottom so it runs at least once" is the answer. Units 4.1 to 4.7.

Q4 b · debug the while loop · 3 MARKS

The paper prints that as a bare fragment. To put it through a real compiler it needs a class and a main around it, so that is what is added below, and nothing else is touched. Every fault you are about to list is the paper's own:

public class WhileDebugBroken {    public static void main(String[] args) {        int count = 1        float output = "";        while(count <=5); {            output = output + count + " ";            Count        }        System.out.println(output);    }}
Compiler outputerror: ';' expected

The errors, listed.

  1. int count = 1 has no semicolon.
  2. float output = ""; is the wrong type. A float is a number; "" is text. They are not interchangeable and Java will not convert one to the other. Fix: String output = "";
  3. while(count <=5); has a stray semicolon. This is the one worth the mark. That semicolon is the loop body: an empty statement. The block below it then runs once, on its own, as an ordinary block. Since count never changes inside the empty body, the condition stays true forever and the program hangs.
  4. Count is not a statement. Wrong case (Java is case sensitive) and, even spelled right, count alone does nothing. Fix: count++; which is what stops the loop.
Trap · The semicolon that eats the loop body

while (condition); and for (...); are both legal Java. The semicolon is an empty statement, and an empty statement is a perfectly good loop body. So the compiler says nothing at all.

What you wrote:

while (count <= 5); { ... }

What Java read:

while (count <= 5) { }   then, separately,   { ... }

The braces you meant as the body became a free-floating block that runs once, after the loop finishes. Except the loop never finishes, because nothing inside an empty body can change count.

This exact trap appears twice on this paper: here, and again in Q6 C as for (int i = 0; i <= n; i++);. The examiner is not being subtle about how much they want you to notice it. Whenever a loop misbehaves, look at the character immediately after the closing bracket. Unit 4.5.

Code · q4 b corrected · VERIFIED ON THE JVM
public class WhileDebug {    public static void main(String[] args) {        int count = 1;        String output = "";        while (count <= 5) {            output = output + count + " ";            count++;        }        System.out.println(output);    }}
Output1 2 3 4 5

There is a trailing space after the 5, because the loop appends count + " " every time including the last. Harmless, and worth writing down if you are asked for the output exactly.

iii.  A do-while loop that prints only the number 10 once.

GivenNothing.
Asked forThree snippets, one per loop type. Snippets, not programs.
The marks3 marks, one per loop.
WatchPart ii counts downwards, so the update is --. Part iii is the classic do-while argument: it runs the body before testing, which is exactly why it prints once.
Taught inUnits 4.4 to 4.6.

blocks.answer:
Q6 a · snippets for the three loop types · 3 MARKS

Part iii is the one being marked. A do-while whose condition is false still runs once, and "print 10 once" is the cleanest possible demonstration of that. Choose a condition that is false immediately, and the body still prints.

Code · q6 a · VERIFIED ON THE JVM
public class ThreeLoopTypes {    public static void main(String[] args) {        // i. a for loop printing 1 to 5        for (int i = 1; i <= 5; i++) {            System.out.print(i + " ");        }        System.out.println();        // ii. a while loop printing 5 down to 1        int j = 5;        while (j >= 1) {            System.out.print(j + " ");            j--;        }        System.out.println();        // iii. a do-while printing only 10, once        int k = 10;        do {            System.out.print(k + " ");            k++;        } while (k <= 10);        System.out.println();    }}
Output1 2 3 4 5
5 4 3 2 1
10

In the do-while, k is 10, the body prints it, k becomes 11, and while (k <= 10) is false, so it stops. The body ran once before the condition was ever looked at, which is the whole difference between do-while and while. Write it as a while with the same condition and nothing prints at all. Unit 4.5.

blocks.answer:
Q6 c · debug evenfinder · 4 MARKS
Compiler outputerror: ';' expected

The errors, listed.

  1. main(String args) is not main. It must be String[] args. Without the brackets it is an ordinary method that the JVM will not recognise as the entry point.
  2. printEven(10.0) has no semicolon.
  3. 10.0 is a double. The method takes an int, and Java will not narrow a double to an int on its own, because that loses information (Unit 3.3). Fix: printEven(10);
  4. printEven(int) has no parameter name. Fix: printEven(int n), which is also why n "does not exist" three lines later.
  5. for (...); has a stray semicolon. The loop body is empty, so the if below is not in the loop. It runs once, after the loop, and it cannot even compile: i was declared in the for, so it is out of scope the moment the for ends.

Error 5 is Q4 B's stray semicolon again, on the same paper, in a for this time. The scope error is what gives it away here: when the compiler says "cannot find symbol: i" about a variable you can plainly see, the loop that declared it has already closed.

The output after correction: 0 2 4 6 8 10

Code · q6 c corrected · VERIFIED ON THE JVM
public class EvenFinder {    public static void main(String[] args) {        printEven(10);    }    public static void printEven(int n) {        for (int i = 0; i <= n; i++) {            if (i % 2 == 0) {                System.out.print(i + " ");            }        }        System.out.println();    }}
Output0 2 4 6 8 10

0 is even, and i <= n means 10 is included, so the answer starts at 0 and ends at 10. Both ends are worth checking: this is the rare loop where <= is correct, because n is a value to reach, not a length.

[7.5 marks]D. Write a program that includes a method called hasEqualAdjacentPairs(int n) which:

i.    Returns true if the number n (a positive integer) contains at least two pairs of equal adjacent digits.

ii.   Returns false otherwise.

iii.  You must:

a.  Write the method hasEqualAdjacentPairs(int n)

b.  Write the main() method to test at least two cases

•  1223 - true (pairs: 22). Only one pair - return false

Reproduced exactly. The second example is self-contradictory as printed: it says "true" and then "return false". The rule in part i is the one to trust. This is discussed in the answer below.

blocks.answer:
Q6 d · hasequaladjacentpairs · 7.5 MARKS

112233 → true (pairs: 11, 22, 33). More than two adjacent pairs.
1223 → true (pairs: 22). Only one pair → return false

Trap · The paper contradicts itself, and you must answer anyway

Read the second example again. It says "1223 - true" and then, in the same line, "Only one pair - return false". Both cannot be right.

The specification says "at least two pairs". 1223 has one pair, the 22. One is not at least two.

The correct return is false. The leading "true" is a slip of the pen.

The examiner's own explanation ("Only one pair") agrees with the specification, so the specification and the reasoning outvote the stray word. This book shows you the paper exactly as printed and tells you what is true, and it never quietly corrects a source (compare the six errors in Module 3, which come from this course's own slides).

What to do in the hall. Do not agonise, and do not answer the typo. Implement the specification, and write one line saying why: "1223 has only one adjacent pair, so by the stated rule of at least two pairs the method returns false; the 'true' in the example appears to be a typographical error." That sentence costs ten seconds and it protects you whichever way the marking scheme reads, because it proves the answer was a decision and not a mistake.

MEMORY HOOK: when a question contradicts itself, follow the specification and say that you did.

Code · q6 d, complete · VERIFIED ON THE JVM
public class AdjacentPairs {    // i/ii. true when n has AT LEAST TWO pairs of equal adjacent digits.    public static boolean hasEqualAdjacentPairs(int n) {        int pairs = 0;        int previous = n % 10;        n = n / 10;        while (n > 0) {            int current = n % 10;            if (current == previous) {                pairs++;            }            previous = current;            n = n / 10;        }        return pairs >= 2;    }    // iii b. main testing more than the two cases the question asks for    public static void main(String[] args) {        int[] tests = {112233, 1223, 1122, 111, 123, 7, 122333};        for (int t : tests) {            System.out.println(t + " -> " + hasEqualAdjacentPairs(t));        }    }}
Output112233 -> true
1223 -> false
1122 -> true
111 -> true
123 -> false
7 -> false
122333 -> true

The paper asks for at least two test cases; there are seven, and each earns its place. 112233 and 1223 are the paper's own. 1122 is the boundary: exactly two pairs, so exactly true. 111 asks what a triple counts as. 123 has no pairs and 7 has no adjacent digits at all, so the loop never runs and pairs stays 0.

Must memorise · Compare adjacent digits by remembering the last one

Take the last digit before the loop and call it previous. Then each turn: take the new current, compare it with previous, and make current the new previous.

That is the whole technique, and it is the same % 10 and / 10 pair as Q6 A on the 2025/26 paper. The only new idea is carrying one value forward so that each digit can see its neighbour. You never need the digits in an array; you need exactly one of them remembered.

111 gives two pairs, not one. The digits are compared in overlapping pairs: positions 1-2 and 2-3. The middle 1 belongs to both. If you think a triple should count once, that is a different specification, and this one does not say so: it says pairs of equal adjacent digits, and 111 contains two of them.

MEMORY HOOK: to compare neighbours, remember one. Peel a digit, compare, then let it become the memory for the next.

frames.teach:
Three loops, and the exam asks you to tell them apart and to convert between them. A for loop when you know how many times, a while when you do not, a do-while when the body must run at least once.

public class Loops {    public static void main(String[] args) {        for (int i = 1; i <= 5; i++) System.out.print(i + " ");        System.out.println();        int j = 5;        while (j >= 1) { System.out.print(j + " "); j--; }        System.out.println();        int k = 10;        do { System.out.print("ran once "); k++; } while (k < 5);        System.out.println();    }}
Output1 2 3 4 5 
5 4 3 2 1 
ran once
frames.ask: What do you expect each of these three to print?

frames.teach:
The do-while is the one to notice: its condition was false from the start and the body still ran, because a do-while tests AFTER. That is a favourite objective question.

Converting a for into a while is on the paper: take the three parts out of the for and put them where they belong.

for (int i = 1; i <= 5; i++) { ... }int i = 1;          // 1. the initialisation goes above the loopwhile (i <= 5) {    // 2. the condition goes in the while    ...    i++;            // 3. the update goes at the END of the body}
frames.ask: If you put the update at the TOP of the while body instead of the bottom, what breaks?

frames.check: The first pass uses the wrong value and the count is off by one.
frames.teach:
The first pass uses the wrong value and the loop runs one fewer time. That is a planted error in a debug question, so check where the update sits every time.

Now the dry run, which is four marks on the 24/25 paper, three times over. The method is a table: one column per variable, one row per pass.

public class Trace {    public static void main(String[] args) {        int sum = 0;        for (int i = 1; i <= 7; i++) {            if (i % 2 == 0) continue;            if (i > 5) break;            sum += i;            System.out.println("i=" + i + " sum=" + sum);        }        System.out.println("final " + sum);    }}
Outputi=1 sum=1
i=3 sum=4
i=5 sum=9
final 9
frames.ask: Trace this one on paper before you run it: what is the final sum?

frames.teach: 9. The even numbers are skipped by continue, and break leaves the loop at i = 7 before it can be added. The two keywords are asked as a pair: continue skips the rest of this pass, break leaves the loop entirely.
frames.ask: Now decisions. In an if-else-if ladder, why does the order of the tests matter?

frames.check: It stops at the first test that is true, so a wide test placed early swallows everything.
frames.teach:
Because the ladder stops at the first true test. A grade ladder must run from the highest boundary down, or a score of 90 matches a test for 45 and above and is graded wrongly.

public class Fall {    public static void main(String[] args) {        int level = 2;        switch (level) {            case 1: System.out.println("Bronze");            case 2: System.out.println("Silver");            case 3: System.out.println("Gold"); break;            default: System.out.println("unranked");        }    }}
OutputSilver
Gold
frames.ask: A switch does the same job for exact values. What happens if you leave out a break inside it?

frames.check: Silver and Gold, because the missing break falls through.
frames.teach:
It falls through: execution carries on into the next case until it meets a break. Level 2 printed Silver AND Gold, because only the third case ends in a break. Deliberate fall through is used to group cases; accidental fall through is a planted error.

Note the rest of the rules: a switch works on int, char, String and enum, default catches everything else, and case labels must be constants.

blocks.big: "A dry run is a table, one column per variable and one row per pass. Never do it in your head."
blocks.sub: A for loop when the count is known, a while when it is not, a do-while when the body must run at least once. break leaves the loop, continue skips to the next pass.

blocks.answer:
GivenNothing. Recall.
Asked forTwo things joined by "and": a definition, then the mechanism. "State precisely the role" is asking how the compiler decides, not what overloading is.
The marks2 marks: one for the definition, one for the mechanism. Answering only the first half caps you at one.
WatchThe word "at compile time" is the hinge. Overloading is resolved statically, by signature; overriding is resolved at run time. Say "compile time" out loud in your answer.

blocks.label: Part 1: the answer you write in the hall
blocks.tag: write yours first, then open this
blocks.problem: Write your answer to the question above in your book first. It carries 2 marks, so write one clear point for every mark. Then open the model answer and mark yourself against it.
blocks.answer:
Q1 a · define method overloading, and the role of the signature · 2 MARKS

Model answer.

Method overloading is a feature that allows a class to have more than one method with the same name but different parameter lists (differing in the number, types, or order of parameters).

The method signature is a method's name together with its parameter list. Its role in resolution is this: at a call such as add(2, 3), the compiler compares the number, types and order of the arguments written at the call site against the parameter list of every candidate with that name, and selects the one whose signature matches (widening the argument types if no exact match exists). Because the resolution uses only what appears at the call site, and the return type is not part of the signature, the return type plays no role: two methods differing only by return type are rejected by the compiler as a duplicate definition. The choice is therefore made entirely at compile time, which is why overloading is called compile-time (static) polymorphism.

Where the marks are: one for the definition, one for "signature = name + parameter list" and the fact that the return type is excluded. Saying "the compiler picks the right one" without saying how is half an answer. See Units 5.1 and 5.6.

blocks.answer:
Q1 a · define method signature, overloading, and void method · 3 MARKS

Model answer. One mark each, and each is one sentence.

  1. Method signature. A method's name together with its parameter list (the number, types and order of its parameters). The return type is not part of the signature. It is what the compiler uses to tell one method from another.
  2. Method overloading. Declaring more than one method with the same name but different parameter lists in the same class, so the compiler chooses between them at compile time by matching the arguments at the call site against each signature.
  3. Void method. A method declared void, meaning it returns no value. It is called as a statement on its own, cannot be used in an expression, and may use a bare return; to exit early.

Where the marks are: the examiner asked for signature and overloading in the same breath deliberately, because the second is defined by the first. Say "signature = name + parameter list, return type excluded" and the overloading definition writes itself. Units 5.1, 5.2 and 5.6.

Compiler outputerror: <identifier> expected

The errors, listed. The question says list and correct, so list them: a correction with no list is half an answer.

public class SquareCalc {    public static void main(String[] args) {        int num = 5;        double result = square(num);        System.out.println("Square is: " + result);    }    public static int square(int n) {        return n * n;    }}

ii.   The area of a rectangle

iii.  The area of a triangle.

blocks.label: What you are asked

GivenNothing. You write the whole program.

The marks7.5 marks. The last sentence is a separate instruction carrying its own marks: three correct methods with no main is an incomplete answer.
WatchOverloading is resolved by the parameter list. Circle takes one argument, rectangle and triangle take two, so rectangle and triangle collide unless you distinguish them. Decide how before you start writing.
Taught inUnits 5.6 and 5.7.

blocks.label: Part 1: the answer you write in the hall
blocks.tag: write yours first, then open this
blocks.problem: Write your answer to the question above in your book first. It carries 7.5 marks, so write one clear point for every mark. Then open the model answer and mark yourself against it.
blocks.answer:
Q1 d · overload area for circle, rectangle and triangle · 7.5 MARKS
Must memorise · The obvious answer to this question does not compile

Circle needs one number. Rectangle needs two. Triangle needs two.

So rectangle is area(double, double), and triangle (base and height) is also area(double, double).

That is the same signature. It will not compile.

Overloading needs different parameter lists, and "base, height" is not different from "length, width": the parameter names are not part of the signature, only the types (Q1 A, which you just answered). Write both and javac says:

error: method area(double,double) is already defined in class

The resolution: give the triangle a three-number formula, so its signature is area(double, double, double) and distinct. Heron's formula takes the three sides:

s = (a + b + c) / 2     and     area = √ s(s-a)(s-b)(s-c) 

MEMORY HOOK: overloads differ by types, not by names. If two of your methods take the same types in the same order, you have one method and a compiler error.

This is the single most valuable thing in Question One, and the examiner may not have noticed it. Say it explicitly in your answer: "base and height would collide with length and width, so the triangle is done by Heron's formula on three sides, giving a distinct signature." That sentence proves you understand overloading, which is what the question is for.

Code · q1 d, complete · VERIFIED ON THE JVM
public class AreaOverload {    // i. circle: one number, so the signature is area(double)    public static double area(double radius) {        return Math.PI * radius * radius;    }    // ii. rectangle: two numbers, so the signature is area(double, double)    public static double area(double length, double width) {        return length * width;    }    // iii. triangle: base and height would ALSO be area(double, double), which is    // the rectangle's signature and will not compile. Three sides gives a distinct    // signature and a genuine formula: Heron's.    public static double area(double sideA, double sideB, double sideC) {        double s = (sideA + sideB + sideC) / 2;        return Math.sqrt(s * (s - sideA) * (s - sideB) * (s - sideC));    }    public static void main(String[] args) {        System.out.println("Circle, radius 7      : " + area(7.0));        System.out.println("Rectangle, 5 by 3     : " + area(5.0, 3.0));        System.out.println("Triangle, sides 3 4 5 : " + area(3.0, 4.0, 5.0));    }}
OutputCircle, radius 7      : 153.93804002589985
Rectangle, 5 by 3     : 15.0
Triangle, sides 3 4 5 : 6.0

Check the triangle without trusting Heron. 3, 4, 5 is a right triangle, so its area must be half of 3 × 4, which is 6. Heron gave exactly 6.0. When you use a formula you cannot see through, feed it a case whose answer you already know. Math.PI and Math.sqrt are Unit 3.6.

blocks.text: Part 2: the method behind these, taught from nothing

blocks.label: Work it frame by frame
blocks.tag: for a reader who has never read the course

frames.teach:
A method is a named block that does one job. The header carries four things in order: modifiers, return type, name, parameter list.

public class Area {    static double area(double r) { return Math.PI * r * r; }    static double area(double l, double w) { return l * w; }    static double area(double b, double h, boolean triangle) { return 0.5 * b * h; }    public static void main(String[] args) {        System.out.printf("circle %.2f%n", area(7));        System.out.printf("rectangle %.2f%n", area(4, 5));        System.out.printf("triangle %.2f%n", area(6, 8, true));    }}
Outputcircle 153.94
rectangle 20.00
triangle 24.00
frames.ask: Which of those four make up the SIGNATURE, the part the compiler uses to tell two methods apart?

frames.check: The name and the parameter list.
frames.teach:
The name and the parameter list, and nothing else. The return type is NOT part of the signature, which is the precise point 25/26 asks for: it is the signature that lets the compiler resolve an overloaded call at compile time.

So overloading is several methods with the same name whose parameter lists differ in number, type or order.
frames.ask: Two methods differ only in return type, int and double. Will that compile?

frames.check: No: same signature, so it will not compile.
frames.teach:
No. The signatures are identical, so the compiler cannot choose, and it is a compile error. That single sentence answers half the overloading questions in the objective half.

Now the distinction the paper asks for in words: a parameter is the name in the header, an argument is the value in the call.
frames.ask: A void method and a value returning one. What is the difference in what the CALL is worth?

frames.check: A void call is not a value; a value returning call is.
frames.teach:
A void method hands nothing back, so its call cannot be assigned or printed. A value returning method ends in return, and its call IS a value. In the exam, prefer a method that returns: Section B and C both say "a method that returns".

public class PassByValue {    static void change(int n, int[] nums) {        n = 99;        nums[0] = 99;    }    public static void main(String[] args) {        int n = 1;        int[] nums = {1, 2, 3};        change(n, nums);        System.out.println(n + " " + nums[0]);    }}
Output1 99
frames.ask: Now pass by value. What does this print, and why does the array behave differently from the int?

frames.teach: 1 and 99. Java always passes by value, but the value of an array variable is a REFERENCE to the array. The copy of that reference still points at the same array, so a change through it is visible to the caller; the copy of the int is just a copy.
frames.ask: Last: static. Why can main call a method directly only if that method is static?

frames.check: main is static, so it has no object to call an instance method on.
frames.teach: Because main is static, so it runs without an object, and it can only call other static methods directly. A non static method needs an object first: new Thing().method(). Marking a helper method static in an exam program is the simplest way to keep it callable from main.

blocks.big: "The signature is the name and the parameter list. The return type is not part of it, which is why two methods cannot differ by return type alone."
blocks.sub: Java passes by value: a method cannot change the caller's int. An array variable holds a reference, so its contents can be changed.

blocks.answer:
Q2 a · define encapsulation · 2 MARKS

Model answer.

Encapsulation is the OOP principle of bundling data (fields) and the methods that operate on them into a single unit (a class), while restricting direct access to some of its components.

In Java it is achieved by declaring the fields private and exposing controlled access through public getter and setter methods. This gives data hiding (unauthorised code cannot read or modify the state), validation (a setter can reject invalid input, for example preventing a negative balance), and flexibility (the internal representation can change without breaking any code that uses the class).

Where the marks are: one for the bundling-plus- restricting definition, one for how it is achieved (private fields, public getters and setters). Add one benefit if you have room. See Unit 6.4.

blocks.answer:
Q2 b · three differences: overloading vs overriding · 3 MARKS

Model answer. Three differences, one mark each:

  1. Where they occur. Overloading happens within a single class: several methods share a name. Overriding happens between a superclass and a subclass: the subclass replaces the inherited method.
  2. The parameter list. Overloaded methods must have different parameter lists. An overriding method must have exactly the same name and parameter list as the one it overrides.
  3. When the method is chosen. Overloading is resolved at compile time by the compiler (static polymorphism); overriding is resolved at run time by the JVM, from the object's actual type (dynamic polymorphism).

Where the marks are: three separate axes. If you have room, add that overriding requires inheritance and overloading does not. See Unit 6.7.

A bank wants a system representing different types of accounts using inheritance and polymorphism.

ii.   CurrentAccount extends BankAccount. Override the withdrawal method so that every successful withdrawal automatically adds a ₦50 reward to the balance afterward. (6 marks)

Part 3: Main Method

ii.   Deposits money into each;

iii.  Performs at least one successful and one unsuccessful/reward-triggering withdrawal on each;

iv.  Displays each account's details before and after the transactions;

v.   Demonstrates polymorphism by storing each object in a BankAccount reference and calling the withdrawal method through it, confirming that the correct overridden version runs.

blocks.answer:
Q4 · inheritance and polymorphism · 25 MARKS

Part 1, BankAccount (9 marks). Private fields for account number, holder name and balance; a constructor initialising all three; a method that adds to the balance; a method that deducts if funds suffice and otherwise rejects with a message; a method that displays the details.

Part 2, subclasses (10 marks). SavingAccount overrides the withdrawal so it is allowed only if the balance after the withdrawal would still be >= 1000. CurrentAccount overrides it so every successful withdrawal adds a 50 reward afterwards.

Part 3, main (6 marks). One of each; deposit into each; at least one successful and one unsuccessful or reward-triggering withdrawal on each; details before and after; and demonstrate polymorphism by storing each object in a BankAccount reference and calling the withdrawal through it, confirming the correct overridden version runs.

Must memorise · The question contains a contradiction, and resolving it is the exam

Part 1 says the balance must be private.

Part 2 says the subclasses must change the balance.

A private field is invisible to a subclass. So the subclass cannot touch it.

This is not the examiner being careless. It is the whole of Units 6.4 and 6.6 arriving in one question: encapsulation says the field is private, and inheritance says the child must still be able to work with it. The way out is the only way out, and it is the answer being marked: the subclass goes through the parent's public methods, using getBalance() to read and super.withdraw(amount) or deposit(amount) to change.

MEMORY HOOK: the child knocks, it does not climb in through the window. getBalance() to look, super.withdraw() to act.

Trap · A subclass cannot see a private field, and it will say so

The tempting move is to write the arithmetic straight into the subclass. Java stops you at the compiler:

class Account {    private double balance = 5000;}class Saving extends Account {    public boolean withdraw(double amount) {        balance = balance - amount;        return true;    }}public class SubclassReach {    public static void main(String[] args) {        new Saving().withdraw(100);    }}
Compiler outputerror: balance has private access in Account

Private means the declaring class only, and a subclass is a different class. Inheritance gives Saving the field (every Saving object really does contain a balance) but not access to it. The field is there and untouchable, which is exactly what private is for (Unit 6.4).

Would protected fix it? It would compile, and it is the wrong answer here, because part 1 said private. Marks are for doing what the question said. Beyond the exam, going through the parent's methods is better anyway: every rule the parent enforces on a withdrawal keeps being enforced. Make the field protected and each subclass has to remember those rules for itself, which is how a bank ends up with an account that can be overdrawn down one code path and not another. See the access table in Unit 6.6.

Teach · Why withdraw returns boolean

The paper does not say what withdraw returns, and the obvious choice is void. Then read part 2 ii again: a CurrentAccount adds the reward on every successful withdrawal. Not on every attempt. So the override has to know whether the withdrawal succeeded, and a void method tells it nothing.

Making withdraw return boolean makes the override three honest lines:

boolean succeeded = super.withdraw(amount);if (succeeded) { deposit(50); }return succeeded;

The alternative, comparing the balance before and after, works but is worse: it re-derives an answer the parent already knew and threw away. When a method knows something the caller needs, it should return it. Notice that this decision is forced by a single word in part 2 ii, which is what "read the question" means in practice.

Code · question four, complete · VERIFIED ON THE JVM
// ===== Part 1: the superclass =====class BankAccount {    private String accountNumber;    private String holderName;    private double balance;    // Part 1 i: a constructor that initialises all three fields.    public BankAccount(String accountNumber, String holderName, double balance) {        this.accountNumber = accountNumber;        this.holderName = holderName;        this.balance = balance;    }    // The private fields are reachable only through these doors (Unit 6.4).    public String getAccountNumber() { return accountNumber; }    public String getHolderName()    { return holderName; }    public double getBalance()       { return balance; }    // Part 1 ii: add a given amount to the balance.    public void deposit(double amount) {        balance = balance + amount;        System.out.println("Deposit " + amount + " -> " + accountNumber            + " balance is now " + balance);    }    // Part 1 iii: deduct if funds are sufficient, otherwise reject with a message.    // Returns whether it succeeded, which is what CurrentAccount needs to know.    public boolean withdraw(double amount) {        if (amount <= balance) {            balance = balance - amount;            System.out.println("Withdraw " + amount + " -> " + accountNumber                + " balance is now " + balance);            return true;        }        System.out.println("REJECTED: " + accountNumber + " holds only " + balance            + ", so " + amount + " cannot be withdrawn");        return false;    }    // Part 1 iv: display the account's current details.    public void displayDetails() {        System.out.println("Account " + accountNumber + " | " + holderName            + " | balance " + balance);    }}// ===== Part 2 i: a saving account must never drop below 1000 =====class SavingAccount extends BankAccount {    public SavingAccount(String accountNumber, String holderName, double balance) {        super(accountNumber, holderName, balance);    }    @Override    public boolean withdraw(double amount) {        if (getBalance() - amount < 1000) {            System.out.println("REJECTED: a saving account must retain 1000. " +                "Withdrawing "                + amount + " from " + getAccountNumber() + " would leave "                + (getBalance() - amount));            return false;        }        return super.withdraw(amount);    }}// ===== Part 2 ii: every successful withdrawal earns a 50 reward =====class CurrentAccount extends BankAccount {    public CurrentAccount(String accountNumber, String holderName, double balance) {        super(accountNumber, holderName, balance);    }    @Override    public boolean withdraw(double amount) {        boolean succeeded = super.withdraw(amount);        if (succeeded) {            System.out.println("Reward earned on " + getAccountNumber() + ":");            deposit(50);        }        return succeeded;    }}// ===== Part 3: the main method =====public class BankSystem {    public static void main(String[] args) {        // Part 3 i: at least one of each.        SavingAccount saving   = new SavingAccount("SA-1001", "Ada Bello", 5000.0);        CurrentAccount current = new CurrentAccount("CA-2002", "Femi Okonkwo",            3000.0);        System.out.println("=== iv: details BEFORE the transactions ===");        saving.displayDetails();        current.displayDetails();        // Part 3 ii: deposit into each.        System.out.println("=== ii: deposit into each ===");        saving.deposit(2000.0);        current.deposit(1000.0);        // Part 3 iii: a successful and an unsuccessful withdrawal on each.        System.out.println("=== iii: a successful and an unsuccessful withdrawal on " +            "each ===");        saving.withdraw(4000.0);        saving.withdraw(2500.0);        current.withdraw(1000.0);        current.withdraw(999999.0);        System.out.println("=== iv: details AFTER the transactions ===");        saving.displayDetails();        current.displayDetails();        // Part 3 v: polymorphism. Same reference type, same call, same amount.        System.out.println("=== v: polymorphism, same reference type, same call, " +            "same amount ===");        BankAccount acc = new SavingAccount("SA-3003", "Ngozi Eze", 1500.0);        acc.withdraw(600.0);        acc.displayDetails();        acc = new CurrentAccount("CA-4004", "Tunde Ade", 1500.0);        acc.withdraw(600.0);        acc.displayDetails();    }}
Output=== iv: details BEFORE the transactions ===
Account SA-1001 | Ada Bello | balance 5000.0
Account CA-2002 | Femi Okonkwo | balance 3000.0
=== ii: deposit into each ===
Deposit 2000.0 -> SA-1001 balance is now 7000.0
Deposit 1000.0 -> CA-2002 balance is now 4000.0
=== iii: a successful and an unsuccessful withdrawal on each ===
Withdraw 4000.0 -> SA-1001 balance is now 3000.0
REJECTED: a saving account must retain 1000. Withdrawing 2500.0 from SA-1001 would leave 500.0
Withdraw 1000.0 -> CA-2002 balance is now 3000.0
Reward earned on CA-2002:
Deposit 50.0 -> CA-2002 balance is now 3050.0
REJECTED: CA-2002 holds only 3050.0, so 999999.0 cannot be withdrawn
=== iv: details AFTER the transactions ===
Account SA-1001 | Ada Bello | balance 3000.0
Account CA-2002 | Femi Okonkwo | balance 3050.0
=== v: polymorphism, same reference type, same call, same amount ===
REJECTED: a saving account must retain 1000. Withdrawing 600.0 from SA-3003 would leave 900.0
Account SA-3003 | Ngozi Eze | balance 1500.0
Withdraw 600.0 -> CA-4004 balance is now 900.0
Reward earned on CA-4004:
Deposit 50.0 -> CA-4004 balance is now 950.0
Account CA-4004 | Tunde Ade | balance 950.0

All four classes live in one file because only one may be public and that one must match the file name: BankSystem.java. In the hall, write them as four classes exactly as they are here, or as four separate files. Both are correct.

Dry run · Every balance, and why each rule fired
Callbalance beforewhich rule decidedallowed?balance after
SA-1001, a SavingAccount, opens at 5000
deposit(2000)5000.0no rule: deposits always landyes7000.0
withdraw(4000)7000.07000 - 4000 = 3000, and 3000 >= 1000yes3000.0
withdraw(2500)3000.03000 - 2500 = 500, and 500 < 1000no3000.0
CA-2002, a CurrentAccount, opens at 3000
deposit(1000)3000.0no ruleyes4000.0
withdraw(1000)4000.0funds suffice, so the reward firesyes3000.0, then +50 = 3050.0
withdraw(999999)3050.0funds do not suffice, so no rewardno3050.0

The last row is the one to study. The reward sits inside if (succeeded), so a rejected withdrawal earns nothing. Had withdraw returned void, that if could not have been written, and CA-2002 would have been paid 50 for a transaction that never happened.

Must memorise · How to prove polymorphism in six lines

Part 3 v asks you to confirm the correct overridden version runs. A proof needs a control: change one thing and show the behaviour changes.

So: same reference type, same method, same amount, same starting balance. Only the object differs.

BankAccount acc = new SavingAccount("SA-3003", "Ngozi Eze", 1500.0);acc.withdraw(600.0);        // rejected: would leave 900, under 1000acc = new CurrentAccount("CA-4004", "Tunde Ade", 1500.0);acc.withdraw(600.0);        // allowed, and pays a 50 reward: 950

Both variables are declared BankAccount. Both calls are acc.withdraw(600.0), character for character. Both accounts hold 1500.0. One is refused and one is paid a bonus.

That is the proof, and here is the sentence that earns the mark: the compiler only knew acc was a BankAccount, so the choice of which withdraw to run could not have been made at compile time. It was made at run time, from the object's actual class. That is dynamic method dispatch, and it is what "polymorphism" names (Unit 6.7).

MEMORY HOOK: the reference decides what you may call. The object decides what actually runs.

Compare this with the TRAP at the end of Unit 6.6, where the same setup silently ran the parent's method because the override was really an overload. Same two lines of code, opposite outcomes, and the difference was one parameter type. That is why @Override sits on every override here.

blocks.answer:
Q4 d · the temperaturecheck class · 7.5 MARKS
Must memorise · "Between 15 and 30 inclusive" needs no upper test

if (t < 15) "Too Cold";
else if (t <= 30) "Normal";
else "Too Hot";

The else if only runs when t < 15 was false, which already means t >= 15. So writing else if (t >= 15 && t <= 30) is not wrong, it is redundant: the ladder has already established the lower bound. Let the structure carry what it has proved (Unit 4.2).

The two boundaries are the marks. "Inclusive" means 15 and 30 are both Normal. Get < and <= the wrong way round and the program is right for 99% of inputs and wrong on exactly the two values the examiner will test.

MEMORY HOOK: test the fences, not the field. When a spec names a boundary, that boundary is the test case.

Code · q4 d, complete · VERIFIED ON THE JVM
import java.util.Scanner;// i. the class, with its one data fieldclass TemperatureCheck {    private double temperature;    // ii. a constructor that sets the temperature    public TemperatureCheck(double temperature) {        this.temperature = temperature;    }    // iii. if-else evaluation    public void evaluateTemperature() {        if (temperature < 15) {            System.out.println("Too Cold");        } else if (temperature <= 30) {            System.out.println("Normal");        } else {            System.out.println("Too Hot");        }    }}public class TemperatureDemo {    public static void main(String[] args) {        Scanner in = new Scanner(System.in);        while (in.hasNextLine()) {            String line = in.nextLine();            if (line.isEmpty()) continue;            double t = Double.parseDouble(line);            System.out.print(t + " -> ");            TemperatureCheck check = new TemperatureCheck(t);            check.evaluateTemperature();        }    }}
Output5.0 -> Too Cold
15.0 -> Normal
22.0 -> Normal
30.0 -> Normal
31.0 -> Too Hot
40.0 -> Too Hot

Read rows 2 and 4: 15.0 and 30.0 are both Normal, which is exactly what "inclusive" demands, and 31.0 is the first Too Hot. The values were chosen to sit on the fences. In the hall this reads double t = Double.parseDouble(JOptionPane.showInputDialog("Enter a temperature:")); and the result goes out through showMessageDialog (F.11); the loop here exists only so one run can show you all six cases.

The field is private and set only by the constructor, which is Unit 6.4's encapsulation arriving without being asked for. The question says "data field (state)"; making it private costs one word and is never wrong.

Asked forThree descriptions.
The marks3 marks, one each.
WatchThese three are a chain, so describe them as one: inheritance gives you the subclass, overriding replaces a method in it, polymorphism is what lets the replacement run through a superclass reference. Do not define overriding as overloading.
