blocks.answer:
Q5 a · describe inheritance, polymorphism and method overriding · 3 MARKS

Model answer.

  1. Inheritance. One class acquiring the fields and methods of another with extends, so the subclass has everything the superclass has without repeating it, and may add or replace behaviour. It models an is-a relationship: a Bicycle is a Vehicle.
  2. Polymorphism. One reference, many behaviours: a variable of the superclass type may hold an object of any subclass, and a call through it runs the object's own version, decided at run time. "Many forms".
  3. Method overriding. A subclass supplying its own version of a method the superclass already has, with the same signature, which replaces the inherited one for objects of that subclass.

Where the marks are: these three are one idea in three parts, and saying so earns the mark. Inheritance makes the family; overriding makes the members differ; polymorphism is what you get when you then hold any of them in one variable and call the method. Distinguish overriding (same signature, subclass, run time) from overloading (different parameters, same class, compile time), which is Q1 of this same paper. Units 6.6 and 6.7.

Q5 c · identify the errors and state the output after correction · 4 MARKS
Compiler outputerror: not a statement

The errors, listed.

  1. int nums = {10, 20, 30}; is not an array. A list in braces needs an array type. Fix: int[] nums = {10, 20, 30};
  2. nums[3] does not exist. Three elements means indexes 0, 1 and 2. And the label says "Middle value", so the intent is nums[1], which is 20. Say both halves: the index is out of bounds and the middle of three is index 1.
  3. i <= nums.length is off by one and would throw at nums[3]. Fix: i < nums.length.
  4. i never increments. Fix: i++.
  5. "Sum is: " + ); has nothing to add. Fix: "Sum is: " + sum.

Q5 d · vehicle and bicycle · 7.5 MARKS
Code · q5 d, complete · VERIFIED ON THE JVM
// i. the superclassclass Vehicle {    protected int speed;    public Vehicle(int speed) {        this.speed = speed;    }    public void displayInfo() {        System.out.println("Vehicle speed: " + speed + " km/h");    }}// ii. the subclass, overriding displayInfo()class Bicycle extends Vehicle {    public Bicycle(int speed) {        super(speed);    }    @Override    public void displayInfo() {        System.out.println("Bicycle speed: " + speed            + " km/h. This is an eco-friendly ride.");    }}public class VehicleDemo {    public static void main(String[] args) {        // iii a/b. one of each        Vehicle car = new Vehicle(80);        Bicycle bike = new Bicycle(25);        // iii c. call displayInfo() on both        car.displayInfo();        bike.displayInfo();        // and the polymorphic form the question is really after        Vehicle[] fleet = {new Vehicle(80), new Bicycle(25)};        System.out.println("-- through a Vehicle reference --");        for (Vehicle v : fleet) {            v.displayInfo();        }    }}
OutputVehicle speed: 80 km/h
Bicycle speed: 25 km/h. This is an eco-friendly ride.
-- through a Vehicle reference --
Vehicle speed: 80 km/h
Bicycle speed: 25 km/h. This is an eco-friendly ride.
Teach · The last four words of the question change the answer

The question says: call displayInfo() on both objects to demonstrate polymorphism. Read literally, parts a to c are satisfied by:

Vehicle car = new Vehicle(80);Bicycle bike = new Bicycle(25);car.displayInfo();bike.displayInfo();

That prints the two required lines, and it demonstrates nothing. Each variable's declared type already matches its object exactly, so the compiler could have picked both methods without any run-time decision. Overriding happened, but polymorphism was never tested.

Polymorphism needs the reference to be the SUPERCLASS type, so that the declared type and the actual object disagree and only the run time can settle it:

Vehicle[] fleet = {new Vehicle(80), new Bicycle(25)};
for (Vehicle v : fleet) v.displayInfo();

Now every element is declared Vehicle, the loop body is one identical call, and it still prints two different lines. That is the demonstration, and it is what the last four words are asking for. The listing above does both: the literal answer first, then the proof.

Same idea as Q4 part 3 v on the 2025/26 paper, where the reference is explicitly required to be a BankAccount. Two papers, two years, one point: the reference decides what you may call, the object decides what runs.

blocks.text: Part 2: the method behind these, taught from nothing

blocks.label: Work it frame by frame
blocks.tag: for a reader who has never read the course

frames.teach:
A class is a blueprint; an object is one thing built from it with new. The exam's class questions always want the same four parts: private fields, a constructor, getters and setters, and a method that does the work.

public class Student {    private String name;    private double cgpa;    public Student(String name, double cgpa) {        this.name = name;        this.cgpa = cgpa;    }    public String getName() { return name; }    public void setCgpa(double cgpa) {        if (cgpa >= 0 && cgpa <= 5) this.cgpa = cgpa;    }    public String classify() {        if (cgpa >= 4.5) return "First Class";        if (cgpa >= 3.5) return "Second Upper";        return "Lower";    }    public static void main(String[] args) {        Student s = new Student("Ada", 4.6);        System.out.println(s.getName() + ": " + s.classify());        s.setCgpa(9.9);        System.out.println("after a bad set: " + s.classify());    }}
OutputAda: First Class
after a bad set: First Class
frames.ask: Read this and say what the constructor is for, and why the fields are private.

frames.check: It sets the fields at creation; private fields force changes through a setter that can check them.
frames.teach:
The constructor sets the fields when the object is created, and it has the class's name and no return type. The fields are private so nothing outside can set a CGPA of 9.9: the setter refused it, which is why the classification did not change.

That is encapsulation: data hidden behind methods that can validate it. Say the word AND the reason in the exam.
frames.ask: What is this. for, in this.name = name?

frames.check: It separates the field from the parameter of the same name.
frames.teach:
this is the object the method was called on, so this.name is the FIELD and name alone is the PARAMETER. Without it the parameter would simply assign to itself and the field would stay empty.

class Vehicle {    protected int speed;    public Vehicle(int speed) { this.speed = speed; }    public void display() { System.out.println("Vehicle at " + speed); }}class Car extends Vehicle {    private int doors;    public Car(int speed, int doors) {        super(speed);        this.doors = doors;    }    @Override    public void display() { System.out.println("Car at " + speed + " with " + doors + " doors"); }}public class Ride {    public static void main(String[] args) {        Vehicle[] fleet = { new Vehicle(80), new Car(120, 4) };        for (Vehicle v : fleet) v.display();    }}
OutputVehicle at 80
Car at 120 with 4 doors
frames.ask: Now inheritance. What does extends give the subclass, and what does super do?

frames.check: extends inherits everything; super() calls the parent constructor first.
frames.teach:
extends gives the subclass every field and method of the superclass, and super(speed) calls the parent constructor, which must be the first line of the child's constructor.

Now look at what the loop did: both objects are held in a Vehicle array, but each printed its OWN version of display.
frames.ask: What is that called, and when does Java decide which display to run?

frames.check: Polymorphism, decided at run time by the actual object.
frames.teach:
Polymorphism, and the decision is made at RUN TIME, from the actual object rather than the declared type. That is dynamic method dispatch, and it is the sentence the 25 mark question is marked on.

The method in the child is an override: same name, same parameters, same return type. @Override is optional but it makes the compiler check you.
frames.ask: Overriding against overloading, three differences. Say them before you read on.

frames.check: Different parameters against identical ones, same class against subclass, compile time against run time.
frames.teach:
Overloading: same name, DIFFERENT parameter lists, in the SAME class, resolved at COMPILE time. Overriding: same name and same parameters, in a SUBCLASS, resolved at RUN time. Overloading is about convenience; overriding is about replacing behaviour.

That is 25/26's three mark question, and it is three lines if you learn the pairs: where, what differs, when it is resolved.

blocks.big: "Private fields, a constructor that sets them, getters and setters, and a method that does the work. That is encapsulation, and it is worth marks before the logic is even read."
blocks.sub: Overriding replaces a superclass method, same signature, in a subclass. Overloading is same name, different parameters, in one class. super() calls the parent constructor and must come first.

blocks.tag: for a reader who has never read the course

frames.teach:
Start with the trap, because it costs whole questions.

public class Compare {    public static void main(String[] args) {        String a = "java";        String b = "java";        String c = new String("java");        System.out.println(a == b);        System.out.println(a == c);        System.out.println(a.equals(c));    }}
Outputtrue
false
true
frames.ask: Both pairs hold the same characters. Do you expect both comparisons to be true?

frames.teach:
true, false, true. == asks whether they are the same OBJECT; equals asks whether they hold the same characters. The literals share one pooled object, so == happened to be true; the moment new is used it is false.

So: always compare strings with equals, and with equalsIgnoreCase when case does not matter.

public class Immutable {    public static void main(String[] args) {        String s = "java";        s.toUpperCase();        System.out.println(s);        s = s.toUpperCase();        System.out.println(s);    }}
Outputjava
JAVA
frames.ask: Now immutability. What does this print, and why?

frames.check: java then JAVA: the first call was thrown away.
frames.teach: java, then JAVA. A String cannot be changed in place, so every method returns a NEW string and leaves the original alone. Calling a method without assigning the result changes nothing.
frames.ask: Which methods are worth memorising for the exam?

frames.teach:
The eight that appear: length(), charAt(i), substring(a, b), indexOf(x), equals, toUpperCase, trim(), split(sep). Note length() is a METHOD on a String but length is a FIELD on an array, with no brackets, which is asked directly.

public class Build {    public static void main(String[] args) {        StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder();        for (int i = 1; i <= 5; i++) sb.append(i).append(",");        sb.setLength(sb.length() - 1);        System.out.println(sb.toString());        System.out.println(sb.reverse());    }}
Output1,2,3,4,5
5,4,3,2,1
frames.ask: Last: why does building a long string inside a loop with + get slow?

frames.check: Every + creates a new String, so the work grows with the length.
frames.teach: Because each + builds a whole new String and throws the old one away, so a loop of n appends copies the text n times. StringBuilder is mutable: append, insert, reverse and setLength all change the one object, and toString hands you the finished String.

blocks.big: "== compares references. equals compares characters. For strings, always equals."
blocks.sub: A String cannot be changed, only rebuilt, so every method returns a new one. Use StringBuilder when you are building in a loop.

blocks.answer:
Q1 c · find the errors · 5 MARKS

Read the output first. "141.0" tells you the sum is a double before you have read a line of code. That single character finds two of the five errors.

Code · the paper's snippet, with every error marked · AS PRINTED
import javax.swing.JOptionPane;public class Snippet {public static void main(String[] args) {int[] arr = {24.0, 40.0, 66.0, 80.0, 98.0};        // ERROR 1 and 2  int sum = 0;                                     // ERROR 2  int matches = 0;  boolean stop = false;  for (int i = 0; i <= arr.length && !stop; i++) {   // ERROR 3      for (int j = i; j < arr.length; j++) {          if (arr[j] % 4 == 0) {                     // ERROR 4              continue;          }          sum += arr[j] - j;                        // ERROR 5          matches++;          if (matches == 3) {              stop = true;          }          break;      }  }  JOptionPane.showMessageDialog(null, "Sum: " + sum);  JOptionPane.showMessageDialog(null, "Matches: " + matches);  System.exit(0);}}
Worked example · The five errors, and why each is one
  1. Line 4: int[] cannot hold 24.0. Those are double literals. This is a compile error: "incompatible types: possible lossy conversion from double to int". Fix: double[] arr. The output confirms it: 141.0 is a double.
  2. Line 5: int sum cannot total doubles, and could never print "141.0". Fix: double sum = 0; Unit 3.3: the type decides what you may do and how it prints.
  3. Line 8: i <= arr.length is off by one. Indexes run 0 to length-1 (F.10). Fix: i < arr.length. Here it would not actually throw, because the inner loop never runs when i = 5, but it is still wrong and it is one of the five marks.
  4. Lines 10 to 12: the continue is inverted. The spec says find numbers that are multiples of 4. This skips them and processes everything else: precisely backwards. Fix: if (arr[j] % 4 != 0) continue; Unit 4.7: read every continue as "unless". This is the error worth the most attention, because it is the one that is pure logic.
  5. Line 13: arr[j] - j subtracts the index. The spec says add (that number - 1). Fix: sum += arr[j] - 1; A subtle one: with j it would give the right answer for j = 1 only, so a spot check could miss it.
Code · corrected, and it reproduces the paper's answer · VERIFIED ON THE JVM
// JOptionPane replaced by println so the output can be printed here;// in the exam, keep the dialogs exactly as the paper has them.public class Q1C {    public static void main(String[] args) {        double[] arr = {24.0, 40.0, 66.0, 80.0, 98.0};   // fix 1        double sum = 0;                                 // fix 2        int matches = 0;        boolean stop = false;        for (int i = 0; i < arr.length && !stop; i++) {  // fix 3            for (int j = i; j < arr.length; j++) {                if (arr[j] % 4 != 0) {                   // fix 4                    continue;                }                sum += arr[j] - 1;                      // fix 5                matches++;                if (matches == 3) {                    stop = true;                }                break;            }        }        System.out.println("Sum: " + sum);        System.out.println("Matches: " + matches);    }}
OutputSum: 141.0
Matches: 3

That is the proof. The paper printed Sum: 141.0 and Matches: 3, and the corrected program produces exactly that. If your five fixes do not reproduce the stated output, one of them is wrong, and the paper has handed you the means to check your own answer.

blocks.answer:
Q2 c · find the errors · 5 MARKS

The same five errors as Q1, in the same order. This is the payoff of the template.

Worked example · The five errors
  1. Line 4: int[] prices = {15.5, ...}. Decimal literals in an int array: a compile error. Fix: double[] prices. The output "202.725" says double before you read anything else.
  2. Line 5: int total = 0; cannot hold 202.725. Fix: double total = 0;
  3. Line 8: i <= prices.length is off by one. Fix: i < prices.length. Unlike Q1, this one would throw ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException at i = 6, because line 9 reads prices[i] straight away. Same error, worse consequence.
  4. Line 9: if (prices[i] > 20) continue; is inverted. The spec says skip anything under 20. This skips everything over 20, i.e. exactly the items to be discounted. Fix: if (prices[i] < 20) continue;
  5. Line 15: if (count == 5). The spec says stop once 4 have been discounted. Fix: if (count == 4). Only four of the six prices are 20 or above anyway, so with == 5 the flag never fires. The count would still be 4, and the total would still be right, which makes this the easiest error to miss: it does not change the answer, it just means the code does not do what it was asked.
Code · corrected, reproducing the paper's answer · VERIFIED ON THE JVM
public class Q2C {    public static void main(String[] args) {        double[] prices = {15.5, 42.0, 8.75, 60.0, 33.25, 90.0};  // fix 1        double total = 0;                                        // fix 2        int count = 0;        boolean done = false;        for (int i = 0; i < prices.length && !done; i++) {         // fix 3            if (prices[i] < 20) {                                 // fix 4                continue;            }            double discount = prices[i] * 0.1;            total += prices[i] - discount;            count++;            if (count == 4) {                                     // fix 5                done = true;            }        }        System.out.println("Total: " + total);        System.out.println("Count: " + count);    }}
OutputTotal: 202.725
Count: 4

Matches the paper exactly.

Q3 a · consecutive duplicates in a sales log · 12 MARKS
Index0123456789
Amount20203540404015606025

Write a program that (i) counts, in one pass, the indices i >= 1 where the amount equals the one before it; (ii) returns a single String listing, in order and comma separated, every amount that equals its predecessor or its successor, built with plain String concatenation only; (iii) displays both in one JOptionPane dialog. The paper adds a hint: it must not flag 35, 15, or 25.

Must memorise · Parts i and ii count DIFFERENT things

Part i counts positions. Part ii lists values. They are not the same question asked twice, and they do not give the same number.

Part i asks how many boundaries have a twin across them. Part ii asks which elements are touching a twin at all.

Look at the three 40s. They contain two boundaries (index 3 to 4, and 4 to 5) but three elements. So part i counts 2 there and part ii lists 3. Read the two parts as one question and you will answer one of them wrong.

MEMORY HOOK: fences and posts. Part i counts the fences between posts, part ii counts the posts. A run of n twins has n posts and n-1 fences, always.

Code · question three, part a · VERIFIED ON THE JVM
public class SalesDuplicates {    // Part i: ONE pass. Count every index i >= 1 whose amount equals the one before.    static int countConsecutiveDuplicates(int[] sales) {        int count = 0;        for (int i = 1; i < sales.length; i++) {            if (sales[i] == sales[i - 1]) {                count++;            }        }        return count;    }    // Part ii: every amount equal to its predecessor OR its successor, in order,    // comma separated, built with plain String concatenation only.    static String flaggedAmounts(int[] sales) {        String result = "";        for (int i = 0; i < sales.length; i++) {            boolean sameAsPrevious = (i > 0) && (sales[i] == sales[i - 1]);            boolean sameAsNext = (i < sales.length - 1) && (sales[i] == sales[i + 1]);            if (sameAsPrevious || sameAsNext) {                if (result.equals("")) {                    result = "" + sales[i];                } else {                    result = result + ", " + sales[i];                }            }        }        return result;    }    // Part iii: one dialog showing both answers.    public static void main(String[] args) {        int[] saleAmounts = {20, 20, 35, 40, 40, 40, 15, 60, 60, 25};        int duplicates = countConsecutiveDuplicates(saleAmounts);        String flagged = flaggedAmounts(saleAmounts);        String message = "Consecutive duplicate count: " + duplicates                       + "\nFlagged amounts: " + flagged;        System.out.println(message);    }}
OutputConsecutive duplicate count: 4
Flagged amounts: 20, 20, 40, 40, 40, 60, 60

Exactly the hand trace, including the three amounts the paper told us not to flag. The dialog is a println here so its text can be printed in this book; in the hall, write JOptionPane.showMessageDialog(null, message); and import javax.swing.JOptionPane (F.11).

Trap · Three ways to lose marks on part A

1. Starting part i's loop at 0. The question says i >= 1, and for a reason: sales[0 - 1] is sales[-1], which throws ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException (Unit 8.1). Index 0 has no predecessor, so the loop starts at 1. This is where "one pass" is easiest to get right and easiest to throw away.

2. Forgetting the boundary guards in part ii. Index 0 has no predecessor and the last index has no successor. The guards (i > 0) and (i < sales.length - 1) are what stop the reads from running off either end. They work because && is short-circuit (Unit 3.6): when i > 0 is false, Java never evaluates sales[i - 1], so it never throws. Swap the two sides of the && and the program crashes on the first element.

3. The leading comma. Concatenating ", " + sales[i] every time gives , 20, 20, 40... with a comma stuck on the front. The test if (result.equals("")) writes the first value bare and every later value with its separator in front. Compare Strings with .equals(), never with == (Unit 7.3).

The question bans StringBuilder deliberately: it wants to see that you can handle the separator yourself. Use StringBuilder anyway and you have answered a question the paper did not ask.

(13 marks)B. A cold-storage warehouse records its internal temperature once every hour, for 24 hours. Write a program, using JOptionPane only for input/output, that checks the day's temperature log for sustained breaches of a safe limit. A reading is a breach if it is above 8°C.

i.    Using a loop, prompt the user 24 times (one dialog per hour) for that hour's temperature. Each input must be validated: it must parse as a number between -20 and 50 inclusive. If invalid, re-prompt for the same hour (using a nested loop/control statement) until a valid value is entered. Store all 24 valid readings in a 1-D array.

ii.   Scan the 24-hour array once to find every maximal run of consecutive breach-hours (temperature > 8°C). Using only loops and conditionals (no extra arrays), determine:

•  the total number of qualifying streaks, where a qualifying streak is any consecutive run of 3 or more breach-hours;

•  the length (in hours) of the single longest breach streak anywhere in the log.

iii.  Using nested if-else logic, classify the day as exactly one of:

•  "CRITICAL": longest streak >= 6 hours

•  "WARNING": longest streak is 3-5 hours (inclusive)

•  "SAFE": no streak of 3 or more consecutive breach-hours occurred

iv.  Show one JOptionPane dialog stating: the total number of qualifying streaks, the longest streak length, and the final classification.

blocks.answer:
Q5 b · sustained breaches of a safe limit · 13 MARKS
  1. prompt 24 times, one dialog per hour. Each input must parse as a number between -20 and 50 inclusive; if invalid, re-prompt for the same hour using a nested loop, until valid. Store all 24 in a 1-D array;
  2. scan the array once, using only loops and conditionals (no extra arrays), to find the number of qualifying streaks (runs of 3 or more consecutive breach-hours) and the length of the longest breach streak;
  3. using nested if-else, classify: CRITICAL if the longest streak is >= 6, WARNING if it is 3 to 5, SAFE if no streak of 3 or more occurred;
  4. show one dialog with the streak count, the longest length, and the classification.
Must memorise · Count the run when it turns 3, and measure it as you go

The whole of part 2 is three variables and one pass:

currentRun: breach hours in a row right now, reset to 0 on any non-breach.
longestStreak: updated every breach hour, not at the end of a run.
qualifyingStreaks: incremented when currentRun == 3, exactly.

Why == 3 and not >= 3. A run passes through 3 exactly once, on its third hour. So == 3 counts each qualifying run once, however long it becomes. Use >= 3 and a 6-hour run is counted four times, giving 4 streaks where there is one.

MEMORY HOOK: a run is counted at the moment it qualifies, not while it continues. The threshold is a door you pass through once, not a room you stay in.

Trap · The streak that is still running when the day ends

The instinct is to close each run in the else, where the non-breach hour is: "the run just ended, so now measure it."

if (readings[hour] > 8) {    currentRun++;} else {    if (currentRun > longestStreak) longestStreak = currentRun;  // non-breach only    if (currentRun >= 3) qualifyingStreaks++;    currentRun = 0;}

It works, until the day ends mid-streak. If hours 18 to 23 are all breaches, the loop finishes with currentRun = 6 and never reaches the else. The longest streak of the day is never measured and never counted. The program reports SAFE on a day the freezer was over temperature for six straight hours.

The fix is not to bolt a copy of the else-block on after the loop. That is the usual patch and it duplicates the logic in two places, so the next edit changes one and forgets the other. Instead, update on every breach hour:

Measure longestStreak as the run grows, and count the run the instant it turns 3. Then a run that is still going when the array ends has already been measured and already been counted, and the end of the array needs no special case at all.

This is worth more than one exam question. A boundary you never treat specially cannot be got wrong at the boundary.

Code · question five, part b · VERIFIED ON THE JVM
import java.util.Scanner;public class ColdStorage {    public static void main(String[] args) {        Scanner in = new Scanner(System.in);        double[] readings = new double[24];        // Part i: 24 prompts, each re-prompted until the value is valid.        for (int hour = 0; hour < 24; hour++) {            boolean valid = false;            while (!valid) {                String typed = in.nextLine();                try {                    double t = Double.parseDouble(typed);                    if (t >= -20 && t <= 50) {                        readings[hour] = t;                        valid = true;                    } else {                        System.out.println("  hour " + hour + ": " + t                            + " is outside -20 to 50. Asking again.");                    }                } catch (NumberFormatException e) {                    System.out.println("  hour " + hour + ": \"" + typed                        + "\" is not a number. Asking again.");                }            }        }        // Part ii: ONE scan, no extra arrays.        int currentRun = 0, longestStreak = 0, qualifyingStreaks = 0;        for (int hour = 0; hour < 24; hour++) {            if (readings[hour] > 8) {                currentRun++;                if (currentRun > longestStreak) {                    longestStreak = currentRun;                }                if (currentRun == 3) {                    qualifyingStreaks++;                }            } else {                currentRun = 0;            }        }        // Part iii: classify.        String classification;        if (longestStreak >= 6) {            classification = "CRITICAL";        } else if (longestStreak >= 3) {            classification = "WARNING";        } else {            classification = "SAFE";        }        // Part iv: one dialog.        String message = "Qualifying streaks (3+ hours): " + qualifyingStreaks                       + "\nLongest breach streak: " + longestStreak + " hour(s)"                       + "\nClassification: " + classification;        System.out.println(message);    }}
Output  hour 0: 99.0 is outside -20 to 50. Asking again.
  hour 0: "abc" is not a number. Asking again.
Qualifying streaks (3+ hours): 3
Longest breach streak: 6 hour(s)
Classification: CRITICAL

The run fed hour 0 a 99, then the text "abc", then a valid 5, so both halves of "must parse as a number between -20 and 50" are shown rejecting input and re-prompting the same hour.

Dry run · The 24 hours, and where the three streaks are
breach = above 8. The bar shows breach hours.
hoursreadingsbreach runcounted?
0 to 35, 9, 10, 42 in a rowno: under 3
4 to 79, 9, 9, 23 in a rowyes, streak 1
8 to 1312, 11, 9, 9, 10, 35 in a rowyes, streak 2
14 to 171, 2, 3, 4noneno
18 to 239, 9, 9, 9, 9, 96 in a row, to the last houryes, streak 3
Answerslongest = 63 streaks, CRITICAL

The first run of 2 is the control: it proves the counter is not simply counting runs. The last run is the trap above, live: it reaches hour 23 and stops because the day stopped, not because the temperature did. It is both the longest streak and the one that decides the classification, and the else-branch version would have missed it entirely and printed WARNING.

(13 marks)B. A university parking garage needs a program, using JOptionPane only for input/output, to process a batch of vehicles exiting on the same day and calculate the total fees owed. The program must use clear separation of concerns; each task below must be its own method. No collection classes (e.g. ArrayList) are allowed anywhere.

i.    Prompt for the number of exiting vehicles, V. Then, using a loop, fill two parallel arrays of length V:

•  the number of hours each vehicle was parked (an integer per vehicle). A value <= 0 is invalid; use a nested control statement to keep re-prompting until a valid value is entered.

•  the permit type for each vehicle (a String per vehicle, either "Staff" or "Visitor").

ii.   Create a method that takes in one vehicle's hours parked and permit type, and computes one vehicle's fee using nested if-else logic (the rules below must be nested together, not checked as separate independent conditions):

•  Staff: first 2 hours free; each additional hour costs 1.00; capped at a maximum of 10.00/day.

•  Visitor: no free period; first 3 hours cost a flat 6.00; each hour beyond 3 costs 2.50; capped at a maximum of 25.00/day.

•  Any permit type that is not exactly "Staff" must be treated as "Visitor".

iii.  Create a method that takes in the array of hours parked, loops over the array and tallies vehicles into three categories: SHORT-STAY (1-2 hrs), STANDARD (3-6 hrs), EXTENDED (>6 hrs). Return these three counts without using any collection class.

iv.  In main(),

•  call the method from part (ii) for every vehicle across both parallel arrays to accumulate the batch's total revenue

•  call the method from part (iii) once

•  display one final JOptionPane showing the total revenue and the three category counts.

blocks.answer:
Q6 b · parking fees for a batch of vehicles · 13 MARKS
  1. prompt for the number of vehicles V, then fill two parallel arrays of length V: hours parked (int per vehicle; a value <= 0 is invalid, so use a nested control statement to re-prompt until valid) and permit type (String per vehicle, "Staff" or "Visitor");
  2. a method taking one vehicle's hours and permit, computing its fee with nested if-else: Staff, first 2 hours free, each additional hour 1.00, capped at 10.00/day; Visitor, no free period, first 3 hours a flat 6.00, each hour beyond 3 costs 2.50, capped at 25.00/day; and any permit that is not exactly "Staff" is treated as Visitor;
  3. a method taking the hours array, tallying SHORT-STAY (1-2), STANDARD (3-6) and EXTENDED (>6), returning the three counts without any collection class;
  4. main(): call (ii) for every vehicle across both arrays to accumulate revenue, call (iii) once, and display one dialog with the total and the three counts.
Must memorise · Three counts, one return, no collections

Part 3 asks for three numbers back. A Java method returns one value. And ArrayList is banned.

So return an int[] of length 3.

An array is not a collection class. That distinction is the question: "collection classes (e.g. ArrayList)" means java.util's List/Set/Map family. An array is a built-in Java type, not a class you import, which is why F.10 and Module 8 exist and why the ban costs you nothing.

Document the slots in a comment ([0] short, [1] standard, [2] extended) and use them in that order. The alternative the ban is steering you away from is three separate fields or three methods walking the same array three times.

MEMORY HOOK: one return value, several numbers, no collections: that is an array.

Teach · Parallel arrays, and the invariant that keeps them honest

Two arrays are parallel when index i in one and index i in the other describe the same thing. hoursParked[3] and permitType[3] are one car.

The whole idea rests on one invariant: they are the same length and they are always written together. The loop in part 1 fills both in the same iteration, which is what keeps them aligned. Fill them in two separate loops, or continue past one but not the other, and vehicle 3's hours are paired with vehicle 4's permit. Nothing throws. Every fee is simply wrong.

In Module 6's terms this is what a class is for: a Vehicle object holding hours and permit together cannot fall out of step, because there is no "step" to fall out of. The paper asks for parallel arrays, so write parallel arrays; but knowing what they are the poor relation of is what Q4 was testing.

Code · question six, part b · VERIFIED ON THE JVM
import java.util.Scanner;public class ParkingGarage {    // Part ii: one vehicle's fee, by NESTED if-else. The permit decides the branch;    // the hours are only examined inside it.    static double feeFor(int hours, String permit) {        double fee;        if (permit.equals("Staff")) {            if (hours <= 2) {                fee = 0.0;            } else {                fee = (hours - 2) * 1.00;                if (fee > 10.00) {                    fee = 10.00;                }            }        } else {            if (hours <= 3) {                fee = 6.00;            } else {                fee = 6.00 + (hours - 3) * 2.50;                if (fee > 25.00) {                    fee = 25.00;                }            }        }        return fee;    }    // Part iii: tally the three categories. Three counts, one return value, and no    // collection class: an int[] of length 3. An array is not a collection.    // [0] SHORT-STAY (1-2), [1] STANDARD (3-6), [2] EXTENDED (>6)    static int[] tally(int[] hoursParked) {        int[] counts = new int[3];        for (int i = 0; i < hoursParked.length; i++) {            if (hoursParked[i] <= 2) {                counts[0]++;            } else if (hoursParked[i] <= 6) {                counts[1]++;            } else {                counts[2]++;            }        }        return counts;    }    public static void main(String[] args) {        Scanner in = new Scanner(System.in);        int vehicles = Integer.parseInt(in.nextLine());        // Part i: two PARALLEL arrays. Index i is one vehicle in both.        int[] hoursParked = new int[vehicles];        String[] permitType = new String[vehicles];        for (int i = 0; i < vehicles; i++) {            int hours = Integer.parseInt(in.nextLine());            while (hours <= 0) {                System.out.println("  vehicle " + i + ": " + hours                    + " is not a valid number of hours. Asking again.");                hours = Integer.parseInt(in.nextLine());            }            hoursParked[i] = hours;            permitType[i] = in.nextLine();        }        // Part iv: accumulate revenue across both arrays, then tally once.        double totalRevenue = 0;        for (int i = 0; i < vehicles; i++) {            double fee = feeFor(hoursParked[i], permitType[i]);            totalRevenue += fee;            System.out.println("Vehicle " + i + ": " + hoursParked[i] + "h, "                + permitType[i] + " -> " + fee);        }        int[] counts = tally(hoursParked);        String message = "Total revenue: " + totalRevenue                       + "\nSHORT-STAY (1-2 hrs): " + counts[0]                       + "\nSTANDARD (3-6 hrs): " + counts[1]                       + "\nEXTENDED (>6 hrs): " + counts[2];        System.out.println(message);    }}
Output  vehicle 0: 0 is not a valid number of hours. Asking again.
Vehicle 0: 2h, Staff -> 0.0
Vehicle 1: 5h, Staff -> 3.0
Vehicle 2: 15h, Staff -> 10.0
Vehicle 3: 1h, Visitor -> 6.0
Vehicle 4: 5h, Visitor -> 11.0
Vehicle 5: 12h, Guest -> 25.0
Total revenue: 55.0
SHORT-STAY (1-2 hrs): 2
STANDARD (3-6 hrs): 2
EXTENDED (>6 hrs): 2
Dry run · Every rule in the fee table, fired once
hourspermitwhich rule, and the arithmeticfee
2Stafffirst 2 hours free, and 2 is not beyond 20.00
5Staff(5 - 2) × 1.00 = 3.00, under the 10.00 cap3.00
15Staff(15 - 2) × 1.00 = 13.00, over the cap10.00
1Visitorflat 6.00 for the first 3 hours, even for 16.00
5Visitor6.00 + (5 - 3) × 2.50 = 11.0011.00
12Guestnot exactly "Staff", so Visitor: 6.00 + 9 × 2.50 = 28.50, over the cap25.00
Total revenue55.00

Every rule in the question fires exactly once in that table, which is how the test data was chosen: both free periods, both per-hour rates, both caps, and the not-Staff-means-Visitor rule. When you invent your own test data, invent it like this: one row per rule, so a single run proves the lot.

Two rows repay a second look. 1 hour as a Visitor costs 6.00: "first 3 hours cost a flat 6.00" is a flat fee, not a rate, so an hour and three hours cost the same, and a Visitor pays more than a Staff member who stayed fifteen. That is not a bug, it is the pricing the question specifies. And Guest at 12 hours is the only row testing the fallback rule; delete it from your test data and a program that crashes on unknown permits would look perfectly healthy.

Must memorise · A cap is a ceiling you apply after, not a rule you fold in

Compute the fee, then clamp it:

fee = 6.00 + (hours - 3) * 2.50;
if (fee > 25.00) { fee = 25.00; }

The temptation is to work out the hour at which the cap bites (for Visitors, 10.6 hours) and branch on that. It gives the same answers and it is a worse answer: you have hidden a magic number that no line of the question contains, and changing the rate to 3.00 silently breaks it, because the crossover moves and your constant does not.

This is the same shape as Q5 A's price floor, which is a cap from below. Both read as one line placed after the sum, and both then say plainly what the question said: capped at a maximum of 25.00/day.

MEMORY HOOK: compute, then clamp. Never solve for where the clamp starts.

blocks.answer:
Q2 a · define dynamic array initialisation, length, and the out of bounds exception · 3 MARKS

Model answer.

  1. Dynamic array initialisation. Creating the array with new and a size decided while the program runs, rather than from a literal list written in the source: int[] a = new int[n]; where n is only known at run time. Every element starts at its default (0 for int, null for objects), and the values are filled in afterwards. Contrast static initialisation, int[] a = {2, 4, 6, 8};, where the size and the values are both fixed in the source.
  2. The length property. a.length gives the number of elements. It is a field, not a method, so there are no brackets: writing a.length() is a compile error. It is final: an array's length is fixed the moment it is created and can never change. A String's length IS a method, s.length(). The examiner knows that catches people; Unit 7.2.
  3. The out-of-bounds exception. ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException, thrown at run time when you use an index below 0 or at or above length. Valid indexes are 0 to length - 1, so a[a.length] always throws. It is unchecked, so the compiler will not warn you about it.

Where the marks are: "length is a field, not a method" and "indexes are 0 to length-1" are the two facts every other part of this question depends on. F.10 and Unit 8.1.

blocks.answer:
Q2 b · debug copyarray · 3 MARKS
Compiler outputerror: not a statement

The errors, listed.

  1. int b; is not an array. It is a single int, and it is never given a value. System.arraycopy needs a destination array that already exists and has room: it copies into an array, it does not create one. Fix: int[] b = new int[a.length]; This is Q2 A part 1 being examined: dynamic initialisation, sized from a.length.
  2. System.arrayCopy has a capital C. The method is System.arraycopy, all lower case. Java is case sensitive, so this is not a typo the compiler forgives: it is a method that does not exist.
  3. i <= b.length is off by one. The last index is length - 1, so this reads b[4] on an array of 4 and throws ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException. Fix: i < b.length. Q2 A part 3, being examined.
  4. i is not an increment. The third slot of the for needs i++. As written it is not even a statement, which is the error javac reports first. Without it the loop would never end.

Notice what this question is. Its three errors are its own part A, in order: dynamic initialisation, the length property, the out-of-bounds exception. Part A is not a warm-up, it is the answer key to part B.

Code · q2 b corrected · VERIFIED ON THE JVM
public class CopyArray {    public static void main(String[] args) {        int[] a = {2, 4, 6, 8};        int[] b = new int[a.length];        System.arraycopy(a, 0, b, 0, a.length);        for (int i = 0; i < b.length; i++) {            System.out.println(b[i]);        }    }}
Output2
4
6
8

System.arraycopy(a, 0, b, 0, a.length) reads: from a starting at 0, into b starting at 0, a.length elements. Source, source position, destination, destination position, count. Unit 8.3.

Q2 d · ten values, evens, odd sum, and the maximum · 7.5 MARKS

Read the verbs: find, count, display is three things, and the even method must do all three. And the maximum must be found in main with a for loop, not in a third method: the question says where to put it.

Code · q2 d, complete · VERIFIED ON THE JVM
import java.util.Scanner;public class ArrayStats {    // ii a. find, count and display the even numbers    public static void evens(int[] values) {        int count = 0;        String found = "";        for (int i = 0; i < values.length; i++) {            if (values[i] % 2 == 0) {                count++;                found = found.equals("") ? "" + values[i] : found + ", " + values[i];            }        }        System.out.println("Even numbers: " + found);        System.out.println("How many even: " + count);    }    // ii b. sum and display the odd numbers    public static void odds(int[] values) {        int sum = 0;        for (int i = 0; i < values.length; i++) {            if (values[i] % 2 != 0) {                sum += values[i];            }        }        System.out.println("Sum of the odd numbers: " + sum);    }    public static void main(String[] args) {        Scanner in = new Scanner(System.in);        // i. prompt for 10 values        int[] values = new int[10];        for (int i = 0; i < values.length; i++) {            values[i] = Integer.parseInt(in.nextLine());        }        evens(values);        odds(values);        // iii. a for loop in main to find and display the maximum        int max = values[0];        for (int i = 1; i < values.length; i++) {            if (values[i] > max) {                max = values[i];            }        }        System.out.println("Maximum: " + max);    }}
OutputEven numbers: 4, 12, 0, -8, 6
How many even: 5
Sum of the odd numbers: 39
Maximum: 15

Input is a Scanner here so the run can be printed. The ten values fed in were 4, 7, -3, 12, 9, 0, 15, -8, 6, 11.

Must memorise · Test for odd with != 0, never == 1

if (v % 2 != 0)   is odd. Always.

if (v % 2 == 1)   is odd only for positives, and silently wrong for negatives.

In Java, % keeps the sign of the left operand, so -3 % 2 is -1, not 1. So -3 % 2 == 1 is false and the == 1 test declares -3 even.

The test data above proves it. The odd numbers are 7, -3, 9, 15 and 11, and they sum to 39. Had the method used == 1, it would have skipped -3 and printed 42: a wrong answer, from a program that runs cleanly and looks right. That is why the ten values include a negative odd number, and why yours should too. Unit 3.6 and Unit 8.4.

MEMORY HOOK: "not even" is safe; "equals one" is not.

Teach · Priming the maximum: why not start at 0

The maximum loop starts int max = values[0]; and then runs from i = 1. The tempting alternative is int max = 0;, and it is a bug waiting for the right data.

If every value is negative, max = 0 never gets replaced and the program reports a maximum of 0, a number that is not in the array. Priming with values[0] cannot do that: the answer starts as a real element and only ever moves to another real element.

The same reasoning as Unit 8.4's minimum, and the same reasoning that makes Integer.MIN_VALUE the other correct prime. Starting at 0 is correct only if you know the data contains a non-negative number, and "I know my data" is how bugs are born.

public class CountNegatives {    // Q5 B: the method the question asks for, and nothing else.    public static int countNegatives(int[] numbers) {        int count = 0;        for (int i = 0; i < numbers.length; i++) {            if (numbers[i] < 0) {                count++;            }        }        return count;    }    // main is not part of the answer; it is here so the method can be run.    public static void main(String[] args) {        int[] a = {3, -1, 0, -7, 8, -2};        int[] b = {1, 2, 3};        int[] c = {};        System.out.println("{3, -1, 0, -7, 8, -2} -> " + countNegatives(a));        System.out.println("{1, 2, 3}             -> " + countNegatives(b));        System.out.println("{} (empty)            -> " + countNegatives(c));    }}
Output{3, -1, 0, -7, 8, -2} -> 3
{1, 2, 3}             -> 0
{} (empty)            -> 0

Only countNegatives is the answer; main is here so the method can be run. Zero is not negative, which is why the first array has a 0 in it and the count is 3, not 4: the test is < 0, never <= 0. And the empty array returns 0 without any special case, since the loop simply never runs.

frames.teach:
An array is a fixed length row of values of one type. Three steps: declare, create with a size, then fill.

public class Walk {    public static void main(String[] args) {        int[] nums = new int[5];        for (int i = 0; i < nums.length; i++) nums[i] = (i + 1) * 10;        int[] given = {4, -2, 7, -9, 3};        System.out.println(nums.length + " " + nums[nums.length - 1]);        try {            System.out.println(given[5]);        } catch (ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException e) {            System.out.println("caught: " + e.getMessage());        }    }}
Output5 50
caught: Index 5 out of bounds for length 5
frames.ask: What is the highest index of an array created with new int[5], and what happens if you use 5?

frames.teach:
The highest index is 4, and index 5 throws ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException, which 24/25 asks you to define by name. The loop condition is therefore i < nums.length, never <=.

length is a field on an array, with no brackets, unlike a String's length().
frames.ask: Now the patterns. Write, in your head, a method that returns the total of an array.

frames.check: A running total set to zero before the loop, added to inside it, returned after it.
frames.teach:
Here are the four the exam wants, each as a method that returns, which is exactly how the papers word it.

public class Patterns {    static int total(int[] a) {        int sum = 0;        for (int x : a) sum += x;        return sum;    }    static int countNegatives(int[] a) {        int count = 0;        for (int x : a) if (x < 0) count++;        return count;    }    static int largest(int[] a) {        int best = a[0];        for (int x : a) if (x > best) best = x;        return best;    }    static int consecutiveDuplicates(int[] a) {        int pairs = 0;        for (int i = 1; i < a.length; i++) if (a[i] == a[i - 1]) pairs++;        return pairs;    }    public static void main(String[] args) {        int[] sales = {12, 12, -5, 30, 30, 30, -1};        System.out.println(total(sales));        System.out.println(countNegatives(sales));        System.out.println(largest(sales));        System.out.println(consecutiveDuplicates(sales));    }}
Output108
2
30
3
frames.ask: Read the four and predict the four printed values.

frames.teach:
108, 2, 30, 3. Notice what the fourth one does differently: it starts at i = 1 and looks BACK at a[i - 1]. Every question about repeats, streaks or rises uses that one line.

Notice too that the best so far pattern starts from a[0], not from zero: start from zero and an array of negatives returns the wrong answer.
frames.ask: A streak question asks for the LONGEST run. What two variables does that need?

frames.check: One for the run you are in, one for the longest seen.
frames.teach:
A current run and a best run: extend current when the test holds, reset it to zero or one when it breaks, and update best whenever current beats it. That is the cold storage temperature question in one sentence.

public class Grid {    public static void main(String[] args) {        int[][] marks = { {70, 65}, {40, 55}, {90, 80} };        for (int r = 0; r < marks.length; r++) {            int sum = 0;            for (int c = 0; c < marks[r].length; c++) sum += marks[r][c];            System.out.println("row " + r + " total " + sum);        }    }}
Outputrow 0 total 135
row 1 total 95
row 2 total 170
frames.ask: Last: two dimensions. How do you walk a table of rows and columns?

frames.check: Nested loops, the inner one bounded by that row's own length.
frames.teach: A loop inside a loop: the outer over marks.length, the rows, the inner over marks[r].length, that row's columns. Writing the inner bound as marks.length is a planted error, and it only shows when the table is not square.

blocks.answer:
Q6 b · what does compute(13) return? show the steps · 3 MARKS

The answer: 3. And the question says show the steps, so the table is the answer, not the number.

Dry run · compute(13), step by step
while (x > 0): count the odd steps, halve each time
xx % 2odd, so count++?x = x / 2count
131yes61
60no31
31yes12
11yes03
0x > 0 is false, so the loop ends3

What the method actually is. Repeatedly halving with x / 2 and testing x % 2 walks the number's binary digits, from the right. So compute counts the 1 bits. 13 in binary is 1101, which has three 1s, so the answer is 3, and you can check it in one second without tracing anything.

Say that in your answer after showing the table. Naming what the code is ("it counts the set bits") is what separates a trace from understanding, and it costs one line.

Code · the paper's own method, run on 13 and on friends · VERIFIED ON THE JVM
public class ComputeBits {    // exactly as the paper prints it    public static int compute(int x) {        int count = 0;        while (x > 0) {            if (x % 2 == 1) count++;            x = x / 2;        }        return count;    }    public static void main(String[] args) {        System.out.println("compute(13) = " + compute(13));        System.out.println("13 in binary is " + Integer.toBinaryString(13));        for (int v : new int[]{1, 2, 3, 7, 8, 255}) {            System.out.println("compute(" + v + ") = " + compute(v)                + "   binary " + Integer.toBinaryString(v));        }    }}
Outputcompute(13) = 3
13 in binary is 1101
compute(1) = 1   binary 1
compute(2) = 1   binary 10
compute(3) = 2   binary 11
compute(7) = 3   binary 111
compute(8) = 1   binary 1000
compute(255) = 8   binary 11111111

Every row is its own proof: the answer always equals the number of 1s printed beside it. compute(255) = 8 and 255 is eight 1s; compute(8) = 1 and 8 is 1000. The claim is not "this looks like a bit count", it is a bit count.

blocks.text: Part 2: the method behind these, taught from nothing

blocks.label: Work it frame by frame
blocks.tag: for a reader who has never read the course

frames.teach:
A recursive method calls itself on a smaller version of the problem. Two parts, always: the base case, which returns without calling itself, and the recursive case, which moves towards the base case.

public class Recurse {    static int factorial(int n) {        if (n <= 1) return 1;        return n * factorial(n - 1);    }    static int digitSum(int n) {        if (n < 10) return n;        return n % 10 + digitSum(n / 10);    }    public static void main(String[] args) {        System.out.println(factorial(5));        System.out.println(digitSum(13));    }}
Output120
4
frames.ask: Find both parts in this, then predict the two printed values.

frames.teach: 120 and 4. In factorial the base case is n <= 1; in digitSum it is n < 10, one digit left. Both recursive cases shrink the argument, which is what guarantees the base case is reached.
frames.ask: What happens if the base case is missing, or never reached?

frames.check: It recurses forever and throws StackOverflowError.
frames.teach: The calls pile up until the call stack is full and the program dies with a StackOverflowError. Naming that error is a mark, and "no base case" is a planted error in a debug question.
frames.ask: Now the trace, which is how the paper asks it. Write out digitSum(13) as calls going down and answers coming back.

frames.teach:
Two columns, and both directions matter:

Going downComing back
digitSum(13) needs 3 + digitSum(1)3 + 1 = 4
digitSum(1), and 1 is under 10returns 1

Write the table, then the answer. The marks in "show the steps" are the steps, not the number.
frames.ask: Last: recursion against iteration. One advantage each.

frames.check: Recursion is clearer for recursive definitions; iteration is faster and safer on memory.
frames.teach: Recursion is shorter and closer to the definition for problems that are naturally recursive, factorials, Fibonacci, tree walks. Iteration uses no call stack, so it is faster and cannot overflow. Any recursive method can be written as a loop, and the exam sometimes asks for both.

blocks.big: "Every recursive method needs a base case that returns without calling itself, and a recursive case that moves towards it."
blocks.sub: Trace it as a table of calls going down and answers coming back up. No base case, or one you never reach, is a StackOverflowError.

blocks.answer:
Q1 b · three differences: checked vs unchecked · 3 MARKS

Model answer. Three differences, one mark each:

  1. When they are detected. Checked exceptions are checked by the compiler at compile time; unchecked exceptions occur at run time and the compiler does not examine them.
  2. Whether you must handle them. A checked exception must be either caught in a try-catch or declared with throws, or the code will not compile. An unchecked exception carries no such obligation.
  3. What causes them. Checked exceptions represent conditions outside the program's control (a missing file, a failed network call), whereas unchecked exceptions represent programming errors (dereferencing null, a bad index, dividing by zero).

Examples (add them; they cost one line and prove the point): checked: IOException, FileNotFoundException, ClassNotFoundException. Unchecked: NullPointerException, ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException, ArithmeticException.

Where the marks are: three distinct axes. Writing "one is checked and one is not" three different ways scores one mark. See Unit 10.1.

(13 marks)B. A college admin office needs a program to record and review student details (ID, name, CGPA) using basic file I/O. Using only java.io.FileWriter, java.io.FileReader, java.io.BufferedReader, java.io.BufferedWriter, and java.io.IOException (or its subclasses), write a complete program that does the following:

i.    Create a file named input.txt and write the details (student ID, name, CGPA) of at least three students into it using FileWriter, one student per line. Wrap the writing logic in a try-catch block that handles any exception that may occur.

ii.   Read student details from a file named output.txt using FileReader and print each line to the console exactly as it appears in the file. Handle any exception that may occur while reading, including the case where output.txt does not exist.

iii.  Create a method that takes in a file name, opens the file, counts the number of lines (student records) it contains, and returns that count. This method must handle its own exceptions internally.

blocks.answer:
Q3 b · student records with basic file i/o · 13 MARKS
  1. creates input.txt and writes at least three students (ID, name, CGPA) into it with FileWriter, one per line, wrapped in try-catch;
  2. reads student details from output.txt with FileReader and prints each line exactly as it appears, handling any exception including the case where output.txt does not exist;
  3. has a method that takes a file name, counts the lines, and returns the count, handling its own exceptions internally;
  4. closes every resource, and prints a clear, specific message in every catch block.
Must memorise · It writes input.txt and reads output.txt

Part 1 writes input.txt. Part 2 reads output.txt. The program never creates output.txt.

That is not a misprint for you to tidy up. It is the question.

Read part 2 again: "handle any exception that may occur while reading, including the case where output.txt does not exist." The examiner has told you, in the question itself, that the file will be missing. The marks are for the catch block running, not for the file being read.

So do not "fix" it by reading input.txt instead. Write exactly what the paper asks, and let the catch block do its job. That is the answer.

MEMORY HOOK: the missing file is the exam. When a question names a file it never created, the catch block is the thing being marked.

Teach · The five classes, and why the list is exactly these five

The restriction looks arbitrary. It is not: the five are exactly what you need and nothing more (Unit 10.3).

ClassDirectionWhat it is for
FileWriteroutWrites characters to a file. On its own it writes one character at a time.
BufferedWriteroutWraps a FileWriter and collects characters, writing them in blocks. Also gives you newLine().
FileReaderinReads characters from a file. On its own it reads one character at a time: it has no readLine().
BufferedReaderinWraps a FileReader and gives you readLine(), which is the whole reason it is on the list.
IOException-The checked exception every one of the above can throw. You must catch it or declare it (Unit 10.1).

The pairing is the point. The question says "read using FileReader" and "one student per line". A FileReader alone cannot give you a line. So you wrap it: new BufferedReader(new FileReader(fileName)). That is why both appear on the list, and it is why the list is not padding.

And read "or its subclasses" carefully. Those three words are permission. FileNotFoundException is a subclass of IOException, so you are explicitly allowed to catch it separately, which is exactly how you answer part 2's "including the case where output.txt does not exist" with a message that says what actually happened.

Trap · Catch the child before the parent, or it will not compile

When you catch both, the subclass must come first. Java tries catch blocks top to bottom and takes the first that fits. Put IOException first and it swallows everything, leaving the FileNotFoundException block unreachable. Java does not let that pass:

import java.io.BufferedReader;import java.io.FileNotFoundException;import java.io.FileReader;import java.io.IOException;public class CatchOrder {    public static void main(String[] args) {        try (BufferedReader in = new BufferedReader(new FileReader("any.txt"))) {            System.out.println(in.readLine());        } catch (IOException e) {            System.out.println("the parent is caught first");        } catch (FileNotFoundException e) {            System.out.println("this line can never run");        }    }}
Compiler outputerror: exception FileNotFoundException has already been caught

This is one of Java's friendlier errors: it refuses to compile code containing a block that could never run. Reverse the two catch blocks and it compiles. Specific first, general last, every time.

Code · question three, part b · VERIFIED ON THE JVM
import java.io.BufferedReader;import java.io.BufferedWriter;import java.io.FileNotFoundException;import java.io.FileReader;import java.io.FileWriter;import java.io.IOException;public class StudentRecords {    // Part i: create input.txt and write three student records, one per line.    static void writeStudents(String fileName) {        try (BufferedWriter out = new BufferedWriter(new FileWriter(fileName))) {            out.write("STU001, Ada Bello, 4.51");            out.newLine();            out.write("STU002, Femi Okonkwo, 3.78");            out.newLine();            out.write("STU003, Ngozi Eze, 4.92");            out.newLine();            System.out.println("Wrote 3 student records to " + fileName);        } catch (IOException e) {            System.out.println("Could not write to " + fileName + ": "                + e.getMessage());        }    }    // Part ii: read a file and print every line exactly as it appears.    static void printStudents(String fileName) {        try (BufferedReader in = new BufferedReader(new FileReader(fileName))) {            String line = in.readLine();            while (line != null) {                System.out.println(line);                line = in.readLine();            }        } catch (FileNotFoundException e) {            System.out.println("Cannot read " + fileName                + ": the file does not exist.");        } catch (IOException e) {            System.out.println("Error while reading " + fileName + ": "                + e.getMessage());        }    }    // Part iii: count a file's records. Handles its own exceptions; never throws.    static int countRecords(String fileName) {        int lines = 0;        try (BufferedReader in = new BufferedReader(new FileReader(fileName))) {            while (in.readLine() != null) {                lines++;            }        } catch (FileNotFoundException e) {            System.out.println("Cannot count " + fileName                + ": the file does not exist.");            return -1;        } catch (IOException e) {            System.out.println("Error while counting " + fileName + ": "                + e.getMessage());            return -1;        }        return lines;    }    public static void main(String[] args) {        writeStudents("input.txt");        System.out.println("--- part ii: reading output.txt, exactly as the paper " +            "asks ---");        printStudents("output.txt");        System.out.println("--- the same method on the file we did write ---");        printStudents("input.txt");        System.out.println("--- part iii: counting records ---");        System.out.println("input.txt holds " + countRecords("input.txt")            + " records");        System.out.println("output.txt holds " + countRecords("output.txt")            + " records");    }}
OutputWrote 3 student records to input.txt
--- part ii: reading output.txt, exactly as the paper asks ---
Cannot read output.txt: the file does not exist.
--- the same method on the file we did write ---
STU001, Ada Bello, 4.51
STU002, Femi Okonkwo, 3.78
STU003, Ngozi Eze, 4.92
--- part iii: counting records ---
input.txt holds 3 records
Cannot count output.txt: the file does not exist.
output.txt holds -1 records

Line 3 of that output is the 13 marks. The program did exactly what the paper asked, the file was not there, and the catch block said so in words a human can read.

Teach · Four decisions in that program worth defending

1. try-with-resources answers part 4 on its own. Writing try (BufferedWriter out = ...) closes the writer automatically, whether the block ends normally or throws (Unit 10.2). The paper allows a finally block instead, and it is worth knowing why the bracket form is better: a close() inside finally can itself throw, and if it does while an earlier exception is already travelling, the second exception replaces the first and the real cause disappears. If you do use finally, the close must sit inside its own try-catch, and it must test for null, because the resource may have failed to open at all.

2. Wrapping means closing one thing, not two. out.close() on the BufferedWriter closes the FileWriter inside it. Closing the wrapper closes what it wraps, so one bracket handles both.

3. countRecords returns -1, not 0, when it fails. The method must "handle its own exceptions internally", so it cannot throw, so it must return something. Return 0 and the caller cannot tell a missing file from an empty one. -1 is impossible as a line count, so it can only mean failure. A value chosen because it cannot be mistaken for a real answer is called a sentinel, and picking a good one is a real skill.

4. Read the last two lines of the output in the right order. "Cannot count output.txt" prints before "output.txt holds -1 records", even though the second is the println that contains the first as an argument. Java evaluates the arguments before it calls the method: countRecords runs to completion, printing its own message, and only then does the outer println receive -1 and print. Argument first, call second, always.

blocks.answer:
Q3 a · define printwriter, files.write(), and try with resources · 3 MARKS

Model answer.

  1. PrintWriter. A character-output class that writes formatted text to a file or stream, giving you the same familiar methods as System.out: print, println and printf. It is a wrapper: you hand it a destination (a file name, or another Writer) and it adds the formatting.
  2. Files.write(). A static method on java.nio.file.Files that writes an entire byte array or collection of lines to a file in a single call, creating the file if needed and closing it for you. It is the one-line alternative to opening a writer, looping, and closing.
  3. try-with-resources. A try with the resource declared in brackets, try (PrintWriter out = ...) { ... }, which automatically closes that resource when the block ends, whether it ends normally or by an exception. It removes the need for a finally block whose only job is closing. Unit 10.2.

Where the marks are: for each, say what it is and what it saves you. "PrintWriter writes formatted text" earns the mark; "PrintWriter is for files" does not distinguish it from FileWriter.

Q3 b · debug filetest · 3 MARKS
Compiler outputerror: class, interface, enum, or record expected

The errors, listed.

  1. Line 1 is missing import. java.io.FileWriter; on its own is not a statement, it is nothing at all, which is why javac's first complaint is that it expected a class. Fix: import java.io.FileWriter;
  2. FileWriter("note.txt") is missing new. Creating an object requires new: without it Java looks for a method called FileWriter and finds none. Fix: new FileWriter("note.txt").
  3. writer.close is missing its brackets and semicolon. A method call needs (). Fix: writer.close(); Naming a method without calling it is not a statement, so it cannot stand on a line by itself.
  4. The IOException is never handled. This is the error the others hide, and it is the one worth the mark. new FileWriter(...), write(...) and close() all throw IOException, which is checked (Unit 10.1), so the code will not compile until you either catch it or declare throws IOException on main. Fix all three syntax errors and it still does not compile.

Error 4 is the one that separates answers. Anyone can see a missing bracket; the examiner wants to know whether you understand that a checked exception is a compile-time obligation.

import java.io.FileWriter;import java.io.IOException;public class FileTest {    public static void main(String[] args) {        try (FileWriter writer = new FileWriter("note.txt")) {            writer.write("Hello from Java!");        } catch (IOException e) {            System.out.println("Could not write note.txt: " + e.getMessage());        }        System.out.println("note.txt written");    }}

blocks.answer:
Q3 c · what is the output of the data.txt file? · 4 MARKS

Note the question: not what the program prints on screen (it prints nothing), but what ends up in the file.

The answer:

data.txtAge: 25
Score: 89.46

Two lines. And three details carry the four marks.

Must memorise · print, println, printf: the three differences

print("Age: ")   writes the text, no line break. So the 25 lands on the same line.

println(25)   writes it and a line break. That break is what ends line 1.

printf("Score: %.2f", 89.456)   formats, and adds no line break unless you write %n.

1. %.2f rounds, it does not truncate. 89.456 to two places is 89.46, not 89.45. Unit 3.11.

2. The file has no trailing newline. printf did not add one, so the file ends immediately after the 6 of 89.46. The file is 21 bytes and its last character is not a line break.

3. Nothing appears on screen. Every call is on pw, not on System.out. A common wrong answer is to write the two lines as program output.

MEMORY HOOK: only println breaks the line. print and printf leave the cursor exactly where it stopped.

Code · the paper's code, plus a dump of the file it wrote · VERIFIED ON THE JVM
import java.io.*;public class PrintWriterExample {    public static void main(String[] args) throws IOException {        PrintWriter pw = new PrintWriter("data.txt");        pw.print("Age: ");        pw.println(25);        pw.printf("Score: %.2f", 89.456);        pw.close();        // show exactly what landed in the file, bytes and all        BufferedReader in = new BufferedReader(new FileReader("data.txt"));        StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder();        int c;        while ((c = in.read()) != -1) sb.append((char) c);        in.close();        System.out.println("--- data.txt verbatim ---");        System.out.print(sb);        System.out.println("\n--- as escaped bytes ---");        System.out.println(sb.toString().replace("\r", "\r").replace("\n", "\n"));        System.out.println("length = " + sb.length());    }}
Output--- data.txt verbatim ---
Age: 25
Score: 89.46
--- as escaped bytes ---
Age: 25
Score: 89.46
length = 21

The paper's four lines are exactly as printed; everything after pw.close() is ours, reading the file back so that this book can show you what landed in it. Length 21 is the proof of the trailing-newline point: "Age: 25" is 7 characters, "Score: 89.46" is 12, which is 19, and the two remaining bytes are the single line break in the middle. There is nothing on the end.

Those two bytes are worth a word. println uses the platform's line separator, which on Windows is carriage-return plus line-feed (two characters) and on Linux is line-feed alone (one). Same program, 21 bytes here and 20 there. The two printed lines are the answer either way; if you are asked for a byte count, say which platform.
