blocks.answer:
Q3 d · write students.txt as a formatted, appended table · 7.5 MARKS
Must memorise · PrintWriter cannot append. The FileWriter under it can

new PrintWriter("students.txt")   truncates the file to empty. Every time. There is no append constructor.

new PrintWriter(new FileWriter("students.txt", true))   appends.

The true is the append flag, and it belongs to FileWriter, not to PrintWriter. So the answer to "append with PrintWriter" is to wrap one around a FileWriter opened in append mode, exactly as Unit 10.3 wraps a BufferedReader around a FileReader to get readLine(). Each wrapper adds what the other lacks.

And it satisfies part i for free. FileWriter creates the file if it does not exist, in either mode. So "create students.txt if it does not exist" needs no if, no File.exists(), no check at all: opening it in append mode does both jobs.

MEMORY HOOK: the flag is on the writer that touches the disk. PrintWriter only formats; FileWriter opens the file, so the mode is its business.

Code · q3 d, complete · VERIFIED ON THE JVM
import java.io.BufferedReader;import java.io.FileReader;import java.io.FileWriter;import java.io.IOException;import java.io.PrintWriter;public class StudentTable {    public static void main(String[] args) {        String[] names = {"John", "Lilian", "Ken"};        int[] ages = {20, 21, 19};        double[] gpas = {3.75, 3.95, 3.65};        // iv. APPEND, not overwrite. new PrintWriter("students.txt") would truncate        // the file each run; the append flag is on the FileWriter beneath.        // i. FileWriter also creates students.txt if it does not already exist.        try (PrintWriter out = new PrintWriter(new FileWriter("students.txt",            true))) {            // iii. printf for column alignment: %-8s is left-aligned in 8 columns.            out.printf("%-8s %-5s %-6s%n", "Name", "Age", "GPA");            for (int i = 0; i < names.length; i++) {                out.printf("%-8s %-5d %-6.2f%n", names[i], ages[i], gpas[i]);            }        } catch (IOException e) {            // v. handle possible exceptions properly            System.out.println("Could not write students.txt: " + e.getMessage());        }        // Not part of the answer: read the file back so this book can show you what        // landed in it. A dot marks each trailing space from printf's padding.        try (BufferedReader in = new BufferedReader(new FileReader("students.txt"))) {            String line = in.readLine();            while (line != null) {                System.out.println(line.replace(' ', '.'));                line = in.readLine();            }        } catch (IOException e) {            System.out.println("Could not read students.txt back: " + e.getMessage());        }    }}
students.txt, read back, every space shown as a dotName.....Age...GPA...
John.....20....3.75..
Lilian...21....3.95..
Ken......19....3.65..

The dots are the marks. %-8s means: a String, left aligned, padded to 8 columns, and you can count the padding: "Name" plus four dots, "Lilian" plus two. The minus sign is what makes it left aligned; drop it and every column is pushed right and the table goes ragged. %-6.2f is the same idea for a double, fixed at 2 decimal places, which is why 3.75 prints as 3.75 and not 3.8. Unit 3.11.

Those trailing dots are real spaces, sitting at the end of every line. printf pads the last column just as faithfully as the others, because it cannot know it is last. Harmless in a text file, and worth knowing before you go looking for why two files that "look identical" are not.

Code · proof that the append flag is doing the work · RUN TWICE, IN ONE PROGRAM

The claim above is that the true is what makes it append and that without it the file is wiped. Here that claim is tested: the same write is done twice each way, and the lines are counted.

import java.io.BufferedReader;import java.io.FileReader;import java.io.FileWriter;import java.io.IOException;import java.io.PrintWriter;public class AppendProof {    static void writeOnce(String file, boolean append) throws IOException {        try (PrintWriter out = append                ? new PrintWriter(new FileWriter(file, true))   // appends                : new PrintWriter(file)) {                      // TRUNCATES            out.printf("%-8s %-5d %-6.2f%n", "John", 20, 3.75);        }    }    static int lines(String file) throws IOException {        int n = 0;        try (BufferedReader in = new BufferedReader(new FileReader(file))) {            while (in.readLine() != null) n++;        }        return n;    }    public static void main(String[] args) throws IOException {        writeOnce("appended.txt", true);        writeOnce("appended.txt", true);        System.out.println("new PrintWriter(new FileWriter(f, true)) twice -> "            + lines("appended.txt") + " lines");        writeOnce("truncated.txt", false);        writeOnce("truncated.txt", false);        System.out.println("new PrintWriter(f)                     twice -> "            + lines("truncated.txt") + " lines");    }}
Outputnew PrintWriter(new FileWriter(f, true)) twice -> 2 lines
new PrintWriter(f)                     twice -> 1 lines

Two lines against one. The appending version kept both records; the plain PrintWriter threw the first away and left only the second. If you write new PrintWriter("students.txt") in the exam, your program passes every other part of this question and still fails part iv, and nothing in its output tells you.

blocks.text: Part 2: the method behind these, taught from nothing

blocks.label: Work it frame by frame
blocks.tag: for a reader who has never read the course

frames.teach:
An exception is an error raised while the program runs. Java splits them in two, and the difference is who is responsible.

public class Kinds {    public static void main(String[] args) {        int[] a = {1, 2, 3};        try {            System.out.println(a[5]);        } catch (ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException e) {            System.out.println("unchecked: " + e.getMessage());        }        try {            System.out.println(Integer.parseInt("ten"));        } catch (NumberFormatException e) {            System.out.println("unchecked: " + e.getMessage());        } finally {            System.out.println("finally always runs");        }    }}
Outputunchecked: Index 5 out of bounds for length 3
unchecked: For input string: "ten"
finally always runs
frames.ask: Which kind does the compiler force you to handle, and what is the other kind usually caused by?

frames.check: Checked ones. Unchecked ones come from bugs in the code.
frames.teach:
Checked exceptions are the ones the compiler forces you to catch or declare, IOException and FileNotFoundException among them, and they are about the world outside the program. Unchecked ones extend RuntimeException, are your own bugs, and the compiler says nothing: the two above are unchecked.

Three differences for the 25/26 question: checked are checked at compile time, unchecked at run time; checked must be handled or declared, unchecked need not be; checked signal outside failures, unchecked signal programming faults.
frames.ask: In that listing, when did finally run, and when would it not?

frames.teach:
It ran after the catch, and it runs whether or not an exception was thrown, which is why it is where files and connections are closed. It is skipped only if the JVM itself exits.

throw raises an exception now; throws in a header declares that this method may raise one and will not handle it. One letter apart, and the exam asks for both.

import java.io.FileWriter;import java.io.BufferedReader;import java.io.FileReader;import java.io.IOException;public class Records {    public static void main(String[] args) {        try (FileWriter out = new FileWriter("students.txt")) {            out.write("20/1234,Ada,4.6\n");            out.write("20/1235,Grace,3.9\n");        } catch (IOException e) {            System.out.println("could not write: " + e.getMessage());        }        try (FileWriter more = new FileWriter("students.txt", true)) {            more.write("20/1236,Chinwe,4.1\n");        } catch (IOException e) {            System.out.println("could not append: " + e.getMessage());        }        try (BufferedReader in = new BufferedReader(new FileReader("students.txt"))) {            String line;            int n = 0;            while ((line = in.readLine()) != null) {                n++;                String[] parts = line.split(",");                System.out.println(n + ". " + parts[1] + " has " + parts[2]);            }            System.out.println(n + " records");        } catch (IOException e) {            System.out.println("could not read: " + e.getMessage());        }    }}
Output1. Ada has 4.6
2. Grace has 3.9
3. Chinwe has 4.1
3 records
frames.ask: Now files. Which class writes, which reads, and what does the second argument true do?

frames.check: FileWriter writes, BufferedReader with FileReader reads, and true appends.
frames.teach:
FileWriter writes, BufferedReader wrapped around a FileReader reads a line at a time, and the second argument true means APPEND. Without it the file is emptied the moment it is opened, which is the difference between adding a record and destroying every record.

Note the loop: while ((line = in.readLine()) != null) is the shape to memorise, because readLine returns null at the end of the file.
frames.ask: Every open above sits inside try (...) rather than before it. What is that called, and what does it save you?

frames.check: try-with-resources: it closes the file for you.
frames.teach:
try-with-resources, which 24/25 asks you to define. Anything opened in those brackets is closed automatically when the block ends, whether it ended normally or by an exception, so no finally block and no forgotten close.

PrintWriter is the other writer to know: it wraps a file and gives you println and printf, so it writes formatted lines the way System.out does.
frames.ask: Last, the one that costs marks in a debug question: what must a method that opens a file either do or declare?

frames.check: Catch IOException or declare throws IOException.
frames.teach: Either catch IOException, or declare throws IOException in its header. IOException is checked, so leaving it out is a compile error and is a favourite planted fault. Check the imports too: java.io.* or the four classes by name.

blocks.big: "Checked exceptions must be caught or declared with throws, and the compiler enforces it. Unchecked ones are your bugs, and it does not."
blocks.sub: FileWriter with true appends, without it overwrites. try-with-resources closes the file for you, whatever happens.

blocks.printed: [2 Marks]A. Define method overloading in Java, and state precisely the role that the method signature plays in enabling the compiler to resolve an overloaded call at compile time.

GivenNothing. Recall.

The marks2 marks: one for the definition, one for the mechanism. Answering only the first half caps you at one.

blocks.label: Model answer
blocks.problem: Write your answer to the question above in your book first. It carries 2 marks, so write one clear point for every mark. Then open the model answer and mark yourself against it.
blocks.working:
Q1 a · define method overloading, and the role of the signature · 2 MARKS

Model answer.

Method overloading is a feature that allows a class to have more than one method with the same name but different parameter lists (differing in the number, types, or order of parameters).

The method signature is a method's name together with its parameter list. Its role in resolution is this: at a call such as add(2, 3), the compiler compares the number, types and order of the arguments written at the call site against the parameter list of every candidate with that name, and selects the one whose signature matches (widening the argument types if no exact match exists). Because the resolution uses only what appears at the call site, and the return type is not part of the signature, the return type plays no role: two methods differing only by return type are rejected by the compiler as a duplicate definition. The choice is therefore made entirely at compile time, which is why overloading is called compile-time (static) polymorphism.

Where the marks are: one for the definition, one for "signature = name + parameter list" and the fact that the return type is excluded. Saying "the compiler picks the right one" without saying how is half an answer. See Units 5.1 and 5.6.

blocks.working:
Q1 b · three differences: checked vs unchecked · 3 MARKS

Model answer. Three differences, one mark each:

  1. When they are detected. Checked exceptions are checked by the compiler at compile time; unchecked exceptions occur at run time and the compiler does not examine them.
  2. Whether you must handle them. A checked exception must be either caught in a try-catch or declared with throws, or the code will not compile. An unchecked exception carries no such obligation.
  3. What causes them. Checked exceptions represent conditions outside the program's control (a missing file, a failed network call), whereas unchecked exceptions represent programming errors (dereferencing null, a bad index, dividing by zero).

Examples (add them; they cost one line and prove the point): checked: IOException, FileNotFoundException, ClassNotFoundException. Unchecked: NullPointerException, ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException, ArithmeticException.

Where the marks are: three distinct axes. Writing "one is checked and one is not" three different ways scores one mark. See Unit 10.1.

blocks.label: As printed

Q1 c · find the errors · 5 MARKS

Read the output first. "141.0" tells you the sum is a double before you have read a line of code. That single character finds two of the five errors.

Code · the paper's snippet, with every error marked · AS PRINTED
import javax.swing.JOptionPane;public class Snippet {public static void main(String[] args) {int[] arr = {24.0, 40.0, 66.0, 80.0, 98.0};        // ERROR 1 and 2  int sum = 0;                                     // ERROR 2  int matches = 0;  boolean stop = false;  for (int i = 0; i <= arr.length && !stop; i++) {   // ERROR 3      for (int j = i; j < arr.length; j++) {          if (arr[j] % 4 == 0) {                     // ERROR 4              continue;          }          sum += arr[j] - j;                        // ERROR 5          matches++;          if (matches == 3) {              stop = true;          }          break;      }  }  JOptionPane.showMessageDialog(null, "Sum: " + sum);  JOptionPane.showMessageDialog(null, "Matches: " + matches);  System.exit(0);}}
Worked example · The five errors, and why each is one
  1. Line 4: int[] cannot hold 24.0. Those are double literals. This is a compile error: "incompatible types: possible lossy conversion from double to int". Fix: double[] arr. The output confirms it: 141.0 is a double.
  2. Line 5: int sum cannot total doubles, and could never print "141.0". Fix: double sum = 0; Unit 3.3: the type decides what you may do and how it prints.
  3. Line 8: i <= arr.length is off by one. Indexes run 0 to length-1 (F.10). Fix: i < arr.length. Here it would not actually throw, because the inner loop never runs when i = 5, but it is still wrong and it is one of the five marks.
  4. Lines 10 to 12: the continue is inverted. The spec says find numbers that are multiples of 4. This skips them and processes everything else: precisely backwards. Fix: if (arr[j] % 4 != 0) continue; Unit 4.7: read every continue as "unless". This is the error worth the most attention, because it is the one that is pure logic.
  5. Line 13: arr[j] - j subtracts the index. The spec says add (that number - 1). Fix: sum += arr[j] - 1; A subtle one: with j it would give the right answer for j = 1 only, so a spot check could miss it.

public class ArmstrongChecker {    public static void main(String[] args) {        int[] numbers = {370, 371, 372, 407, 408};        for (int idx = 0; idx < numbers.length; idx++) {            int n = numbers[idx], digits = 0, temp = n, sum = 0;            while (temp > 0) { digits++; temp /= 10; }            temp = n;            while (temp > 0) {                int d = temp % 10, power = 1;                for (int p = 0; p < digits; p++) power *= d;                sum += power;                temp /= 10;            }            System.out.println(n + " -> "                + (sum == n ? "ARMSTRONG" : "NOT ARMSTRONG"));        }    }}

371 -> ARMSTRONG
372 -> NOT ARMSTRONG
407 -> ARMSTRONG

Q1 d ii · convert the loops · 10 MARKS, PART TWO

Read it precisely. The original has three loops:

LoopCurrentlyBecomes
the outer one over idxforwhile
counting the digitswhilefor
summing the powerswhilefor
the inner p loopforwhile

"The For Loop" (singular) is the outer one; "the While loops" (plural) are the two digit loops. The innermost p loop is also a for, so convert it too: the safest reading is that every for becomes a while and every while becomes a for. Apply Unit 4.6's recipe to each.

Code · every loop converted, same output · VERIFIED ON THE JVM
public class ArmstrongConverted {    public static void main(String[] args) {        int[] numbers = {370, 371, 372, 407, 408};        // FOR -> WHILE: init out, condition in, update at the bottom        int idx = 0;        while (idx < numbers.length) {            int n = numbers[idx], digits = 0, temp = n, sum = 0;            // WHILE -> FOR: no init needed, temp is the counter            for (; temp > 0; temp /= 10) {                digits++;            }            temp = n;            // WHILE -> FOR            for (; temp > 0; temp /= 10) {                int d = temp % 10, power = 1;                // FOR -> WHILE                int p = 0;                while (p < digits) {                    power *= d;                    p++;                }                sum += power;            }            System.out.println(n + " -> "                + (sum == n ? "ARMSTRONG" : "NOT ARMSTRONG"));            idx++;                      // the update, at the bottom        }    }}
Output370 -> ARMSTRONG
371 -> ARMSTRONG
372 -> NOT ARMSTRONG
407 -> ARMSTRONG
408 -> NOT ARMSTRONG

Identical output to the original. That is the test of a conversion: same program, different clothes.

Two points a marker looks for. The for (; temp > 0; temp /= 10) has an empty initialisation, which is legal and is the honest conversion: the original while had nothing to initialise, because temp already existed. Do not invent a variable to fill the slot. And idx++ sits at the bottom of the while body, which is Unit 4.6's step 3 and the one people forget: leave it out and the program runs forever.

Q2 a · define encapsulation · 2 MARKS

Model answer.

Encapsulation is the OOP principle of bundling data (fields) and the methods that operate on them into a single unit (a class), while restricting direct access to some of its components.

In Java it is achieved by declaring the fields private and exposing controlled access through public getter and setter methods. This gives data hiding (unauthorised code cannot read or modify the state), validation (a setter can reject invalid input, for example preventing a negative balance), and flexibility (the internal representation can change without breaking any code that uses the class).

Where the marks are: one for the bundling-plus- restricting definition, one for how it is achieved (private fields, public getters and setters). Add one benefit if you have room. See Unit 6.4.

Q2 b · three differences: overloading vs overriding · 3 MARKS

Model answer. Three differences, one mark each:

  1. Where they occur. Overloading happens within a single class: several methods share a name. Overriding happens between a superclass and a subclass: the subclass replaces the inherited method.
  2. The parameter list. Overloaded methods must have different parameter lists. An overriding method must have exactly the same name and parameter list as the one it overrides.
  3. When the method is chosen. Overloading is resolved at compile time by the compiler (static polymorphism); overriding is resolved at run time by the JVM, from the object's actual type (dynamic polymorphism).

Where the marks are: three separate axes. If you have room, add that overriding requires inheritance and overloading does not. See Unit 6.7.

Q2 c · find the errors · 5 MARKS

The same five errors as Q1, in the same order. This is the payoff of the template.

Worked example · The five errors
  1. Line 4: int[] prices = {15.5, ...}. Decimal literals in an int array: a compile error. Fix: double[] prices. The output "202.725" says double before you read anything else.
  2. Line 5: int total = 0; cannot hold 202.725. Fix: double total = 0;
  3. Line 8: i <= prices.length is off by one. Fix: i < prices.length. Unlike Q1, this one would throw ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException at i = 6, because line 9 reads prices[i] straight away. Same error, worse consequence.
  4. Line 9: if (prices[i] > 20) continue; is inverted. The spec says skip anything under 20. This skips everything over 20, i.e. exactly the items to be discounted. Fix: if (prices[i] < 20) continue;
  5. Line 15: if (count == 5). The spec says stop once 4 have been discounted. Fix: if (count == 4). Only four of the six prices are 20 or above anyway, so with == 5 the flag never fires. The count would still be 4, and the total would still be right, which makes this the easiest error to miss: it does not change the answer, it just means the code does not do what it was asked.

Q2 d i · state the output · 10 MARKS, PART ONE

The answer: Perfect: 2, Abundant: 5, Deficient: 23

The reasoning, which is worth writing out because "no need to show workings" does not mean "do not check":

ClassCountWhich
Perfect26 (1+2+3 = 6) and 28 (1+2+4+7+14 = 28)
Abundant512 (16), 18 (21), 20 (22), 24 (36), 30 (42)
Deficient23everything else, including every prime, and 1

Two checks that catch mistakes. 2 + 5 + 23 = 30, so every number is classified exactly once. And 1 is deficient: its proper divisors sum to 0, because 1 has no proper divisor, and the loop for (div = 1; div < num; div++) never runs for num = 1. Forget that and you get 22, not 23.

Code · confirmed, with the classification printed · VERIFIED ON THE JVM
public class NumberClassifier {    public static void main(String[] args) {        int perfectCount = 0, abundantCount = 0, deficientCount = 0;        for (int num = 1; num <= 30; num++) {            int sum = 0;            for (int div = 1; div < num; div++) {                if (num % div == 0) sum += div;            }            if (sum == num) perfectCount++;            else if (sum > num) abundantCount++;            else deficientCount++;        }        System.out.println("Perfect: " + perfectCount + ", Abundant: " + abundantCount            + ", Deficient: " + deficientCount);        System.out.println("check: " + (perfectCount + abundantCount + deficientCount)            + " numbers classified");    }}
OutputPerfect: 2, Abundant: 5, Deficient: 23
check: 30 numbers classified
Code · q2 d ii · for loops converted to while loops · VERIFIED ON THE JVM
public class NumberClassifierWhile {    public static void main(String[] args) {        int perfectCount = 0, abundantCount = 0, deficientCount = 0;        int num = 1;                        // 1. init above        while (num <= 30) {                 // 2. condition            int sum = 0;            int div = 1;                    // the inner one too            while (div < num) {                if (num % div == 0) sum += div;                div++;                      // 3. update at the bottom            }            if (sum == num) perfectCount++;            else if (sum > num) abundantCount++;            else deficientCount++;            num++;                          // 3. update at the bottom        }        System.out.println("Perfect: " + perfectCount + ", Abundant: " + abundantCount            + ", Deficient: " + deficientCount);    }}
OutputPerfect: 2, Abundant: 5, Deficient: 23

Identical output, which is the whole test. Note int sum = 0; stays inside the outer loop: it must be reset for every number, and moving it out is the classic way to wreck this conversion. The recipe only moves the loop's own three parts; everything else stays exactly where it was, which is what "retain other things" means.

Q3 a · consecutive duplicates in a sales log · 12 MARKS
Index0123456789
Amount20203540404015606025

Write a program that (i) counts, in one pass, the indices i >= 1 where the amount equals the one before it; (ii) returns a single String listing, in order and comma separated, every amount that equals its predecessor or its successor, built with plain String concatenation only; (iii) displays both in one JOptionPane dialog. The paper adds a hint: it must not flag 35, 15, or 25.

Must memorise · Parts i and ii count DIFFERENT things

Part i counts positions. Part ii lists values. They are not the same question asked twice, and they do not give the same number.

Part i asks how many boundaries have a twin across them. Part ii asks which elements are touching a twin at all.

Look at the three 40s. They contain two boundaries (index 3 to 4, and 4 to 5) but three elements. So part i counts 2 there and part ii lists 3. Read the two parts as one question and you will answer one of them wrong.

MEMORY HOOK: fences and posts. Part i counts the fences between posts, part ii counts the posts. A run of n twins has n posts and n-1 fences, always.

Dry run · Both answers, by hand, before writing any code

Check it against the hint. The paper told you 35, 15 and 25 must not be flagged, and they are the only three that are not. The examiner has handed you a way to test your own trace before you write a line of code, which is exactly what the hint is for.

And check the two answers against each other. The runs are 20-20 (2 long), 40-40-40 (3 long) and 60-60 (2 long). Part ii flags 2 + 3 + 2 = 7 values. Part i counts 1 + 2 + 1 = 4 positions. They differ by exactly 3, the number of runs, because each run loses one to the fences-and-posts rule. If your two answers do not differ by the number of runs, one of them is wrong.

Code · question three, part a · VERIFIED ON THE JVM
public class SalesDuplicates {    // Part i: ONE pass. Count every index i >= 1 whose amount equals the one before.    static int countConsecutiveDuplicates(int[] sales) {        int count = 0;        for (int i = 1; i < sales.length; i++) {            if (sales[i] == sales[i - 1]) {                count++;            }        }        return count;    }    // Part ii: every amount equal to its predecessor OR its successor, in order,    // comma separated, built with plain String concatenation only.    static String flaggedAmounts(int[] sales) {        String result = "";        for (int i = 0; i < sales.length; i++) {            boolean sameAsPrevious = (i > 0) && (sales[i] == sales[i - 1]);            boolean sameAsNext = (i < sales.length - 1) && (sales[i] == sales[i + 1]);            if (sameAsPrevious || sameAsNext) {                if (result.equals("")) {                    result = "" + sales[i];                } else {                    result = result + ", " + sales[i];                }            }        }        return result;    }    // Part iii: one dialog showing both answers.    public static void main(String[] args) {        int[] saleAmounts = {20, 20, 35, 40, 40, 40, 15, 60, 60, 25};        int duplicates = countConsecutiveDuplicates(saleAmounts);        String flagged = flaggedAmounts(saleAmounts);        String message = "Consecutive duplicate count: " + duplicates                       + "\nFlagged amounts: " + flagged;        System.out.println(message);    }}
OutputConsecutive duplicate count: 4
Flagged amounts: 20, 20, 40, 40, 40, 60, 60

Exactly the hand trace, including the three amounts the paper told us not to flag. The dialog is a println here so its text can be printed in this book; in the hall, write JOptionPane.showMessageDialog(null, message); and import javax.swing.JOptionPane (F.11).

Trap · Three ways to lose marks on part A

1. Starting part i's loop at 0. The question says i >= 1, and for a reason: sales[0 - 1] is sales[-1], which throws ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException (Unit 8.1). Index 0 has no predecessor, so the loop starts at 1. This is where "one pass" is easiest to get right and easiest to throw away.

2. Forgetting the boundary guards in part ii. Index 0 has no predecessor and the last index has no successor. The guards (i > 0) and (i < sales.length - 1) are what stop the reads from running off either end. They work because && is short-circuit (Unit 3.6): when i > 0 is false, Java never evaluates sales[i - 1], so it never throws. Swap the two sides of the && and the program crashes on the first element.

3. The leading comma. Concatenating ", " + sales[i] every time gives , 20, 20, 40... with a comma stuck on the front. The test if (result.equals("")) writes the first value bare and every later value with its separator in front. Compare Strings with .equals(), never with == (Unit 7.3).

The question bans StringBuilder deliberately: it wants to see that you can handle the separator yourself. Use StringBuilder anyway and you have answered a question the paper did not ask.

Using only java.io.FileWriter, java.io.FileReader, java.io.BufferedReader, java.io.BufferedWriter, and java.io.IOException (or its subclasses), write a complete program that does the following:

i.    Create a file named input.txt and write the details (student ID, name, CGPA) of at least three students into it using FileWriter, one student per line. Wrap the writing logic in a try-catch block that handles any exception that may occur.

ii.   Read student details from a file named output.txt using FileReader and print each line to the console exactly as it appears in the file. Handle any exception that may occur while reading, including the case where output.txt does not exist.

iii.  Create a method that takes in a file name, opens the file, counts the number of lines (student records) it contains, and returns that count. This method must handle its own exceptions internally.

iv.  Ensure every file resource opened is properly closed (either in a finally block or via try-with-resources) and that every catch block prints a clear, specific message describing what went wrong.

Console output (System.out) is acceptable throughout.

blocks.working:
Q3 b · student records with basic file i/o · 13 MARKS
  1. creates input.txt and writes at least three students (ID, name, CGPA) into it with FileWriter, one per line, wrapped in try-catch;
  2. reads student details from output.txt with FileReader and prints each line exactly as it appears, handling any exception including the case where output.txt does not exist;
  3. has a method that takes a file name, counts the lines, and returns the count, handling its own exceptions internally;
  4. closes every resource, and prints a clear, specific message in every catch block.
Must memorise · It writes input.txt and reads output.txt

Part 1 writes input.txt. Part 2 reads output.txt. The program never creates output.txt.

That is not a misprint for you to tidy up. It is the question.

Read part 2 again: "handle any exception that may occur while reading, including the case where output.txt does not exist." The examiner has told you, in the question itself, that the file will be missing. The marks are for the catch block running, not for the file being read.

So do not "fix" it by reading input.txt instead. Write exactly what the paper asks, and let the catch block do its job. That is the answer.

MEMORY HOOK: the missing file is the exam. When a question names a file it never created, the catch block is the thing being marked.

Teach · The five classes, and why the list is exactly these five

The restriction looks arbitrary. It is not: the five are exactly what you need and nothing more (Unit 10.3).

ClassDirectionWhat it is for
FileWriteroutWrites characters to a file. On its own it writes one character at a time.
BufferedWriteroutWraps a FileWriter and collects characters, writing them in blocks. Also gives you newLine().
FileReaderinReads characters from a file. On its own it reads one character at a time: it has no readLine().
BufferedReaderinWraps a FileReader and gives you readLine(), which is the whole reason it is on the list.
IOException-The checked exception every one of the above can throw. You must catch it or declare it (Unit 10.1).

The pairing is the point. The question says "read using FileReader" and "one student per line". A FileReader alone cannot give you a line. So you wrap it: new BufferedReader(new FileReader(fileName)). That is why both appear on the list, and it is why the list is not padding.

And read "or its subclasses" carefully. Those three words are permission. FileNotFoundException is a subclass of IOException, so you are explicitly allowed to catch it separately, which is exactly how you answer part 2's "including the case where output.txt does not exist" with a message that says what actually happened.

Trap · Catch the child before the parent, or it will not compile

When you catch both, the subclass must come first. Java tries catch blocks top to bottom and takes the first that fits. Put IOException first and it swallows everything, leaving the FileNotFoundException block unreachable. Java does not let that pass:

import java.io.BufferedReader;import java.io.FileNotFoundException;import java.io.FileReader;import java.io.IOException;public class CatchOrder {    public static void main(String[] args) {        try (BufferedReader in = new BufferedReader(new FileReader("any.txt"))) {            System.out.println(in.readLine());        } catch (IOException e) {            System.out.println("the parent is caught first");        } catch (FileNotFoundException e) {            System.out.println("this line can never run");        }    }}
Compiler outputerror: exception FileNotFoundException has already been caught

This is one of Java's friendlier errors: it refuses to compile code containing a block that could never run. Reverse the two catch blocks and it compiles. Specific first, general last, every time.

Code · question three, part b · VERIFIED ON THE JVM
import java.io.BufferedReader;import java.io.BufferedWriter;import java.io.FileNotFoundException;import java.io.FileReader;import java.io.FileWriter;import java.io.IOException;public class StudentRecords {    // Part i: create input.txt and write three student records, one per line.    static void writeStudents(String fileName) {        try (BufferedWriter out = new BufferedWriter(new FileWriter(fileName))) {            out.write("STU001, Ada Bello, 4.51");            out.newLine();            out.write("STU002, Femi Okonkwo, 3.78");            out.newLine();            out.write("STU003, Ngozi Eze, 4.92");            out.newLine();            System.out.println("Wrote 3 student records to " + fileName);        } catch (IOException e) {            System.out.println("Could not write to " + fileName + ": "                + e.getMessage());        }    }    // Part ii: read a file and print every line exactly as it appears.    static void printStudents(String fileName) {        try (BufferedReader in = new BufferedReader(new FileReader(fileName))) {            String line = in.readLine();            while (line != null) {                System.out.println(line);                line = in.readLine();            }        } catch (FileNotFoundException e) {            System.out.println("Cannot read " + fileName                + ": the file does not exist.");        } catch (IOException e) {            System.out.println("Error while reading " + fileName + ": "                + e.getMessage());        }    }    // Part iii: count a file's records. Handles its own exceptions; never throws.    static int countRecords(String fileName) {        int lines = 0;        try (BufferedReader in = new BufferedReader(new FileReader(fileName))) {            while (in.readLine() != null) {                lines++;            }        } catch (FileNotFoundException e) {            System.out.println("Cannot count " + fileName                + ": the file does not exist.");            return -1;        } catch (IOException e) {            System.out.println("Error while counting " + fileName + ": "                + e.getMessage());            return -1;        }        return lines;    }    public static void main(String[] args) {        writeStudents("input.txt");        System.out.println("--- part ii: reading output.txt, exactly as the paper " +            "asks ---");        printStudents("output.txt");        System.out.println("--- the same method on the file we did write ---");        printStudents("input.txt");        System.out.println("--- part iii: counting records ---");        System.out.println("input.txt holds " + countRecords("input.txt")            + " records");        System.out.println("output.txt holds " + countRecords("output.txt")            + " records");    }}
OutputWrote 3 student records to input.txt
--- part ii: reading output.txt, exactly as the paper asks ---
Cannot read output.txt: the file does not exist.
--- the same method on the file we did write ---
STU001, Ada Bello, 4.51
STU002, Femi Okonkwo, 3.78
STU003, Ngozi Eze, 4.92
--- part iii: counting records ---
input.txt holds 3 records
Cannot count output.txt: the file does not exist.
output.txt holds -1 records

Line 3 of that output is the 13 marks. The program did exactly what the paper asked, the file was not there, and the catch block said so in words a human can read.

Teach · Four decisions in that program worth defending

1. try-with-resources answers part 4 on its own. Writing try (BufferedWriter out = ...) closes the writer automatically, whether the block ends normally or throws (Unit 10.2). The paper allows a finally block instead, and it is worth knowing why the bracket form is better: a close() inside finally can itself throw, and if it does while an earlier exception is already travelling, the second exception replaces the first and the real cause disappears. If you do use finally, the close must sit inside its own try-catch, and it must test for null, because the resource may have failed to open at all.

2. Wrapping means closing one thing, not two. out.close() on the BufferedWriter closes the FileWriter inside it. Closing the wrapper closes what it wraps, so one bracket handles both.

3. countRecords returns -1, not 0, when it fails. The method must "handle its own exceptions internally", so it cannot throw, so it must return something. Return 0 and the caller cannot tell a missing file from an empty one. -1 is impossible as a line count, so it can only mean failure. A value chosen because it cannot be mistaken for a real answer is called a sentinel, and picking a good one is a real skill.

4. Read the last two lines of the output in the right order. "Cannot count output.txt" prints before "output.txt holds -1 records", even though the second is the println that contains the first as an argument. Java evaluates the arguments before it calls the method: countRecords runs to completion, printing its own message, and only then does the outer println receive -1 and print. Argument first, call second, always.

ii.   CurrentAccount extends BankAccount. Override the withdrawal method so that every successful withdrawal automatically adds a ₦50 reward to the balance afterward. (6 marks)

blocks.working:
Q4 · inheritance and polymorphism · 25 MARKS

Part 1, BankAccount (9 marks). Private fields for account number, holder name and balance; a constructor initialising all three; a method that adds to the balance; a method that deducts if funds suffice and otherwise rejects with a message; a method that displays the details.

Part 2, subclasses (10 marks). SavingAccount overrides the withdrawal so it is allowed only if the balance after the withdrawal would still be >= 1000. CurrentAccount overrides it so every successful withdrawal adds a 50 reward afterwards.

Part 3, main (6 marks). One of each; deposit into each; at least one successful and one unsuccessful or reward-triggering withdrawal on each; details before and after; and demonstrate polymorphism by storing each object in a BankAccount reference and calling the withdrawal through it, confirming the correct overridden version runs.

Must memorise · The question contains a contradiction, and resolving it is the exam

Part 1 says the balance must be private.

Part 2 says the subclasses must change the balance.

A private field is invisible to a subclass. So the subclass cannot touch it.

This is not the examiner being careless. It is the whole of Units 6.4 and 6.6 arriving in one question: encapsulation says the field is private, and inheritance says the child must still be able to work with it. The way out is the only way out, and it is the answer being marked: the subclass goes through the parent's public methods, using getBalance() to read and super.withdraw(amount) or deposit(amount) to change.

MEMORY HOOK: the child knocks, it does not climb in through the window. getBalance() to look, super.withdraw() to act.

Trap · A subclass cannot see a private field, and it will say so

The tempting move is to write the arithmetic straight into the subclass. Java stops you at the compiler:

class Account {    private double balance = 5000;}class Saving extends Account {    public boolean withdraw(double amount) {        balance = balance - amount;        return true;    }}public class SubclassReach {    public static void main(String[] args) {        new Saving().withdraw(100);    }}
Compiler outputerror: balance has private access in Account

Private means the declaring class only, and a subclass is a different class. Inheritance gives Saving the field (every Saving object really does contain a balance) but not access to it. The field is there and untouchable, which is exactly what private is for (Unit 6.4).

Would protected fix it? It would compile, and it is the wrong answer here, because part 1 said private. Marks are for doing what the question said. Beyond the exam, going through the parent's methods is better anyway: every rule the parent enforces on a withdrawal keeps being enforced. Make the field protected and each subclass has to remember those rules for itself, which is how a bank ends up with an account that can be overdrawn down one code path and not another. See the access table in Unit 6.6.

Teach · Why withdraw returns boolean

The paper does not say what withdraw returns, and the obvious choice is void. Then read part 2 ii again: a CurrentAccount adds the reward on every successful withdrawal. Not on every attempt. So the override has to know whether the withdrawal succeeded, and a void method tells it nothing.

Making withdraw return boolean makes the override three honest lines:

boolean succeeded = super.withdraw(amount);if (succeeded) { deposit(50); }return succeeded;

The alternative, comparing the balance before and after, works but is worse: it re-derives an answer the parent already knew and threw away. When a method knows something the caller needs, it should return it. Notice that this decision is forced by a single word in part 2 ii, which is what "read the question" means in practice.

Code · question four, complete · VERIFIED ON THE JVM
// ===== Part 1: the superclass =====class BankAccount {    private String accountNumber;    private String holderName;    private double balance;    // Part 1 i: a constructor that initialises all three fields.    public BankAccount(String accountNumber, String holderName, double balance) {        this.accountNumber = accountNumber;        this.holderName = holderName;        this.balance = balance;    }    // The private fields are reachable only through these doors (Unit 6.4).    public String getAccountNumber() { return accountNumber; }    public String getHolderName()    { return holderName; }    public double getBalance()       { return balance; }    // Part 1 ii: add a given amount to the balance.    public void deposit(double amount) {        balance = balance + amount;        System.out.println("Deposit " + amount + " -> " + accountNumber            + " balance is now " + balance);    }    // Part 1 iii: deduct if funds are sufficient, otherwise reject with a message.    // Returns whether it succeeded, which is what CurrentAccount needs to know.    public boolean withdraw(double amount) {        if (amount <= balance) {            balance = balance - amount;            System.out.println("Withdraw " + amount + " -> " + accountNumber                + " balance is now " + balance);            return true;        }        System.out.println("REJECTED: " + accountNumber + " holds only " + balance            + ", so " + amount + " cannot be withdrawn");        return false;    }    // Part 1 iv: display the account's current details.    public void displayDetails() {        System.out.println("Account " + accountNumber + " | " + holderName            + " | balance " + balance);    }}// ===== Part 2 i: a saving account must never drop below 1000 =====class SavingAccount extends BankAccount {    public SavingAccount(String accountNumber, String holderName, double balance) {        super(accountNumber, holderName, balance);    }    @Override    public boolean withdraw(double amount) {        if (getBalance() - amount < 1000) {            System.out.println("REJECTED: a saving account must retain 1000. " +                "Withdrawing "                + amount + " from " + getAccountNumber() + " would leave "                + (getBalance() - amount));            return false;        }        return super.withdraw(amount);    }}// ===== Part 2 ii: every successful withdrawal earns a 50 reward =====class CurrentAccount extends BankAccount {    public CurrentAccount(String accountNumber, String holderName, double balance) {        super(accountNumber, holderName, balance);    }    @Override    public boolean withdraw(double amount) {        boolean succeeded = super.withdraw(amount);        if (succeeded) {            System.out.println("Reward earned on " + getAccountNumber() + ":");            deposit(50);        }        return succeeded;    }}// ===== Part 3: the main method =====public class BankSystem {    public static void main(String[] args) {        // Part 3 i: at least one of each.        SavingAccount saving   = new SavingAccount("SA-1001", "Ada Bello", 5000.0);        CurrentAccount current = new CurrentAccount("CA-2002", "Femi Okonkwo",            3000.0);        System.out.println("=== iv: details BEFORE the transactions ===");        saving.displayDetails();        current.displayDetails();        // Part 3 ii: deposit into each.        System.out.println("=== ii: deposit into each ===");        saving.deposit(2000.0);        current.deposit(1000.0);        // Part 3 iii: a successful and an unsuccessful withdrawal on each.        System.out.println("=== iii: a successful and an unsuccessful withdrawal on " +            "each ===");        saving.withdraw(4000.0);        saving.withdraw(2500.0);        current.withdraw(1000.0);        current.withdraw(999999.0);        System.out.println("=== iv: details AFTER the transactions ===");        saving.displayDetails();        current.displayDetails();        // Part 3 v: polymorphism. Same reference type, same call, same amount.        System.out.println("=== v: polymorphism, same reference type, same call, " +            "same amount ===");        BankAccount acc = new SavingAccount("SA-3003", "Ngozi Eze", 1500.0);        acc.withdraw(600.0);        acc.displayDetails();        acc = new CurrentAccount("CA-4004", "Tunde Ade", 1500.0);        acc.withdraw(600.0);        acc.displayDetails();    }}
Output=== iv: details BEFORE the transactions ===
Account SA-1001 | Ada Bello | balance 5000.0
Account CA-2002 | Femi Okonkwo | balance 3000.0
=== ii: deposit into each ===
Deposit 2000.0 -> SA-1001 balance is now 7000.0
Deposit 1000.0 -> CA-2002 balance is now 4000.0
=== iii: a successful and an unsuccessful withdrawal on each ===
Withdraw 4000.0 -> SA-1001 balance is now 3000.0
REJECTED: a saving account must retain 1000. Withdrawing 2500.0 from SA-1001 would leave 500.0
Withdraw 1000.0 -> CA-2002 balance is now 3000.0
Reward earned on CA-2002:
Deposit 50.0 -> CA-2002 balance is now 3050.0
REJECTED: CA-2002 holds only 3050.0, so 999999.0 cannot be withdrawn
=== iv: details AFTER the transactions ===
Account SA-1001 | Ada Bello | balance 3000.0
Account CA-2002 | Femi Okonkwo | balance 3050.0
=== v: polymorphism, same reference type, same call, same amount ===
REJECTED: a saving account must retain 1000. Withdrawing 600.0 from SA-3003 would leave 900.0
Account SA-3003 | Ngozi Eze | balance 1500.0
Withdraw 600.0 -> CA-4004 balance is now 900.0
Reward earned on CA-4004:
Deposit 50.0 -> CA-4004 balance is now 950.0
Account CA-4004 | Tunde Ade | balance 950.0

All four classes live in one file because only one may be public and that one must match the file name: BankSystem.java. In the hall, write them as four classes exactly as they are here, or as four separate files. Both are correct.

Dry run · Every balance, and why each rule fired
Callbalance beforewhich rule decidedallowed?balance after
SA-1001, a SavingAccount, opens at 5000
deposit(2000)5000.0no rule: deposits always landyes7000.0
withdraw(4000)7000.07000 - 4000 = 3000, and 3000 >= 1000yes3000.0
withdraw(2500)3000.03000 - 2500 = 500, and 500 < 1000no3000.0
CA-2002, a CurrentAccount, opens at 3000
deposit(1000)3000.0no ruleyes4000.0
withdraw(1000)4000.0funds suffice, so the reward firesyes3000.0, then +50 = 3050.0
withdraw(999999)3050.0funds do not suffice, so no rewardno3050.0

The last row is the one to study. The reward sits inside if (succeeded), so a rejected withdrawal earns nothing. Had withdraw returned void, that if could not have been written, and CA-2002 would have been paid 50 for a transaction that never happened.

Must memorise · How to prove polymorphism in six lines

Part 3 v asks you to confirm the correct overridden version runs. A proof needs a control: change one thing and show the behaviour changes.

So: same reference type, same method, same amount, same starting balance. Only the object differs.

BankAccount acc = new SavingAccount("SA-3003", "Ngozi Eze", 1500.0);acc.withdraw(600.0);        // rejected: would leave 900, under 1000acc = new CurrentAccount("CA-4004", "Tunde Ade", 1500.0);acc.withdraw(600.0);        // allowed, and pays a 50 reward: 950

Both variables are declared BankAccount. Both calls are acc.withdraw(600.0), character for character. Both accounts hold 1500.0. One is refused and one is paid a bonus.

That is the proof, and here is the sentence that earns the mark: the compiler only knew acc was a BankAccount, so the choice of which withdraw to run could not have been made at compile time. It was made at run time, from the object's actual class. That is dynamic method dispatch, and it is what "polymorphism" names (Unit 6.7).

MEMORY HOOK: the reference decides what you may call. The object decides what actually runs.

Compare this with the TRAP at the end of Unit 6.6, where the same setup silently ran the parent's method because the override was really an overload. Same two lines of code, opposite outcomes, and the difference was one parameter type. That is why @Override sits on every override here.

blocks.html:
Section C does not merely ask for a working program. It tells you which construct to use, and using a different one loses the mark even when the output is right.

"Use a switch" · "use nested if-else (not a switch, and not independent/separate if checks)" · "using a nested control statement" · "no StringBuilder" · "no collection classes" · "JOptionPane only" · "each task must be its own method".

And from the front page: use comments in Section B and Section C to say what each block does. That is an instruction, and it is free marks.

MEMORY HOOK: underline every noun that names a construct before you write anything. Those nouns are the marking scheme.

blocks.label: As printed
blocks.printed:
(12 marks)A. A conference organiser needs a program (using JOptionPane only, for all input/output) that prices tickets for a 3-day conference and produces a sales summary. Implement the following four methods.

i.    Create a method that takes in a day number. Use a switch statement to return a base ticket price for Day 1, Day 2, or Day 3 (pick any three distinct prices and state them clearly). If the day number is not 1, 2, or 3, throw an IllegalArgumentException.

ii.   Create a method that takes in a tier and a number of days attending. Use nested if-else statements (not a switch, and not independent/separate if checks) to return a discount percentage:

•  Gold, attending all 3 days -> 25%

•  Gold, attending 1-2 days -> 15%

•  Silver, attending all 3 days -> 15%

•  Silver, attending 1-2 days -> 5%

•  Bronze (any days) -> 0%

•  Any tier string that is not "Gold" or "Silver" must be treated as "Bronze"

The nesting must reflect that "days attending" is only checked within each tier branch, not as a separate top-level check.

iii.  Create a method that takes in a base price total and a discount percentage and applies the discount to the base price total. If the discounted amount is below 50.0, the method should return 50.0 instead (a price floor).

iv.  main()

•  Ask the user for the number of attendees N (a positive integer).

•  Loop exactly N times. In each iteration, ask for that attendee's number of days attending (an integer from 1 to 3, inclusive) and tier. For each day from 1 up to that attendee's days attending, call the method from part (i) and add the result to that attendee's running base price total (a running total that starts at 0 for each new attendee). Then call the method from part (ii) to get the discount percentage, and the method from part (iii) to get that attendee's final price.

•  Accumulate: (a) total revenue across all attendees, and (b) a running count of how many attendees were Gold, Silver, and Bronze.

v.   After the loop, show one summary dialog with total revenue and the three tier counts.

blocks.working:
Q5 a · conference ticket pricing · 12 MARKS
  1. takes a day number, uses a switch to return a base price for Day 1, 2 or 3 (pick any three distinct prices and state them clearly); any other day throws IllegalArgumentException;
  2. takes a tier and days attending, and uses nested if-else to return a discount: Gold 3 days 25%, Gold 1-2 days 15%, Silver 3 days 15%, Silver 1-2 days 5%, Bronze 0%, and any tier that is not "Gold" or "Silver" is Bronze. The nesting must reflect that days are only checked within each tier branch;
  3. takes a base total and a discount percentage, applies it, and returns 50.0 if the result would fall below 50.0 (a price floor);
  4. main(): ask for N attendees; loop N times asking days and tier; sum the day prices into a per-attendee base total; get the discount; get the final price; accumulate total revenue and a count of Gold, Silver and Bronze; then show one summary dialog.
Must memorise · Choose prices that let the floor fire

The question lets you pick the three prices. That freedom is a trap with a right answer.

Pick 15000, 12000 and 9000 and part 3's price floor can never fire. The largest possible discount is 25%, so nothing ever falls near 50.0. You will have written a floor you cannot demonstrate and the examiner cannot see work.

Pick 30.0, 25.0 and 20.0 and the floor becomes live: one Gold day is 30, less 15% is 25.50, which is below 50.0, so the method returns 50.0. The 50.0 floor is itself the hint about the scale the examiner had in mind.

MEMORY HOOK: when a question lets you choose the numbers, choose numbers that make every rule visible. A rule that never fires is a rule you cannot be shown to have written correctly.

Teach · What "nested, not separate" actually means here

Part 2 is unusually explicit: nested if-else, not a switch, not independent if checks, and "the nesting must reflect that days attending is only checked within each tier branch, not as a separate top-level check."

So the shape is forced. The tier decides the branch; the days are examined inside it:

What the question demandsWhat loses the mark
if (Gold) { if (days == 3) 25 else 15 }
else if (Silver) { if (days == 3) 15 else 5 }
else { 0 }		 if (Gold && days == 3) 25;
if (Gold && days < 3) 15;
if (Silver && days == 3) 15;
Right answers, wrong structure: days is tested at the top level, four separate times. This is what "not independent checks" forbids.

Why the final else is the whole Bronze rule. "Any tier string that is not Gold or Silver must be treated as Bronze" is not an extra check you add: it is what a bare else already means. Write else if (tier.equals("Bronze")) and you have broken the rule, because "Platinum" would then match nothing and fall through with no discount assigned. The bare else catches Bronze, Platinum, "gold" in lower case, and an empty string, which is exactly what was asked (Unit 4.4).

The same else must also do the counting. If "Platinum" is treated as Bronze for the discount, it is a Bronze attendee in the summary too. Count it anywhere else and your dialog contradicts your own pricing.

Code · question five, part a · VERIFIED ON THE JVM
import java.util.Scanner;public class ConferenceTickets {    // Part i: a switch returning the base price for a day. Any other day is illegal.    static double basePriceForDay(int day) {        switch (day) {            case 1:  return 30.0;            case 2:  return 25.0;            case 3:  return 20.0;            default: throw new IllegalArgumentException(                         "Day must be 1, 2 or 3 but was " + day);        }    }    // Part ii: NESTED if-else. Days are only examined inside a tier branch.    static double discountPercent(String tier, int daysAttending) {        if (tier.equals("Gold")) {            if (daysAttending == 3) {                return 25.0;            } else {                return 15.0;            }        } else if (tier.equals("Silver")) {            if (daysAttending == 3) {                return 15.0;            } else {                return 5.0;            }        } else {            return 0.0;        }    }    // Part iii: apply the discount, with a price floor of 50.0.    static double applyDiscount(double baseTotal, double percent) {        double discounted = baseTotal - (baseTotal * percent / 100.0);        if (discounted < 50.0) {            return 50.0;        }        return discounted;    }    public static void main(String[] args) {        Scanner in = new Scanner(System.in);        int attendees = Integer.parseInt(in.nextLine());        double totalRevenue = 0;        int goldCount = 0, silverCount = 0, bronzeCount = 0;        for (int a = 1; a <= attendees; a++) {            int days = Integer.parseInt(in.nextLine());            String tier = in.nextLine();            double baseTotal = 0;            for (int d = 1; d <= days; d++) {                baseTotal += basePriceForDay(d);            }            double percent = discountPercent(tier, days);            double finalPrice = applyDiscount(baseTotal, percent);            totalRevenue += finalPrice;            if (tier.equals("Gold")) {                goldCount++;            } else if (tier.equals("Silver")) {                silverCount++;            } else {                bronzeCount++;            }            System.out.println("Attendee " + a + ": " + tier + ", " + days                + " day(s), base "                + baseTotal + ", discount " + percent + "%, pays " + finalPrice);        }        System.out.println("SUMMARY");        System.out.println("Total revenue: " + totalRevenue);        System.out.println("Gold: " + goldCount + ", Silver: " + silverCount            + ", Bronze: " + bronzeCount);    }}
OutputAttendee 1: Gold, 3 day(s), base 75.0, discount 25.0%, pays 56.25
Attendee 2: Gold, 1 day(s), base 30.0, discount 15.0%, pays 50.0
Attendee 3: Silver, 2 day(s), base 55.0, discount 5.0%, pays 52.25
Attendee 4: Bronze, 1 day(s), base 30.0, discount 0.0%, pays 50.0
Attendee 5: Platinum, 3 day(s), base 75.0, discount 0.0%, pays 75.0
SUMMARY
Total revenue: 283.5
Gold: 2, Silver: 1, Bronze: 2

Read attendees 2 and 4: both would have paid less than 50 and both paid exactly 50.0, so the floor is visibly working. Read attendee 5: "Platinum" got a 0% discount and was counted as Bronze, so the two Bronze rules agree. Input is a Scanner here so the run can be printed; in the hall, every prompt is JOptionPane.showInputDialog and the summary is one showMessageDialog (F.11).

Trap · The switch must return, or fall through

Part 1's method must give back a price for 1, 2 and 3 and throw otherwise. Writing return inside each case is what makes that safe: a return leaves the method immediately, so no break is needed and there is no fall-through to worry about (Unit 4.3).

Use double price; with assignments instead and you must not forget the breaks, and the compiler will additionally complain that price "might not have been initialized" unless every path assigns it. The default: throw is what convinces the compiler every path is covered: an exception is a legitimate way to leave a method that promised to return a double, because it does not return at all.

Note also that throw needs no throws clause here. IllegalArgumentException is unchecked (Unit 10.1), which is Q1 B's distinction being examined a second time on the same paper.

blocks.text: The cold-storage log, and the streak that ends at midnight

blocks.label: As printed
blocks.printed:
(13 marks)B. A cold-storage warehouse records its internal temperature once every hour, for 24 hours. Write a program, using JOptionPane only for input/output, that checks the day's temperature log for sustained breaches of a safe limit. A reading is a breach if it is above 8°C.

i.    Using a loop, prompt the user 24 times (one dialog per hour) for that hour's temperature. Each input must be validated: it must parse as a number between -20 and 50 inclusive. If invalid, re-prompt for the same hour (using a nested loop/control statement) until a valid value is entered. Store all 24 valid readings in a 1-D array.

ii.   Scan the 24-hour array once to find every maximal run of consecutive breach-hours (temperature > 8°C). Using only loops and conditionals (no extra arrays), determine:

•  the total number of qualifying streaks, where a qualifying streak is any consecutive run of 3 or more breach-hours;

•  the length (in hours) of the single longest breach streak anywhere in the log.

iii.  Using nested if-else logic, classify the day as exactly one of:

•  "CRITICAL": longest streak >= 6 hours

•  "WARNING": longest streak is 3-5 hours (inclusive)

•  "SAFE": no streak of 3 or more consecutive breach-hours occurred

iv.  Show one JOptionPane dialog stating: the total number of qualifying streaks, the longest streak length, and the final classification.

blocks.label: Break it down first
blocks.question: What is this question actually asking, what have you been given, and what do the marks tell you about how much to write? Decide, then check.
blocks.answer:
GivenA 24-hour log, a breach threshold, and three classifications.
Asked forValidated input, a single scan, a classification, and one dialog.
The marks13 marks.
WatchTwo constraints do the real work: "scan once" and "no extra arrays", which together forbid the obvious approach of collecting streak lengths into a list. Track the current run and the best run as you go. Note also that a breach is strictly above 8, so exactly 8 is safe.
Taught inUnits 4.2 to 4.6, 6.3 and F.11.

blocks.working:
Q5 b · sustained breaches of a safe limit · 13 MARKS
  1. prompt 24 times, one dialog per hour. Each input must parse as a number between -20 and 50 inclusive; if invalid, re-prompt for the same hour using a nested loop, until valid. Store all 24 in a 1-D array;
  2. scan the array once, using only loops and conditionals (no extra arrays), to find the number of qualifying streaks (runs of 3 or more consecutive breach-hours) and the length of the longest breach streak;
  3. using nested if-else, classify: CRITICAL if the longest streak is >= 6, WARNING if it is 3 to 5, SAFE if no streak of 3 or more occurred;
  4. show one dialog with the streak count, the longest length, and the classification.
Must memorise · Count the run when it turns 3, and measure it as you go

The whole of part 2 is three variables and one pass:

currentRun: breach hours in a row right now, reset to 0 on any non-breach.
longestStreak: updated every breach hour, not at the end of a run.
qualifyingStreaks: incremented when currentRun == 3, exactly.

Why == 3 and not >= 3. A run passes through 3 exactly once, on its third hour. So == 3 counts each qualifying run once, however long it becomes. Use >= 3 and a 6-hour run is counted four times, giving 4 streaks where there is one.

MEMORY HOOK: a run is counted at the moment it qualifies, not while it continues. The threshold is a door you pass through once, not a room you stay in.

Trap · The streak that is still running when the day ends

The instinct is to close each run in the else, where the non-breach hour is: "the run just ended, so now measure it."

if (readings[hour] > 8) {    currentRun++;} else {    if (currentRun > longestStreak) longestStreak = currentRun;  // non-breach only    if (currentRun >= 3) qualifyingStreaks++;    currentRun = 0;}

It works, until the day ends mid-streak. If hours 18 to 23 are all breaches, the loop finishes with currentRun = 6 and never reaches the else. The longest streak of the day is never measured and never counted. The program reports SAFE on a day the freezer was over temperature for six straight hours.

The fix is not to bolt a copy of the else-block on after the loop. That is the usual patch and it duplicates the logic in two places, so the next edit changes one and forgets the other. Instead, update on every breach hour:

Measure longestStreak as the run grows, and count the run the instant it turns 3. Then a run that is still going when the array ends has already been measured and already been counted, and the end of the array needs no special case at all.

This is worth more than one exam question. A boundary you never treat specially cannot be got wrong at the boundary.

Code · question five, part b · VERIFIED ON THE JVM
import java.util.Scanner;public class ColdStorage {    public static void main(String[] args) {        Scanner in = new Scanner(System.in);        double[] readings = new double[24];        // Part i: 24 prompts, each re-prompted until the value is valid.        for (int hour = 0; hour < 24; hour++) {            boolean valid = false;            while (!valid) {                String typed = in.nextLine();                try {                    double t = Double.parseDouble(typed);                    if (t >= -20 && t <= 50) {                        readings[hour] = t;                        valid = true;                    } else {                        System.out.println("  hour " + hour + ": " + t                            + " is outside -20 to 50. Asking again.");                    }                } catch (NumberFormatException e) {                    System.out.println("  hour " + hour + ": \"" + typed                        + "\" is not a number. Asking again.");                }            }        }        // Part ii: ONE scan, no extra arrays.        int currentRun = 0, longestStreak = 0, qualifyingStreaks = 0;        for (int hour = 0; hour < 24; hour++) {            if (readings[hour] > 8) {                currentRun++;                if (currentRun > longestStreak) {                    longestStreak = currentRun;                }                if (currentRun == 3) {                    qualifyingStreaks++;                }            } else {                currentRun = 0;            }        }        // Part iii: classify.        String classification;        if (longestStreak >= 6) {            classification = "CRITICAL";        } else if (longestStreak >= 3) {            classification = "WARNING";        } else {            classification = "SAFE";        }        // Part iv: one dialog.        String message = "Qualifying streaks (3+ hours): " + qualifyingStreaks                       + "\nLongest breach streak: " + longestStreak + " hour(s)"                       + "\nClassification: " + classification;        System.out.println(message);    }}
Output  hour 0: 99.0 is outside -20 to 50. Asking again.
  hour 0: "abc" is not a number. Asking again.
Qualifying streaks (3+ hours): 3
Longest breach streak: 6 hour(s)
Classification: CRITICAL

The run fed hour 0 a 99, then the text "abc", then a valid 5, so both halves of "must parse as a number between -20 and 50" are shown rejecting input and re-prompting the same hour.

Dry run · The 24 hours, and where the three streaks are
breach = above 8. The bar shows breach hours.
hoursreadingsbreach runcounted?
0 to 35, 9, 10, 42 in a rowno: under 3
4 to 79, 9, 9, 23 in a rowyes, streak 1
8 to 1312, 11, 9, 9, 10, 35 in a rowyes, streak 2
14 to 171, 2, 3, 4noneno
18 to 239, 9, 9, 9, 9, 96 in a row, to the last houryes, streak 3
Answerslongest = 63 streaks, CRITICAL

The first run of 2 is the control: it proves the counter is not simply counting runs. The last run is the trap above, live: it reaches hour 23 and stops because the day stopped, not because the temperature did. It is both the longest streak and the one that decides the classification, and the else-branch version would have missed it entirely and printed WARNING.

blocks.label: As printed
blocks.printed:
(12 marks)A. Design and implement a program, using JOptionPane only for input and output, that classifies a single user-supplied positive integer N according to its digit pattern (Palindrome).

Definition: A number is a palindrome if it reads the same forwards and backwards (i.e. it is equal to its own digit-reversed value). For example, 4884 and 7 are palindromes; 4821 is not.

Constraints: The entire task must be implemented inside main() only, using loops and nested/chained if-else and/or switch logic. No arrays and no user-defined helper methods are permitted; everything must be inline.

i.    Using a loop built only on the % and / operators (no converting N to a String or array), compute, in the same loop:

•  the digit sum of N, and

•  the value of N with its digits reversed (e.g. for N = 4821, the reversed value is 1284).

ii.   Determine whether N is a palindrome by comparing N directly to the reversed value computed in step 1.

iii.  Inline in main() (not a separate method), determine whether the digit sum from step 1 is itself a prime number. Use a loop that tests divisibility only up to the square root of the digit sum.

iv.  Using nested/chained conditional logic, classify N into exactly one of the following categories, checked strictly in this priority order:

•  "PALINDROME-PRIME-SUM": if N is a palindrome AND its digit sum is prime

•  "PALINDROME": if N is a palindrome but its digit sum is not prime

•  "HARSHAD": if N is not a palindrome but N is exactly divisible by its own digit sum

•  "STANDARD": in every other case

v.   Display N, its digit sum, its reversed value, and its final classification in a single JOptionPane message dialog.
