blocks.question: What is this question actually asking, what have you been given, and what do the marks tell you about how much to write? Decide, then check.
blocks.answer:
GivenA definition, worked examples, and a hard set of constraints.
Asked forOne inline program. No helper methods and no arrays, which is unusual and deliberate.
The marks12 marks.
WatchPart i says compute both values in the same loop, so one pass produces the digit sum and the reversal together. Part iv says "checked strictly in this priority order": an if-else chain in that exact order, because a number can satisfy two categories at once.
Taught inUnits 3.6, 4.2 to 4.5 and F.11.

blocks.label: Model answer
blocks.problem: Write your answer to the question above in your book first. It carries 12 marks, so write one clear point for every mark. Then open the model answer and mark yourself against it.
blocks.working:
Q6 a · classify a number by its digit pattern · 12 MARKS
  1. in one loop, built only on % and / (no converting N to a String or array), compute both the digit sum of N and N with its digits reversed;
  2. N is a palindrome if it equals its reversed value;
  3. inline, decide whether the digit sum is prime, testing divisibility only up to its square root;
  4. classify, strictly in this priority order: PALINDROME-PRIME-SUM (palindrome and sum prime), PALINDROME (palindrome, sum not prime), HARSHAD (not a palindrome, but N divides exactly by its digit sum), STANDARD otherwise;
  5. show N, its digit sum, its reversed value and its classification in a single dialog.
Must memorise · The digit loop, and the copy that saves it

Peeling digits off a number is three lines you should be able to write without thinking:

int digit = temp % 10;   takes the last digit
reversed = reversed * 10 + digit;   pushes it onto the right of the answer
temp = temp / 10;   drops the last digit

Loop while (temp > 0). Both answers fall out of one pass.

The line the marks hang on is int temp = n;. The loop destroys whatever it walks: temp ends at 0. Walk n itself and by step 2 there is nothing left to compare the reversed value against, and nothing left to divide in step 4. Copy it, consume the copy.

reversed * 10 + digit is worth a moment. Take 4821: the loop pulls 1, then 2, then 8, then 4. Start at 0, and each step shifts what you have one place left and drops the new digit into the units: 1, then 12, then 128, then 1284. The digits come off backwards, which is exactly why pushing them on in the order they arrive reverses the number.

MEMORY HOOK: % takes the last digit, / removes it. Every digit problem in this course is those two lines and a loop.

Teach · The square root test, without Math.sqrt

Part 3 says test divisibility only up to the square root of the digit sum. The clean way needs no square root at all:

boolean sumIsPrime = (digitSum >= 2);for (int f = 2; f * f <= digitSum; f++) {    if (digitSum % f == 0) { sumIsPrime = false; break; }}

f * f <= digitSum is "f is at most the square root of digitSum", squared on both sides. It stays in whole numbers, so there is no Math.sqrt, no double, and no floating-point comparison to get wrong at the boundary (Unit 3.6).

Why stopping at the square root is correct, not just faster. If digitSum = a * b, then a and b cannot both be above the square root, or their product would exceed digitSum. So every factor pairs with one at or below the square root. Find none there and there are none at all.

And the initialiser is the whole edge case. digitSum >= 2 is what makes 1 not prime and 0 not prime. The loop cannot help you: for digitSum = 1 it never runs, so whatever you started with survives. Start at true and the program declares 1 prime, and then N = 1 (a palindrome with digit sum 1) is misclassified. See the table below, last row.

Code · question six, part a · VERIFIED ON THE JVM
import java.util.Scanner;public class PalindromeClassifier {    public static void main(String[] args) {        Scanner in = new Scanner(System.in);        int n = Integer.parseInt(in.nextLine());        // Step i: ONE loop, using only % and /, computing BOTH the digit sum and        // the reversed value. temp is consumed; n must survive for step ii.        int temp = n;        int digitSum = 0;        int reversed = 0;        while (temp > 0) {            int digit = temp % 10;            digitSum = digitSum + digit;            reversed = reversed * 10 + digit;            temp = temp / 10;        }        // Step ii: palindrome is a comparison against the ORIGINAL n.        boolean isPalindrome = (n == reversed);        // Step iii: is digitSum prime? Test factors only up to its square root.        boolean sumIsPrime = (digitSum >= 2);        for (int f = 2; f * f <= digitSum; f++) {            if (digitSum % f == 0) {                sumIsPrime = false;                break;            }        }        // Step iv: classify, in the paper's priority order.        String classification;        if (isPalindrome) {            if (sumIsPrime) {                classification = "PALINDROME-PRIME-SUM";            } else {                classification = "PALINDROME";            }        } else if (n % digitSum == 0) {            classification = "HARSHAD";        } else {            classification = "STANDARD";        }        // Step v: one dialog with all four facts.        String message = "N: " + n                       + "\nDigit sum: " + digitSum                       + "\nReversed: " + reversed                       + "\nClassification: " + classification;        System.out.println(message);    }}
OutputN: 4884
Digit sum: 24
Reversed: 4884
Classification: PALINDROME

4884 is the paper's own example. It is a palindrome, and 24 = 2 × 12 is not prime, so it is PALINDROME and not PALINDROME-PRIME-SUM. That is the priority order doing its job.

Code · the same statements, run over every case · SO THE TABLE IS REAL

This is not the exam answer: the question forbids helper methods and demands a single N. It is the identical block of statements with a loop around it, so that every row below is real output rather than someone's arithmetic.

import java.util.Scanner;// The SAME statements as the answer, with a loop around them, so that every row// of the table in this book is real output rather than someone's arithmetic.public class ClassifierBench {    public static void main(String[] args) {        Scanner in = new Scanner(System.in);        System.out.println("     N | sum | reversed | classification");        while (in.hasNextLine()) {            String line = in.nextLine();            if (line.isEmpty()) {                continue;            }            int n = Integer.parseInt(line);            int temp = n, digitSum = 0, reversed = 0;            while (temp > 0) {                int digit = temp % 10;                digitSum = digitSum + digit;                reversed = reversed * 10 + digit;                temp = temp / 10;            }            boolean isPalindrome = (n == reversed);            boolean sumIsPrime = (digitSum >= 2);            for (int f = 2; f * f <= digitSum; f++) {                if (digitSum % f == 0) {                    sumIsPrime = false;                    break;                }            }            String classification;            if (isPalindrome) {                classification = sumIsPrime ? "PALINDROME-PRIME-SUM" : "PALINDROME";            } else if (n % digitSum == 0) {                classification = "HARSHAD";            } else {                classification = "STANDARD";            }            System.out.printf("%6d | %3d | %8d | %s%n", n, digitSum, reversed,                classification);        }    }}
Output     N | sum | reversed | classification
  4884 |  24 |     4884 | PALINDROME
     7 |   7 |        7 | PALINDROME-PRIME-SUM
  4821 |  15 |     1284 | STANDARD
    21 |   3 |       12 | HARSHAD
   131 |   5 |      131 | PALINDROME-PRIME-SUM
     1 |   1 |        1 | PALINDROME

Six rows, and every branch of part 4 is exercised. 4884 and 4821 are the paper's own two examples and both come out as the paper says. 7 is its one-digit palindrome. 4821: the digit sum is 15 and 4821 = 15 × 321 + 6, so it is not a Harshad number either, and it falls to STANDARD. 1 is the row worth staring at: a palindrome whose digit sum is 1, and 1 is not prime, so PALINDROME. Get the initialiser wrong and this row alone would read PALINDROME-PRIME-SUM.

Trap · "Priority order" means else-if, not four ifs

Part 4 says checked strictly in this priority order and exactly one category. Both phrases point at the same structure: one chain, where reaching a test means every test above it already failed.

Write four independent ifs and a palindrome with a prime digit sum matches the first, then falls into the others too, and your single dialog reports whichever assignment landed last. The chain is what makes "exactly one" true, and it is also what makes HARSHAD's rule readable: HARSHAD never has to say "and is not a palindrome", because it is only ever reached when the palindrome test failed. The order does that work, which is precisely why the question fixes it (Unit 4.2).

Watch n % digitSum in the HARSHAD test. It is safe here only because N is a positive integer, so digitSum is at least 1 and never 0. Take that guarantee away and it throws ArithmeticException (Unit 3.6): a division by zero hiding in a remainder.

blocks.text: The parking garage, and three counts from one method

blocks.label: As printed
blocks.printed:
(13 marks)B. A university parking garage needs a program, using JOptionPane only for input/output, to process a batch of vehicles exiting on the same day and calculate the total fees owed. The program must use clear separation of concerns; each task below must be its own method. No collection classes (e.g. ArrayList) are allowed anywhere.

i.    Prompt for the number of exiting vehicles, V. Then, using a loop, fill two parallel arrays of length V:

•  the number of hours each vehicle was parked (an integer per vehicle). A value <= 0 is invalid; use a nested control statement to keep re-prompting until a valid value is entered.

•  the permit type for each vehicle (a String per vehicle, either "Staff" or "Visitor").

ii.   Create a method that takes in one vehicle's hours parked and permit type, and computes one vehicle's fee using nested if-else logic (the rules below must be nested together, not checked as separate independent conditions):

•  Staff: first 2 hours free; each additional hour costs 1.00; capped at a maximum of 10.00/day.

•  Visitor: no free period; first 3 hours cost a flat 6.00; each hour beyond 3 costs 2.50; capped at a maximum of 25.00/day.

•  Any permit type that is not exactly "Staff" must be treated as "Visitor".

iii.  Create a method that takes in the array of hours parked, loops over the array and tallies vehicles into three categories: SHORT-STAY (1-2 hrs), STANDARD (3-6 hrs), EXTENDED (>6 hrs). Return these three counts without using any collection class.

iv.  In main(),

•  call the method from part (ii) for every vehicle across both parallel arrays to accumulate the batch's total revenue

•  call the method from part (iii) once

•  display one final JOptionPane showing the total revenue and the three category counts.

blocks.question: What is this question actually asking, what have you been given, and what do the marks tell you about how much to write? Decide, then check.
blocks.answer:
GivenTwo fee schedules and three stay categories.
Asked forParallel arrays, one fee method, one tally method, and a main that calls them.
The marks13 marks.
WatchPart iii asks one method to return three counts with no collection class allowed, which is the real puzzle: an int[] of three is the intended way out. Note also the caps are on the fee, not the hours, so compute then clamp.
Taught inUnits 6.3 to 6.6, 5.4, 4.2 and F.11.

blocks.label: Model answer
blocks.problem: Write your answer to the question above in your book first. It carries 13 marks, so write one clear point for every mark. Then open the model answer and mark yourself against it.
blocks.working:
Q6 b · parking fees for a batch of vehicles · 13 MARKS
  1. prompt for the number of vehicles V, then fill two parallel arrays of length V: hours parked (int per vehicle; a value <= 0 is invalid, so use a nested control statement to re-prompt until valid) and permit type (String per vehicle, "Staff" or "Visitor");
  2. a method taking one vehicle's hours and permit, computing its fee with nested if-else: Staff, first 2 hours free, each additional hour 1.00, capped at 10.00/day; Visitor, no free period, first 3 hours a flat 6.00, each hour beyond 3 costs 2.50, capped at 25.00/day; and any permit that is not exactly "Staff" is treated as Visitor;
  3. a method taking the hours array, tallying SHORT-STAY (1-2), STANDARD (3-6) and EXTENDED (>6), returning the three counts without any collection class;
  4. main(): call (ii) for every vehicle across both arrays to accumulate revenue, call (iii) once, and display one dialog with the total and the three counts.
Must memorise · Three counts, one return, no collections

Part 3 asks for three numbers back. A Java method returns one value. And ArrayList is banned.

So return an int[] of length 3.

An array is not a collection class. That distinction is the question: "collection classes (e.g. ArrayList)" means java.util's List/Set/Map family. An array is a built-in Java type, not a class you import, which is why F.10 and Module 8 exist and why the ban costs you nothing.

Document the slots in a comment ([0] short, [1] standard, [2] extended) and use them in that order. The alternative the ban is steering you away from is three separate fields or three methods walking the same array three times.

MEMORY HOOK: one return value, several numbers, no collections: that is an array.

Teach · Parallel arrays, and the invariant that keeps them honest

Two arrays are parallel when index i in one and index i in the other describe the same thing. hoursParked[3] and permitType[3] are one car.

The whole idea rests on one invariant: they are the same length and they are always written together. The loop in part 1 fills both in the same iteration, which is what keeps them aligned. Fill them in two separate loops, or continue past one but not the other, and vehicle 3's hours are paired with vehicle 4's permit. Nothing throws. Every fee is simply wrong.

In Module 6's terms this is what a class is for: a Vehicle object holding hours and permit together cannot fall out of step, because there is no "step" to fall out of. The paper asks for parallel arrays, so write parallel arrays; but knowing what they are the poor relation of is what Q4 was testing.

Code · question six, part b · VERIFIED ON THE JVM
import java.util.Scanner;public class ParkingGarage {    // Part ii: one vehicle's fee, by NESTED if-else. The permit decides the branch;    // the hours are only examined inside it.    static double feeFor(int hours, String permit) {        double fee;        if (permit.equals("Staff")) {            if (hours <= 2) {                fee = 0.0;            } else {                fee = (hours - 2) * 1.00;                if (fee > 10.00) {                    fee = 10.00;                }            }        } else {            if (hours <= 3) {                fee = 6.00;            } else {                fee = 6.00 + (hours - 3) * 2.50;                if (fee > 25.00) {                    fee = 25.00;                }            }        }        return fee;    }    // Part iii: tally the three categories. Three counts, one return value, and no    // collection class: an int[] of length 3. An array is not a collection.    // [0] SHORT-STAY (1-2), [1] STANDARD (3-6), [2] EXTENDED (>6)    static int[] tally(int[] hoursParked) {        int[] counts = new int[3];        for (int i = 0; i < hoursParked.length; i++) {            if (hoursParked[i] <= 2) {                counts[0]++;            } else if (hoursParked[i] <= 6) {                counts[1]++;            } else {                counts[2]++;            }        }        return counts;    }    public static void main(String[] args) {        Scanner in = new Scanner(System.in);        int vehicles = Integer.parseInt(in.nextLine());        // Part i: two PARALLEL arrays. Index i is one vehicle in both.        int[] hoursParked = new int[vehicles];        String[] permitType = new String[vehicles];        for (int i = 0; i < vehicles; i++) {            int hours = Integer.parseInt(in.nextLine());            while (hours <= 0) {                System.out.println("  vehicle " + i + ": " + hours                    + " is not a valid number of hours. Asking again.");                hours = Integer.parseInt(in.nextLine());            }            hoursParked[i] = hours;            permitType[i] = in.nextLine();        }        // Part iv: accumulate revenue across both arrays, then tally once.        double totalRevenue = 0;        for (int i = 0; i < vehicles; i++) {            double fee = feeFor(hoursParked[i], permitType[i]);            totalRevenue += fee;            System.out.println("Vehicle " + i + ": " + hoursParked[i] + "h, "                + permitType[i] + " -> " + fee);        }        int[] counts = tally(hoursParked);        String message = "Total revenue: " + totalRevenue                       + "\nSHORT-STAY (1-2 hrs): " + counts[0]                       + "\nSTANDARD (3-6 hrs): " + counts[1]                       + "\nEXTENDED (>6 hrs): " + counts[2];        System.out.println(message);    }}
Output  vehicle 0: 0 is not a valid number of hours. Asking again.
Vehicle 0: 2h, Staff -> 0.0
Vehicle 1: 5h, Staff -> 3.0
Vehicle 2: 15h, Staff -> 10.0
Vehicle 3: 1h, Visitor -> 6.0
Vehicle 4: 5h, Visitor -> 11.0
Vehicle 5: 12h, Guest -> 25.0
Total revenue: 55.0
SHORT-STAY (1-2 hrs): 2
STANDARD (3-6 hrs): 2
EXTENDED (>6 hrs): 2
Dry run · Every rule in the fee table, fired once
hourspermitwhich rule, and the arithmeticfee
2Stafffirst 2 hours free, and 2 is not beyond 20.00
5Staff(5 - 2) × 1.00 = 3.00, under the 10.00 cap3.00
15Staff(15 - 2) × 1.00 = 13.00, over the cap10.00
1Visitorflat 6.00 for the first 3 hours, even for 16.00
5Visitor6.00 + (5 - 3) × 2.50 = 11.0011.00
12Guestnot exactly "Staff", so Visitor: 6.00 + 9 × 2.50 = 28.50, over the cap25.00
Total revenue55.00

Every rule in the question fires exactly once in that table, which is how the test data was chosen: both free periods, both per-hour rates, both caps, and the not-Staff-means-Visitor rule. When you invent your own test data, invent it like this: one row per rule, so a single run proves the lot.

Two rows repay a second look. 1 hour as a Visitor costs 6.00: "first 3 hours cost a flat 6.00" is a flat fee, not a rate, so an hour and three hours cost the same, and a Visitor pays more than a Staff member who stayed fifteen. That is not a bug, it is the pricing the question specifies. And Guest at 12 hours is the only row testing the fallback rule; delete it from your test data and a program that crashes on unknown permits would look perfectly healthy.

Must memorise · A cap is a ceiling you apply after, not a rule you fold in

Compute the fee, then clamp it:

fee = 6.00 + (hours - 3) * 2.50;
if (fee > 25.00) { fee = 25.00; }

The temptation is to work out the hour at which the cap bites (for Visitors, 10.6 hours) and branch on that. It gives the same answers and it is a worse answer: you have hidden a magic number that no line of the question contains, and changing the rate to 3.00 silently breaks it, because the crossover moves and your constant does not.

This is the same shape as Q5 A's price floor, which is a cap from below. Both read as one line placed after the sum, and both then say plainly what the question said: capped at a maximum of 25.00/day.

MEMORY HOOK: compute, then clamp. Never solve for where the clamp starts.

title: The 2024/2025 Paper, Every Question
lead: Every question on this paper, printed exactly as the examiner set it. For each one: read it, write your full answer in your book, and only then open the model answer. Reading an answer you have not attempted teaches you almost nothing.

blocks.text: The 2024/25 paper, and why you are reading it

blocks.label: Must memorise
blocks.tag: The format changed; the skills did not
blocks.html:
2024/25: six questions at 17.5 marks, attempt any four. No sections.
2025/26: three sections, one question from each, 20 + 25 + 25.

Both are 70 marks over 3 hours. Both test exactly four things: define, debug, dry run, write a program.

The course was even retitled between the two: "Object-Oriented Programming (Java)" became "Computer Programming I (Java)". Same code, COS221, same lecturer, same syllabus.

So do not learn a paper. Learn the four skills. A format can change again between the writing of this book and the day you sit down; the four things being tested have not changed in two years and will not.

MEMORY HOOK: define, debug, dry run, write. Every question on both papers is one of those four, or a bundle of all four.

blocks.label: Teach
blocks.html:
Each of the six questions is the same four parts, in the same order, for the same marks. Recognising this is worth as much as any single answer:

PartMarksWhat it always is
A3Define or describe three terms. One mark each, one sentence each.
B3Debug: list and correct the errors in a snippet.
C4Dry run: state the output, sometimes per iteration.
D7.5Write a program to a specification.

Q5 and Q6 shuffle the order slightly (Q5 B asks you to write a method; Q6 A asks for loop snippets), but the marks are identical and so is the intent.

This book answers all six. The paper says attempt four, and in the hall you will. But a question you skip is a topic you can be examined on next year, and the 25/26 paper proves it: it took this paper's file I/O, its inheritance and its digit-loops and asked them again in a different costume.

The marks3 marks, three terms: one mark, one sentence each. An essay on overloading cannot earn the mark for void method.

Taught inUnits 5.1, 5.2 and 5.6.

blocks.working:
Q1 a · define method signature, overloading, and void method · 3 MARKS

Model answer. One mark each, and each is one sentence.

  1. Method signature. A method's name together with its parameter list (the number, types and order of its parameters). The return type is not part of the signature. It is what the compiler uses to tell one method from another.
  2. Method overloading. Declaring more than one method with the same name but different parameter lists in the same class, so the compiler chooses between them at compile time by matching the arguments at the call site against each signature.
  3. Void method. A method declared void, meaning it returns no value. It is called as a statement on its own, cannot be used in an expression, and may use a bare return; to exit early.

Where the marks are: the examiner asked for signature and overloading in the same breath deliberately, because the second is defined by the first. Say "signature = name + parameter list, return type excluded" and the overloading definition writes itself. Units 5.1, 5.2 and 5.6.

Q1 b · debug squarecalc · 3 MARKS
Compiler outputerror: <identifier> expected

The errors, listed. The question says list and correct, so list them: a correction with no list is half an answer.

  1. Line 2: main(String[] ) has no parameter name. A parameter needs a type and a name. Fix: main(String[] args).
  2. Line 4: no semicolon after double result = square(num).
  3. Line 8: square(int) has no parameter name. Fix: square(int n).
  4. Line 9: n does not exist. It is the symptom of error 3: name the parameter and n exists. Worth saying out loud in your answer, because it shows you understand the cause rather than listing every red squiggle.
  5. The braces are missing for both square and the class.

Three marks, five errors. Do not stop at three: the marker is looking for the set, and errors 3 and 4 are one fault with two faces.

Code · q1 b corrected · VERIFIED ON THE JVM
public class SquareCalc {    public static void main(String[] args) {        int num = 5;        double result = square(num);        System.out.println("Square is: " + result);    }    public static int square(int n) {        return n * n;    }}
OutputSquare is: 25.0

Look hard at that output: 25.0, not 25. square returns an int, and 25 is stored into a double result. Java widens the int to a double on the way in (Unit 5.7), so what gets printed is a double, and a double always prints its point. Nothing is wrong; but if you wrote "Square is: 25" you have missed a mark that costs nothing to get right.

Q1 c · dry run sumseries with 3, 4, 5, 7 · 4 MARKS

The answer is 0. For all four values.

Must memorise · Four values, one answer, and that is the question

j and j + 1 are both int, so j / (j + 1) is integer division.

j is always smaller than j + 1. A smaller int divided by a larger int is always 0. Every term is 0. The sum is 0.

1/2 is 0. 2/3 is 0. 3/4 is 0. Not 0.5, 0.67, 0.75: 0, because integer division throws the remainder away (Unit 3.6). It does not round; it truncates.

Why the examiner gave you four values. Being handed 3, 4, 5 and 7 shouts "four different answers". It is bait. The four values are there so that you either notice the types once and answer all four in one line, or trace fractions by hand for ten minutes and write four confident wrong numbers.

MEMORY HOOK: int / int is an int. Before you trace any division, look at the two types. One double anywhere on top and the answer changes completely: 1.0 / 2 is 0.5.

Code · the paper's own method, run · VERIFIED ON THE JVM
public class SumSeriesTrace {    // exactly as the paper prints it    public static int sumSeries(int i) {        int sum = 0;        for (int j = 1; j <= i; j++) {            sum += j / (j + 1);        }        return sum;    }    public static void main(String[] args) {        System.out.println("sumSeries(3) = " + sumSeries(3));        System.out.println("sumSeries(4) = " + sumSeries(4));        System.out.println("sumSeries(5) = " + sumSeries(5));        System.out.println("sumSeries(7) = " + sumSeries(7));        System.out.println("and the terms themselves: 1/2 = " + (1 / 2)            + ", 2/3 = " + (2 / 3) + ", 3/4 = " + (3 / 4));        System.out.println("with a double on top:     1.0/2 = " + (1.0 / 2));    }}
OutputsumSeries(3) = 0
sumSeries(4) = 0
sumSeries(5) = 0
sumSeries(7) = 0
and the terms themselves: 1/2 = 0, 2/3 = 0, 3/4 = 0
with a double on top:     1.0/2 = 0.5

Four inputs, one answer. The last two lines are the whole explanation: every term really is 0, and the single change that would rescue the method is a double on top.

Dry run · How to write this up for 4 marks

Do not just write "0" four times. Show the trace for one value and generalise; that is what the marks are for.

sumSeries(3): the loop runs for j = 1, 2, 3
jj / (j + 1)in real arithmeticas int divisionsum
11 / 20.500
22 / 30.66700
33 / 40.7500

Then one sentence: "for any i, every term j/(j+1) has j < j+1, so integer division gives 0 every time; therefore sumSeries returns 0 for 3, 4, 5 and 7 alike." That sentence is the answer to all four values, and it is worth more than four traced tables.

blocks.printed:
[7.5 marks]D. Write a program that overloads a method named area to compute:

i.    The area of a circle

ii.   The area of a rectangle

iii.  The area of a triangle.

Call these methods and print out their values in the main method.

blocks.label: Break it down first
blocks.question: What is this question actually asking, what have you been given, and what do the marks tell you about how much to write? Decide, then check.
blocks.answer:
GivenNothing. You write the whole program.
Asked forThree methods that share the name area and differ in parameter list, plus a main that calls them and prints.
The marks7.5 marks. The last sentence is a separate instruction carrying its own marks: three correct methods with no main is an incomplete answer.
WatchOverloading is resolved by the parameter list. Circle takes one argument, rectangle and triangle take two, so rectangle and triangle collide unless you distinguish them. Decide how before you start writing.
Taught inUnits 5.6 and 5.7.

blocks.working:
Q1 d · overload area for circle, rectangle and triangle · 7.5 MARKS
Must memorise · The obvious answer to this question does not compile

Circle needs one number. Rectangle needs two. Triangle needs two.

So rectangle is area(double, double), and triangle (base and height) is also area(double, double).

That is the same signature. It will not compile.

Overloading needs different parameter lists, and "base, height" is not different from "length, width": the parameter names are not part of the signature, only the types (Q1 A, which you just answered). Write both and javac says:

error: method area(double,double) is already defined in class

The resolution: give the triangle a three-number formula, so its signature is area(double, double, double) and distinct. Heron's formula takes the three sides:

s = (a + b + c) / 2     and     area = √ s(s-a)(s-b)(s-c) 

MEMORY HOOK: overloads differ by types, not by names. If two of your methods take the same types in the same order, you have one method and a compiler error.

This is the single most valuable thing in Question One, and the examiner may not have noticed it. Say it explicitly in your answer: "base and height would collide with length and width, so the triangle is done by Heron's formula on three sides, giving a distinct signature." That sentence proves you understand overloading, which is what the question is for.

Code · q1 d, complete · VERIFIED ON THE JVM
public class AreaOverload {    // i. circle: one number, so the signature is area(double)    public static double area(double radius) {        return Math.PI * radius * radius;    }    // ii. rectangle: two numbers, so the signature is area(double, double)    public static double area(double length, double width) {        return length * width;    }    // iii. triangle: base and height would ALSO be area(double, double), which is    // the rectangle's signature and will not compile. Three sides gives a distinct    // signature and a genuine formula: Heron's.    public static double area(double sideA, double sideB, double sideC) {        double s = (sideA + sideB + sideC) / 2;        return Math.sqrt(s * (s - sideA) * (s - sideB) * (s - sideC));    }    public static void main(String[] args) {        System.out.println("Circle, radius 7      : " + area(7.0));        System.out.println("Rectangle, 5 by 3     : " + area(5.0, 3.0));        System.out.println("Triangle, sides 3 4 5 : " + area(3.0, 4.0, 5.0));    }}
OutputCircle, radius 7      : 153.93804002589985
Rectangle, 5 by 3     : 15.0
Triangle, sides 3 4 5 : 6.0

Check the triangle without trusting Heron. 3, 4, 5 is a right triangle, so its area must be half of 3 × 4, which is 6. Heron gave exactly 6.0. When you use a formula you cannot see through, feed it a case whose answer you already know. Math.PI and Math.sqrt are Unit 3.6.

blocks.label: Break it down first
blocks.question: What is this question actually asking, what have you been given, and what do the marks tell you about how much to write? Decide, then check.
blocks.answer:
GivenNothing. Recall.
Asked forThree definitions again, one per term.
The marks3 marks, one per term, one sentence each.
Watchlength is a property (a field), not a method, so it takes no brackets. Saying "length()" in a definition question throws the mark away.
Taught inUnits 6.1 to 6.4.

blocks.problem: Write your answer to the question above in your book first. It carries 3 marks, so write one clear point for every mark. Then open the model answer and mark yourself against it.
blocks.working:
Q2 a · define dynamic array initialisation, length, and the out of bounds exception · 3 MARKS

Model answer.

  1. Dynamic array initialisation. Creating the array with new and a size decided while the program runs, rather than from a literal list written in the source: int[] a = new int[n]; where n is only known at run time. Every element starts at its default (0 for int, null for objects), and the values are filled in afterwards. Contrast static initialisation, int[] a = {2, 4, 6, 8};, where the size and the values are both fixed in the source.
  2. The length property. a.length gives the number of elements. It is a field, not a method, so there are no brackets: writing a.length() is a compile error. It is final: an array's length is fixed the moment it is created and can never change. A String's length IS a method, s.length(). The examiner knows that catches people; Unit 7.2.
  3. The out-of-bounds exception. ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException, thrown at run time when you use an index below 0 or at or above length. Valid indexes are 0 to length - 1, so a[a.length] always throws. It is unchecked, so the compiler will not warn you about it.

Where the marks are: "length is a field, not a method" and "indexes are 0 to length-1" are the two facts every other part of this question depends on. F.10 and Unit 8.1.

blocks.working:
Q2 b · debug copyarray · 3 MARKS
Compiler outputerror: not a statement

The errors, listed.

  1. int b; is not an array. It is a single int, and it is never given a value. System.arraycopy needs a destination array that already exists and has room: it copies into an array, it does not create one. Fix: int[] b = new int[a.length]; This is Q2 A part 1 being examined: dynamic initialisation, sized from a.length.
  2. System.arrayCopy has a capital C. The method is System.arraycopy, all lower case. Java is case sensitive, so this is not a typo the compiler forgives: it is a method that does not exist.
  3. i <= b.length is off by one. The last index is length - 1, so this reads b[4] on an array of 4 and throws ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException. Fix: i < b.length. Q2 A part 3, being examined.
  4. i is not an increment. The third slot of the for needs i++. As written it is not even a statement, which is the error javac reports first. Without it the loop would never end.

Notice what this question is. Its three errors are its own part A, in order: dynamic initialisation, the length property, the out-of-bounds exception. Part A is not a warm-up, it is the answer key to part B.

Code · q2 b corrected · VERIFIED ON THE JVM
public class CopyArray {    public static void main(String[] args) {        int[] a = {2, 4, 6, 8};        int[] b = new int[a.length];        System.arraycopy(a, 0, b, 0, a.length);        for (int i = 0; i < b.length; i++) {            System.out.println(b[i]);        }    }}
Output2
4
6
8

System.arraycopy(a, 0, b, 0, a.length) reads: from a starting at 0, into b starting at 0, a.length elements. Source, source position, destination, destination position, count. Unit 8.3.

blocks.working:
Q2 c · dry run the subtraction loop · 4 MARKS

The question asks for the output of each iteration and the final output, which is a specific instruction: it wants the table, not just the number.

Dry run · x = x - nums[i], starting from nums[0]
nums = {2, 4, 6, 8}, and x starts at nums[0] = 2
inums[i]x = x - nums[i]x after
--x = nums[0]2
142 - 4-2
26-2 - 6-8
38-8 - 8-16
Final output-16

Two things the marker is watching for. First, the loop starts at i = 1, not 0, because x was already primed with nums[0]; start at 0 and you subtract 2 from itself and get -18. Second, the loop prints nothing: the println is outside it, so "the output of each iteration" is a trace of x, and the only thing the program actually prints is -16. Say both.

This is the "prime with the first element, then start the loop at 1" idiom you use for maximum and minimum (Unit 8.4). Here it is used for a running subtraction, which is the same shape with a different operator.

Code · the paper's own code, run · VERIFIED ON THE JVM
public class SubtractDown {    public static void main(String[] args) {        int[] nums = {2, 4, 6, 8};        int x = nums[0];        for (int i = 1; i < nums.length; i++) {            x = x - nums[i];        }        System.out.println(x);    }}
Output-16

Asked forThree deliverables: input of 10 values, two methods, and a maximum found in main.
The marks7.5 marks split across the three numbered parts. Part iii says "in the main method" and "use a for loop", so a method call or a while loop there is not what was asked.

blocks.working:
Q2 d · ten values, evens, odd sum, and the maximum · 7.5 MARKS

Read the verbs: find, count, display is three things, and the even method must do all three. And the maximum must be found in main with a for loop, not in a third method: the question says where to put it.

import java.util.Scanner;public class ArrayStats {    // ii a. find, count and display the even numbers    public static void evens(int[] values) {        int count = 0;        String found = "";        for (int i = 0; i < values.length; i++) {            if (values[i] % 2 == 0) {                count++;                found = found.equals("") ? "" + values[i] : found + ", " + values[i];            }        }        System.out.println("Even numbers: " + found);        System.out.println("How many even: " + count);    }    // ii b. sum and display the odd numbers    public static void odds(int[] values) {        int sum = 0;        for (int i = 0; i < values.length; i++) {            if (values[i] % 2 != 0) {                sum += values[i];            }        }        System.out.println("Sum of the odd numbers: " + sum);    }    public static void main(String[] args) {        Scanner in = new Scanner(System.in);        // i. prompt for 10 values        int[] values = new int[10];        for (int i = 0; i < values.length; i++) {            values[i] = Integer.parseInt(in.nextLine());        }        evens(values);        odds(values);        // iii. a for loop in main to find and display the maximum        int max = values[0];        for (int i = 1; i < values.length; i++) {            if (values[i] > max) {                max = values[i];            }        }        System.out.println("Maximum: " + max);    }}

How many even: 5
Sum of the odd numbers: 39
Maximum: 15

Input is a Scanner here so the run can be printed. The ten values fed in were 4, 7, -3, 12, 9, 0, 15, -8, 6, 11.

Must memorise · Test for odd with != 0, never == 1

if (v % 2 != 0)   is odd. Always.

if (v % 2 == 1)   is odd only for positives, and silently wrong for negatives.

In Java, % keeps the sign of the left operand, so -3 % 2 is -1, not 1. So -3 % 2 == 1 is false and the == 1 test declares -3 even.

The test data above proves it. The odd numbers are 7, -3, 9, 15 and 11, and they sum to 39. Had the method used == 1, it would have skipped -3 and printed 42: a wrong answer, from a program that runs cleanly and looks right. That is why the ten values include a negative odd number, and why yours should too. Unit 3.6 and Unit 8.4.

MEMORY HOOK: "not even" is safe; "equals one" is not.

Teach · Priming the maximum: why not start at 0

The maximum loop starts int max = values[0]; and then runs from i = 1. The tempting alternative is int max = 0;, and it is a bug waiting for the right data.

If every value is negative, max = 0 never gets replaced and the program reports a maximum of 0, a number that is not in the array. Priming with values[0] cannot do that: the answer starts as a real element and only ever moves to another real element.

The same reasoning as Unit 8.4's minimum, and the same reasoning that makes Integer.MIN_VALUE the other correct prime. Starting at 0 is correct only if you know the data contains a non-negative number, and "I know my data" is how bugs are born.

Q3 a · define printwriter, files.write(), and try with resources · 3 MARKS

Model answer.

  1. PrintWriter. A character-output class that writes formatted text to a file or stream, giving you the same familiar methods as System.out: print, println and printf. It is a wrapper: you hand it a destination (a file name, or another Writer) and it adds the formatting.
  2. Files.write(). A static method on java.nio.file.Files that writes an entire byte array or collection of lines to a file in a single call, creating the file if needed and closing it for you. It is the one-line alternative to opening a writer, looping, and closing.
  3. try-with-resources. A try with the resource declared in brackets, try (PrintWriter out = ...) { ... }, which automatically closes that resource when the block ends, whether it ends normally or by an exception. It removes the need for a finally block whose only job is closing. Unit 10.2.

Where the marks are: for each, say what it is and what it saves you. "PrintWriter writes formatted text" earns the mark; "PrintWriter is for files" does not distinguish it from FileWriter.

The errors, listed.

Q3 c · what is the output of the data.txt file? · 4 MARKS

Note the question: not what the program prints on screen (it prints nothing), but what ends up in the file.

The answer:

data.txtAge: 25
Score: 89.46

Two lines. And three details carry the four marks.

Must memorise · print, println, printf: the three differences

print("Age: ")   writes the text, no line break. So the 25 lands on the same line.

println(25)   writes it and a line break. That break is what ends line 1.

printf("Score: %.2f", 89.456)   formats, and adds no line break unless you write %n.

1. %.2f rounds, it does not truncate. 89.456 to two places is 89.46, not 89.45. Unit 3.11.

2. The file has no trailing newline. printf did not add one, so the file ends immediately after the 6 of 89.46. The file is 21 bytes and its last character is not a line break.

3. Nothing appears on screen. Every call is on pw, not on System.out. A common wrong answer is to write the two lines as program output.

MEMORY HOOK: only println breaks the line. print and printf leave the cursor exactly where it stopped.

Code · the paper's code, plus a dump of the file it wrote · VERIFIED ON THE JVM
import java.io.*;public class PrintWriterExample {    public static void main(String[] args) throws IOException {        PrintWriter pw = new PrintWriter("data.txt");        pw.print("Age: ");        pw.println(25);        pw.printf("Score: %.2f", 89.456);        pw.close();        // show exactly what landed in the file, bytes and all        BufferedReader in = new BufferedReader(new FileReader("data.txt"));        StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder();        int c;        while ((c = in.read()) != -1) sb.append((char) c);        in.close();        System.out.println("--- data.txt verbatim ---");        System.out.print(sb);        System.out.println("\n--- as escaped bytes ---");        System.out.println(sb.toString().replace("\r", "\r").replace("\n", "\n"));        System.out.println("length = " + sb.length());    }}
Output--- data.txt verbatim ---
Age: 25
Score: 89.46
--- as escaped bytes ---
Age: 25
Score: 89.46
length = 21

The paper's four lines are exactly as printed; everything after pw.close() is ours, reading the file back so that this book can show you what landed in it. Length 21 is the proof of the trailing-newline point: "Age: 25" is 7 characters, "Score: 89.46" is 12, which is 19, and the two remaining bytes are the single line break in the middle. There is nothing on the end.

Those two bytes are worth a word. println uses the platform's line separator, which on Windows is carriage-return plus line-feed (two characters) and on Linux is line-feed alone (one). Same program, 21 bytes here and 20 there. The two printed lines are the answer either way; if you are asked for a byte count, say which platform.

Q3 d · write students.txt as a formatted, appended table · 7.5 MARKS
Must memorise · PrintWriter cannot append. The FileWriter under it can

new PrintWriter("students.txt")   truncates the file to empty. Every time. There is no append constructor.

new PrintWriter(new FileWriter("students.txt", true))   appends.

The true is the append flag, and it belongs to FileWriter, not to PrintWriter. So the answer to "append with PrintWriter" is to wrap one around a FileWriter opened in append mode, exactly as Unit 10.3 wraps a BufferedReader around a FileReader to get readLine(). Each wrapper adds what the other lacks.

And it satisfies part i for free. FileWriter creates the file if it does not exist, in either mode. So "create students.txt if it does not exist" needs no if, no File.exists(), no check at all: opening it in append mode does both jobs.

MEMORY HOOK: the flag is on the writer that touches the disk. PrintWriter only formats; FileWriter opens the file, so the mode is its business.

import java.io.BufferedReader;import java.io.FileReader;import java.io.FileWriter;import java.io.IOException;import java.io.PrintWriter;public class StudentTable {    public static void main(String[] args) {        String[] names = {"John", "Lilian", "Ken"};        int[] ages = {20, 21, 19};        double[] gpas = {3.75, 3.95, 3.65};        // iv. APPEND, not overwrite. new PrintWriter("students.txt") would truncate        // the file each run; the append flag is on the FileWriter beneath.        // i. FileWriter also creates students.txt if it does not already exist.        try (PrintWriter out = new PrintWriter(new FileWriter("students.txt",            true))) {            // iii. printf for column alignment: %-8s is left-aligned in 8 columns.            out.printf("%-8s %-5s %-6s%n", "Name", "Age", "GPA");            for (int i = 0; i < names.length; i++) {                out.printf("%-8s %-5d %-6.2f%n", names[i], ages[i], gpas[i]);            }        } catch (IOException e) {            // v. handle possible exceptions properly            System.out.println("Could not write students.txt: " + e.getMessage());        }        // Not part of the answer: read the file back so this book can show you what        // landed in it. A dot marks each trailing space from printf's padding.        try (BufferedReader in = new BufferedReader(new FileReader("students.txt"))) {            String line = in.readLine();            while (line != null) {                System.out.println(line.replace(' ', '.'));                line = in.readLine();            }        } catch (IOException e) {            System.out.println("Could not read students.txt back: " + e.getMessage());        }    }}

John.....20....3.75..
Lilian...21....3.95..
Ken......19....3.65..

The dots are the marks. %-8s means: a String, left aligned, padded to 8 columns, and you can count the padding: "Name" plus four dots, "Lilian" plus two. The minus sign is what makes it left aligned; drop it and every column is pushed right and the table goes ragged. %-6.2f is the same idea for a double, fixed at 2 decimal places, which is why 3.75 prints as 3.75 and not 3.8. Unit 3.11.

Those trailing dots are real spaces, sitting at the end of every line. printf pads the last column just as faithfully as the others, because it cannot know it is last. Harmless in a text file, and worth knowing before you go looking for why two files that "look identical" are not.

Code · proof that the append flag is doing the work · RUN TWICE, IN ONE PROGRAM

The claim above is that the true is what makes it append and that without it the file is wiped. Here that claim is tested: the same write is done twice each way, and the lines are counted.

import java.io.BufferedReader;import java.io.FileReader;import java.io.FileWriter;import java.io.IOException;import java.io.PrintWriter;public class AppendProof {    static void writeOnce(String file, boolean append) throws IOException {        try (PrintWriter out = append                ? new PrintWriter(new FileWriter(file, true))   // appends                : new PrintWriter(file)) {                      // TRUNCATES            out.printf("%-8s %-5d %-6.2f%n", "John", 20, 3.75);        }    }    static int lines(String file) throws IOException {        int n = 0;        try (BufferedReader in = new BufferedReader(new FileReader(file))) {            while (in.readLine() != null) n++;        }        return n;    }    public static void main(String[] args) throws IOException {        writeOnce("appended.txt", true);        writeOnce("appended.txt", true);        System.out.println("new PrintWriter(new FileWriter(f, true)) twice -> "            + lines("appended.txt") + " lines");        writeOnce("truncated.txt", false);        writeOnce("truncated.txt", false);        System.out.println("new PrintWriter(f)                     twice -> "            + lines("truncated.txt") + " lines");    }}
Outputnew PrintWriter(new FileWriter(f, true)) twice -> 2 lines
new PrintWriter(f)                     twice -> 1 lines

Two lines against one. The appending version kept both records; the plain PrintWriter threw the first away and left only the second. If you write new PrintWriter("students.txt") in the exam, your program passes every other part of this question and still fails part iv, and nothing in its output tells you.

Q4 a · describe decision making, looping and branching · 3 MARKS

Model answer. These are the three families of control structure (Unit 4.1): the statements that decide which code runs and how often, rather than doing the work themselves.

  1. Decision-making. Choosing between paths by testing a condition, so that some code runs and some does not: if, if-else, the if-else ladder, and switch.
  2. Looping (iteration). Repeating a block while a condition holds: for, while and do-while. The do-while is the one that always runs at least once, because it tests at the bottom.
  3. Branching (jumping). Transferring control out of the normal flow: break leaves a loop or a switch case, continue skips to the next iteration, and return leaves the method entirely.

Where the marks are: name the actual keywords. "Looping means repeating" is the idea; "for, while, do-while, and do-while tests at the bottom so it runs at least once" is the answer. Units 4.1 to 4.7.

Q4 b · debug the while loop · 3 MARKS

The paper prints that as a bare fragment. To put it through a real compiler it needs a class and a main around it, so that is what is added below, and nothing else is touched. Every fault you are about to list is the paper's own:

public class WhileDebugBroken {    public static void main(String[] args) {        int count = 1        float output = "";        while(count <=5); {            output = output + count + " ";            Count        }        System.out.println(output);    }}
Compiler outputerror: ';' expected

The errors, listed.

  1. int count = 1 has no semicolon.
  2. float output = ""; is the wrong type. A float is a number; "" is text. They are not interchangeable and Java will not convert one to the other. Fix: String output = "";
  3. while(count <=5); has a stray semicolon. This is the one worth the mark. That semicolon is the loop body: an empty statement. The block below it then runs once, on its own, as an ordinary block. Since count never changes inside the empty body, the condition stays true forever and the program hangs.
  4. Count is not a statement. Wrong case (Java is case sensitive) and, even spelled right, count alone does nothing. Fix: count++; which is what stops the loop.
Trap · The semicolon that eats the loop body

while (condition); and for (...); are both legal Java. The semicolon is an empty statement, and an empty statement is a perfectly good loop body. So the compiler says nothing at all.

What you wrote:

while (count <= 5); { ... }

What Java read:

while (count <= 5) { }   then, separately,   { ... }

The braces you meant as the body became a free-floating block that runs once, after the loop finishes. Except the loop never finishes, because nothing inside an empty body can change count.

This exact trap appears twice on this paper: here, and again in Q6 C as for (int i = 0; i <= n; i++);. The examiner is not being subtle about how much they want you to notice it. Whenever a loop misbehaves, look at the character immediately after the closing bracket. Unit 4.5.

The else if only runs when t < 15 was false, which already means t >= 15. So writing else if (t >= 15 && t <= 30) is not wrong, it is redundant: the ladder has already established the lower bound. Let the structure carry what it has proved (Unit 4.2).

Q5 a · describe inheritance, polymorphism and method overriding · 3 MARKS

Model answer.

  1. Inheritance. One class acquiring the fields and methods of another with extends, so the subclass has everything the superclass has without repeating it, and may add or replace behaviour. It models an is-a relationship: a Bicycle is a Vehicle.
  2. Polymorphism. One reference, many behaviours: a variable of the superclass type may hold an object of any subclass, and a call through it runs the object's own version, decided at run time. "Many forms".
  3. Method overriding. A subclass supplying its own version of a method the superclass already has, with the same signature, which replaces the inherited one for objects of that subclass.

Where the marks are: these three are one idea in three parts, and saying so earns the mark. Inheritance makes the family; overriding makes the members differ; polymorphism is what you get when you then hold any of them in one variable and call the method. Distinguish overriding (same signature, subclass, run time) from overloading (different parameters, same class, compile time), which is Q1 of this same paper. Units 6.6 and 6.7.

public class CountNegatives {    // Q5 B: the method the question asks for, and nothing else.    public static int countNegatives(int[] numbers) {        int count = 0;        for (int i = 0; i < numbers.length; i++) {            if (numbers[i] < 0) {                count++;            }        }        return count;    }    // main is not part of the answer; it is here so the method can be run.    public static void main(String[] args) {        int[] a = {3, -1, 0, -7, 8, -2};        int[] b = {1, 2, 3};        int[] c = {};        System.out.println("{3, -1, 0, -7, 8, -2} -> " + countNegatives(a));        System.out.println("{1, 2, 3}             -> " + countNegatives(b));        System.out.println("{} (empty)            -> " + countNegatives(c));    }}
Output{3, -1, 0, -7, 8, -2} -> 3
{1, 2, 3}             -> 0
{} (empty)            -> 0

Only countNegatives is the answer; main is here so the method can be run. Zero is not negative, which is why the first array has a 0 in it and the count is 3, not 4: the test is < 0, never <= 0. And the empty array returns 0 without any special case, since the loop simply never runs.

Code · q5 d, complete · VERIFIED ON THE JVM
// i. the superclassclass Vehicle {    protected int speed;    public Vehicle(int speed) {        this.speed = speed;    }    public void displayInfo() {        System.out.println("Vehicle speed: " + speed + " km/h");    }}// ii. the subclass, overriding displayInfo()class Bicycle extends Vehicle {    public Bicycle(int speed) {        super(speed);    }    @Override    public void displayInfo() {        System.out.println("Bicycle speed: " + speed            + " km/h. This is an eco-friendly ride.");    }}public class VehicleDemo {    public static void main(String[] args) {        // iii a/b. one of each        Vehicle car = new Vehicle(80);        Bicycle bike = new Bicycle(25);        // iii c. call displayInfo() on both        car.displayInfo();        bike.displayInfo();        // and the polymorphic form the question is really after        Vehicle[] fleet = {new Vehicle(80), new Bicycle(25)};        System.out.println("-- through a Vehicle reference --");        for (Vehicle v : fleet) {            v.displayInfo();        }    }}
OutputVehicle speed: 80 km/h
Bicycle speed: 25 km/h. This is an eco-friendly ride.
-- through a Vehicle reference --
Vehicle speed: 80 km/h
Bicycle speed: 25 km/h. This is an eco-friendly ride.
Teach · The last four words of the question change the answer

The question says: call displayInfo() on both objects to demonstrate polymorphism. Read literally, parts a to c are satisfied by:

Vehicle car = new Vehicle(80);Bicycle bike = new Bicycle(25);car.displayInfo();bike.displayInfo();

That prints the two required lines, and it demonstrates nothing. Each variable's declared type already matches its object exactly, so the compiler could have picked both methods without any run-time decision. Overriding happened, but polymorphism was never tested.

Polymorphism needs the reference to be the SUPERCLASS type, so that the declared type and the actual object disagree and only the run time can settle it:

Vehicle[] fleet = {new Vehicle(80), new Bicycle(25)};
for (Vehicle v : fleet) v.displayInfo();

Now every element is declared Vehicle, the loop body is one identical call, and it still prints two different lines. That is the demonstration, and it is what the last four words are asking for. The listing above does both: the literal answer first, then the proof.

Same idea as Q4 part 3 v on the 2025/26 paper, where the reference is explicitly required to be a BankAccount. Two papers, two years, one point: the reference decides what you may call, the object decides what runs.

Q6 a · snippets for the three loop types · 3 MARKS

Part iii is the one being marked. A do-while whose condition is false still runs once, and "print 10 once" is the cleanest possible demonstration of that. Choose a condition that is false immediately, and the body still prints.

Code · q6 a · VERIFIED ON THE JVM
public class ThreeLoopTypes {    public static void main(String[] args) {        // i. a for loop printing 1 to 5        for (int i = 1; i <= 5; i++) {            System.out.print(i + " ");        }        System.out.println();        // ii. a while loop printing 5 down to 1        int j = 5;        while (j >= 1) {            System.out.print(j + " ");            j--;        }        System.out.println();        // iii. a do-while printing only 10, once        int k = 10;        do {            System.out.print(k + " ");            k++;        } while (k <= 10);        System.out.println();    }}
Output1 2 3 4 5
5 4 3 2 1
10

In the do-while, k is 10, the body prints it, k becomes 11, and while (k <= 10) is false, so it stops. The body ran once before the condition was ever looked at, which is the whole difference between do-while and while. Write it as a while with the same condition and nothing prints at all. Unit 4.5.

Q6 b · what does compute(13) return? show the steps · 3 MARKS

The answer: 3. And the question says show the steps, so the table is the answer, not the number.

Dry run · compute(13), step by step
while (x > 0): count the odd steps, halve each time
xx % 2odd, so count++?x = x / 2count
131yes61
60no31
31yes12
11yes03
0x > 0 is false, so the loop ends3

What the method actually is. Repeatedly halving with x / 2 and testing x % 2 walks the number's binary digits, from the right. So compute counts the 1 bits. 13 in binary is 1101, which has three 1s, so the answer is 3, and you can check it in one second without tracing anything.

Say that in your answer after showing the table. Naming what the code is ("it counts the set bits") is what separates a trace from understanding, and it costs one line.

Code · the paper's own method, run on 13 and on friends · VERIFIED ON THE JVM
public class ComputeBits {    // exactly as the paper prints it    public static int compute(int x) {        int count = 0;        while (x > 0) {            if (x % 2 == 1) count++;            x = x / 2;        }        return count;    }    public static void main(String[] args) {        System.out.println("compute(13) = " + compute(13));        System.out.println("13 in binary is " + Integer.toBinaryString(13));        for (int v : new int[]{1, 2, 3, 7, 8, 255}) {            System.out.println("compute(" + v + ") = " + compute(v)                + "   binary " + Integer.toBinaryString(v));        }    }}
Outputcompute(13) = 3
13 in binary is 1101
compute(1) = 1   binary 1
compute(2) = 1   binary 10
compute(3) = 2   binary 11
compute(7) = 3   binary 111
compute(8) = 1   binary 1000
compute(255) = 8   binary 11111111

Every row is its own proof: the answer always equals the number of 1s printed beside it. compute(255) = 8 and 255 is eight 1s; compute(8) = 1 and 8 is 1000. The claim is not "this looks like a bit count", it is a bit count.

Q6 c · debug evenfinder · 4 MARKS
Compiler outputerror: ';' expected

The errors, listed.

  1. main(String args) is not main. It must be String[] args. Without the brackets it is an ordinary method that the JVM will not recognise as the entry point.
  2. printEven(10.0) has no semicolon.
  3. 10.0 is a double. The method takes an int, and Java will not narrow a double to an int on its own, because that loses information (Unit 3.3). Fix: printEven(10);
  4. printEven(int) has no parameter name. Fix: printEven(int n), which is also why n "does not exist" three lines later.
  5. for (...); has a stray semicolon. The loop body is empty, so the if below is not in the loop. It runs once, after the loop, and it cannot even compile: i was declared in the for, so it is out of scope the moment the for ends.

Error 5 is Q4 B's stray semicolon again, on the same paper, in a for this time. The scope error is what gives it away here: when the compiler says "cannot find symbol: i" about a variable you can plainly see, the loop that declared it has already closed.

The output after correction: 0 2 4 6 8 10

Code · q6 c corrected · VERIFIED ON THE JVM
public class EvenFinder {    public static void main(String[] args) {        printEven(10);    }    public static void printEven(int n) {        for (int i = 0; i <= n; i++) {            if (i % 2 == 0) {                System.out.print(i + " ");            }        }        System.out.println();    }}
Output0 2 4 6 8 10

0 is even, and i <= n means 10 is included, so the answer starts at 0 and ends at 10. Both ends are worth checking: this is the rare loop where <= is correct, because n is a value to reach, not a length.

[7.5 marks]D. Write a program that includes a method called hasEqualAdjacentPairs(int n) which:

blocks.working:
Q6 d · hasequaladjacentpairs · 7.5 MARKS

112233 → true (pairs: 11, 22, 33). More than two adjacent pairs.
1223 → true (pairs: 22). Only one pair → return false

Trap · The paper contradicts itself, and you must answer anyway

Read the second example again. It says "1223 - true" and then, in the same line, "Only one pair - return false". Both cannot be right.

The specification says "at least two pairs". 1223 has one pair, the 22. One is not at least two.

The correct return is false. The leading "true" is a slip of the pen.

The examiner's own explanation ("Only one pair") agrees with the specification, so the specification and the reasoning outvote the stray word. This book shows you the paper exactly as printed and tells you what is true, and it never quietly corrects a source (compare the six errors in Module 3, which come from this course's own slides).

What to do in the hall. Do not agonise, and do not answer the typo. Implement the specification, and write one line saying why: "1223 has only one adjacent pair, so by the stated rule of at least two pairs the method returns false; the 'true' in the example appears to be a typographical error." That sentence costs ten seconds and it protects you whichever way the marking scheme reads, because it proves the answer was a decision and not a mistake.

MEMORY HOOK: when a question contradicts itself, follow the specification and say that you did.

Code · q6 d, complete · VERIFIED ON THE JVM
public class AdjacentPairs {    // i/ii. true when n has AT LEAST TWO pairs of equal adjacent digits.    public static boolean hasEqualAdjacentPairs(int n) {        int pairs = 0;        int previous = n % 10;        n = n / 10;        while (n > 0) {            int current = n % 10;            if (current == previous) {                pairs++;            }            previous = current;            n = n / 10;        }        return pairs >= 2;    }    // iii b. main testing more than the two cases the question asks for    public static void main(String[] args) {        int[] tests = {112233, 1223, 1122, 111, 123, 7, 122333};        for (int t : tests) {            System.out.println(t + " -> " + hasEqualAdjacentPairs(t));        }    }}
Output112233 -> true
1223 -> false
1122 -> true
111 -> true
123 -> false
7 -> false
122333 -> true

The paper asks for at least two test cases; there are seven, and each earns its place. 112233 and 1223 are the paper's own. 1122 is the boundary: exactly two pairs, so exactly true. 111 asks what a triple counts as. 123 has no pairs and 7 has no adjacent digits at all, so the loop never runs and pairs stays 0.

Must memorise · Compare adjacent digits by remembering the last one

Take the last digit before the loop and call it previous. Then each turn: take the new current, compare it with previous, and make current the new previous.

That is the whole technique, and it is the same % 10 and / 10 pair as Q6 A on the 2025/26 paper. The only new idea is carrying one value forward so that each digit can see its neighbour. You never need the digits in an array; you need exactly one of them remembered.

111 gives two pairs, not one. The digits are compared in overlapping pairs: positions 1-2 and 2-3. The middle 1 belongs to both. If you think a triple should count once, that is a different specification, and this one does not say so: it says pairs of equal adjacent digits, and 111 contains two of them.

MEMORY HOOK: to compare neighbours, remember one. Peel a digit, compare, then let it become the memory for the next.

An automorphic number is a positive integer whose square ends in the number itself. For example, 25 is automorphic because 25 squared is 625, which ends in 25. 6 is automorphic because 6 squared is 36, which ends in 6.

Q1 a · define a constructor · 2 MARKS

Model answer.

A constructor is a special member of a class that runs once, when an object of that class is created with new, and whose job is to put the new object's fields into a valid starting state.

The compiler tells it apart from an ordinary method by two facts, and both are needed for the mark: its name is exactly the class name, and it declares no return type at all, not even void. Those are not two ways of saying the same thing. Write void MeterAccount(...) and you have not written a constructor: you have written an ordinary method that happens to be called MeterAccount, it compiles, it is never called by new, and your fields stay at their defaults.

Where the marks are: one for what it is for, one for how it is recognised. "It has the same name as the class" alone is half the rule and often half the mark.

Q1 b · three differences: while against do while · 3 MARKS

A three-row table beats a paragraph under time pressure, and it is easier to mark, which is the same thing.

 whiledo-while
When it tests Before the body: it is a pre-test loop. After the body: it is a post-test loop.
Fewest runs Zero. If the condition is false at the start, the body never runs. One. The body always runs at least once, whatever the condition.
Syntax No semicolon after the closing brace. Ends with while (condition); and that semicolon is required.

Where the marks are: one per row. The middle row is the one that decides which to use: "must this run at least once?" is the only question that matters, and it is why input validation is usually a do-while.

Q1 c · find the errors · 5 MARKS

Five errors, one per mark, and they are the same five kinds that both real papers plant. Run the TTOIS checklist from S.1 and they fall out in about a minute.

  1. T for Type. Line 4: int[] arr cannot hold 15.0. The required output is 93.0, with a point, which is the question telling you the array is double[]. Fix: double[] arr.
  2. T for Total. Line 5: int sum cannot accumulate decimals. Fix: double sum.
  3. O for Off-by-one. Line 8: i <= arr.length would reach arr[6] in an array of 6. Fix: i < arr.length.
  4. I for Inverted. Line 10: if (arr[j] % 3 == 0) continue; skips exactly the multiples of 3 it was told to find. Fix: % 3 != 0.
  5. S for Stop. Line 14: if (matches == 4) stops after four, and the specification says three. Fix: matches == 3.

What the compiler actually said: errors 1 and 2 only, as six repeats of "incompatible types: possible lossy conversion from double to int". Errors 3, 4 and 5 are not compile errors at all. Fix the types and this program compiles, runs, and prints a confident wrong answer. That is 3 of the 5 marks sitting in code the compiler is perfectly happy with.

Code · q1 c corrected, all five fixes marked · VERIFIED ON THE JVM
// JOptionPane replaced by println so the output can be printed here;// in the exam, keep the dialogs exactly as the paper has them.public class MB1C {    public static void main(String[] args) {        double[] arr = {15.0, 22.0, 36.0, 41.0, 54.0, 60.0};   // fix 1        double sum = 0;                                        // fix 2        int matches = 0;        boolean stop = false;        for (int i = 0; i < arr.length && !stop; i++) {        // fix 3            for (int j = i; j < arr.length; j++) {                if (arr[j] % 3 != 0) {                         // fix 4                    continue;                }                sum += arr[j] + 2;                matches++;                if (matches == 3) {                            // fix 5                    stop = true;                }                break;            }        }        System.out.println("Sum: " + sum);        System.out.println("Matches: " + matches);    }}
OutputSum: 93.0
Matches: 3

Check it by hand, because the examiner gave you the answer and expects you to work back to it. The multiples of 3 are 15, 36, 54 and 60. Starting at i=0 the first one found is 15, giving 17. At i=1 it is 36, giving 38. At i=2 it is 36 again, giving 38, and that is the third match, so it stops. 17 + 38 + 38 = 93.0, and 3 matches.

Q1 d i · the five outputs · 10 MARKS, part one

Square it, then keep as many digits off the right-hand end as the number itself has, and compare.

ndigits n * npower = 10^digits tail = square % poweroutput
51251025 % 10 = 5AUTOMORPHIC
61361036 % 10 = 6AUTOMORPHIC
71491049 % 10 = 9NOT AUTOMORPHIC
252625100625 % 100 = 25AUTOMORPHIC
76257761005776 % 100 = 76AUTOMORPHIC

% power is the whole trick: % 10 keeps the last digit, % 100 keeps the last two. "Ends in" is a remainder, and that is the idea the question is testing.

Code · q1 d, the original, run for real · VERIFIED ON THE JVM
public class AutomorphicChecker {    public static void main(String[] args) {        int[] numbers = {5, 6, 7, 25, 76};        for (int idx = 0; idx < numbers.length; idx++) {            int n = numbers[idx], digits = 0, temp = n;            while (temp > 0) { digits++; temp /= 10; }            int power = 1;            for (int p = 0; p < digits; p++) power *= 10;            int tail = (n * n) % power;            System.out.println(n + " -> "                + (tail == n ? "AUTOMORPHIC" : "NOT AUTOMORPHIC"));        }    }}
Output5 -> AUTOMORPHIC
6 -> AUTOMORPHIC
7 -> NOT AUTOMORPHIC
25 -> AUTOMORPHIC
76 -> AUTOMORPHIC
Must memorise · Loop conversion is mechanical. Move the three parts, change nothing else

A for is a while with its three parts collected onto one line:

for (INIT; TEST; UPDATE) { BODY }

is exactly

INIT; while (TEST) { BODY UPDATE }

So the conversion has three moves and no thinking: INIT goes above the loop, TEST stays in the brackets, UPDATE goes to the bottom of the body. Going the other way, collect all three back onto the header line. A for with an empty init and update, for (; temp > 0; ), is a legal and honest way to write a While as a For.

MEMORY HOOK: INIT up, UPDATE down. Ten marks on the real paper and there is no idea in it at all, only care.

Code · q1 d ii, converted: the for became a while, the whiles became fors · VERIFIED ON THE JVM
public class AutomorphicConverted {    public static void main(String[] args) {        int[] numbers = {5, 6, 7, 25, 76};        // the outer For became a While        int idx = 0;        while (idx < numbers.length) {            int n = numbers[idx], digits = 0, temp = n;            // this While became a For: same init, same test, same update            for (; temp > 0; ) { digits++; temp /= 10; }            // this For became a While: the update moves down into the body            int power = 1;            int p = 0;            while (p < digits) { power *= 10; p++; }            int tail = (n * n) % power;            System.out.println(n + " -> "                + (tail == n ? "AUTOMORPHIC" : "NOT AUTOMORPHIC"));            idx++;        }    }}
Output, identical to the original5 -> AUTOMORPHIC
6 -> AUTOMORPHIC
7 -> NOT AUTOMORPHIC
25 -> AUTOMORPHIC
76 -> AUTOMORPHIC

The output is byte for byte the output of the original, and that is the entire test. A conversion that changes the answer is not a conversion. Both versions were run and their outputs compared, which is exactly what you should do on paper: trace one line of each and check they agree.

Trap · The update must survive the move, especially past a continue

The commonest way to lose these ten marks is to move INIT up and then forget UPDATE, leaving while (idx < numbers.length) with no idx++ anywhere. It compiles. It hangs forever. The marker sees an infinite loop where a conversion was asked for.

And there is a sharper version, worth knowing because "INIT up, UPDATE down" is not always safe: it breaks the moment the body contains a continue. A for runs its update on every way round, including the ones continue cuts short. A while has no update slot, so the one you moved to the bottom of the body gets jumped over, and the loop stops advancing.

Both halves were compiled and run. This for, summing the odd numbers below 6 by skipping the even ones with continue, prints total = 9. Converted to a while by the rule above, with i++ at the bottom of the body, it hangs forever: at i = 0 the continue fires, i++ is never reached, and i is 0 for eternity.

Neither loop in this question contains a continue, so the rule is safe here. Check that before you apply it. If the body does have one, the update must be repeated before the continue as well, or the loop must stay a for.
